Start S1Read this first

Start here

This guide teaches you the six papers and the twelve tools behind our Cybermed project. You read it in two days. When you finish, you can explain every step of our pipeline to the engineers who will ask about it.

The short version
  • Cybermed has a 3D CT scan of a patient's face and a normal photo of the same face. We paint the photo onto the scan.
  • To paint it you must know where the camera stood when the photo was taken. Finding that camera is the hard part.
  • Follow the two day plan below. The 23 pages take about 13 hours.
  • Colours mean the same thing in every figure. Teal is 3D, orange is 2D and magenta is a match.

What this guide is

CT is an X-ray scan that builds a 3D picture of the head. Cybermed cuts the skin surface out of it as a mesh, a net of small triangles measured in millimetres. Our job was to paint a studio photo of the same person onto that surface. Most of this guide is about finding the photo's camera, because that is the hard part.

The Start pages explain the task and our results. The Building blocks teach one tool each, with math and worked numbers. The Papers say what each paper does and what we took from it. Two Wrap up pages compare the papers and define every term.

How to read

Read in the order of the plan below. Each paper page assumes you have read the building blocks it uses. If a word is new, its first use links to the page that explains it, and the glossary has a one line version.

The two day reading plan

The plan splits the site into six sittings of about two hours. The minutes match the reading time at the top of each page.

Use the Mark as read button at the bottom of each page. A tick then shows up next to it in the sidebar.

How the colours work

  • Teal is the CT surface or anything in 3D.
  • Orange is the photo or anything in 2D pixels.
  • Magenta is a landmark or a match between the two.
  • Ink blue is a camera, a ray or a highlight.
  • Green and red are inliers and outliers, the matches we keep and the ones we throw away.

A method here means one complete way of finding the camera. We built 15 of them. They come in families, and the chips use their own colours. A1 to A7 are landmark methods, which match a few named face points. B1 to B4 are dense image methods, which compare whole images instead of a few points. C1 to C4 rebuild the face from the photos and then line it up with the CT.

How to use the animations

Most figures are steppers that play by themselves when they scroll into view. The caption box under the drawing explains the current step.

  1. Pause and step

    Press Pause, then use Back and Next to move one step at a time. The numbered dots jump to any step.

  2. Drag the sliders

    Figures with a slider row recompute as you drag, so you can try a longer lens or more outliers yourself.

  3. Reduced motion

    If your system asks for reduced motion, nothing autoplays. Press Play or step by hand.

The drawings use a generic average face. It is the MediaPipe canonical face model, a 468 point mesh that ships with Google's face landmark detector. No patient image appears anywhere in this guide.

The six papers

Park et al. 2023

Render a 3D face, find landmarks with a 2D detector, lift them to 3D. Fed A1 and the whole A family.

Paulsen et al. 2018

Detect landmarks in many rendered views and keep the 3D point most views agree on. Fed A2.

Amberg et al. 2007

Bend a template mesh onto a scan, stiff first and softer later. Fed A3.

Corsini et al. 2009

Find the camera by comparing renders with the photo through mutual information. Fed B2.

FoundPose 2024

Match DINOv2 patch features between photo and render, then solve the pose. Fed B3 and the refinement in A7.

DUSt3R 2024

A network that turns uncalibrated photos into 3D point maps. Fed C1.

Start S2Used in all 15 methods

The task and our pipeline

Cybermed gave us a CT skin surface and three photos of the same person. They wanted the photo painted onto the surface. This page explains what came in, what had to go out, why the camera is the hard part, and how our recommended pipeline A7 gets there.

The short version
  • Input is a colourless CT skin mesh (eyes closed) and three photos (eyes open) with no lens information.
  • Output is the same mesh with the photo painted on, still in the CT's own coordinates.
  • Painting is easy once you know the camera. Finding the camera is the hard part.
  • The focal length (lens zoom) is the hardest unknown, because a long lens far away looks almost like a short lens close up.
  • Our recommended pipeline A7 finds the camera in nine stages, from rendering the CT to exporting the textured mesh.

The task in plain words

Cybermed is a Korean company that makes dental 3D imaging software. A dental CT scan gives them the bone, the teeth and the skin of a patient's head. The skin comes out as a mesh, a surface made of many small triangles. It is accurate to the millimetre, but it looks like a grey mask.

They also take a studio photo, and doctors want to see the real face on the 3D model. So we paint the photo onto the CT surface and hand back a textured mesh in the CT's own coordinates. It then drops onto the bone model with no extra transform.

Painting is routine once you know where the camera stood, which way it pointed and how zoomed in its lens was. That is the camera pose and focal length. Almost all of our work went into finding it.

What we were given

Every method has to cope with these quirks of the data.

ItemFacts
CT skin meshBinary STL, a common file format for triangle meshes. 302,628 vertices (the corner points of the triangles) and 606,496 triangles. Units are millimetres. The head spans 172 by 221 by 160 mm. The origin sits at a corner of the scan volume, not at the head.
Mesh qualityNot watertight, so the surface has holes and is not one closed skin. 817 separate pieces, and the largest holds 88 percent of the triangles. The rest is debris plus inner shells of the nose, sinuses and airway.
ExpressionEyes closed and mouth closed, because the patient was being scanned.
Chin restA flat plate under the chin, fused into the skin surface. It must not receive skin colour.
ClippingThe scan volume cut the nose tip flat, a patch about 6 mm wide and 11 mm tall. The top of the skull is cut flat too. There is no hair.
Front photo1500 by 1234 px. Eyes open, mouth closed, slight smile. Soft, even studio light.
Two side photos1500 by 1326 px and 1500 by 1332 px. The head is turned about 20 to 25 degrees each way.
EXIFNone. The photos were resized and stripped, so the focal length is unknown.
Wanted outputface.obj, face.mtl and face_texture.png, in the original CT coordinates.

EXIF is the small block of camera data a phone or camera writes into a JPEG. It usually holds the focal length. Without it, the lens zoom becomes one more unknown, and as you will see it is the hardest one.

What Cybermed had already tried

Cybermed had tried the obvious route. Render the CT surface as a grey picture and run MediaPipe, Google's face detector, on it. It finds landmarks, named points such as the nose tip and eye corners. Use those as the 3D side of the match. They found the landmarks on the mesh side too imprecise.

We measured why. We rendered the CT (drew it as a picture from a virtual camera) from 45 angles and lights and detected landmarks on each render. With the camera fixed and only the light moved, the central landmarks shifted 1 to 2 mm typically and 5 to 10 mm in bad cases. The jaw and face outline points slid 10 to 30 mm. Those outline points are not fixed spots on the skin. The detector puts them on the edge of the visible face, and that edge moves when the view moves.

Why finding the camera is the hard part

A camera has seven unknowns here. Three say which way it points (a rotation). Three say where it stands (a translation). One is the focal length. The CT mesh has no colour, so you cannot match photo pixels to mesh points by how they look. Every method on this site is a different way to get those matches.

The focal length is the stubborn one. A long lens far away and a short lens close up make almost the same picture of a face. Only small perspective differences tell them apart, such as how much bigger the nose tip looks than the ears.

On our case the camera fit stays nearly as good over a factor of 3.7 to 6.8 in focal length, depending on the method. We call that range the plateau. The few points that do pin the focal length are the jaw points, the least reliable ones. In method A5, removing either jaw landmark 172 or 136 made the focal length fall to about 2350 px.

So we looked for focal length evidence from outside the landmarks. Two learned estimators, GeoCalib and Depth Pro, read a focal length from a single photo. GeoCalib gave 4665, 4192 and 3800 px for the three photos. Depth Pro gave 3319, 4474 and 4391 px. Together with methods C3 and C4, four independent estimates cluster at 3300 to 4700 px. Our joint solve A6 lands at 4050 px, inside that cluster.

Watch out

A camera can fit the front photo well and still be wrong. A wrong focal length is absorbed by a wrong distance. That is why our results page tests every camera on a second photo.

The coordinate frames

A coordinate frame is a choice of origin, axes and units for writing down positions. Three frames appear in every method. Mixing them up is the most common bug, so learn them once.

  • The CT frame. Millimetres, as the scanner wrote them. The x axis runs toward the patient's left, y runs toward the back of the head, and z runs up. This is the DICOM LPS convention (left, posterior, superior), the standard for medical scans. The face points toward minus y.
  • The camera frame. The camera sits at the origin. x points right in the image, y points down, and z points forward out of the lens. This is the OpenCV convention.
  • The image frame. Pixels. u runs right and v runs down, starting at the top left corner. The principal point is where the lens axis hits the image. We assume it is the image centre.

From a CT point to a pixel

A CT point \(X\) first moves into the camera frame by a rotation and a shift.

\[ X_c = R\,X + t \]

In words, turn the point with \(R\) and slide it by \(t\) so that it is measured from the camera.

Then the pinhole camera divides by depth and scales by the focal length.

\[ u = f\,\frac{X_c}{Z_c} + c_x, \qquad v = f\,\frac{Y_c}{Z_c} + c_y \]

In words, a point twice as far away lands twice as close to the image centre, and a longer lens spreads everything out by \(f\).

X
a point in the CT frame, in mm
R, t
the camera rotation (3 by 3) and translation (3 numbers), together the pose
X_c, Y_c, Z_c
the same point in the camera frame, in mm; Z_c is its depth
f
the focal length in pixels
c_x, c_y
the principal point, the image centre

A small worked example. Take \(f = 4050\) px, the front photo's centre \(c_x = 749.5\), and a point in the camera frame at \(X_c = 30\) mm, \(Z_c = 1000\) mm. Then \(u = 4050 \times 30 / 1000 + 749.5 = 871\) px. Move the point to 2000 mm and double the focal length, and you get the same pixel. That is the trade in Figure 3.

The output OBJ must stay in the CT frame. We never move the mesh. We only find \(R\), \(t\) and \(f\), and look up colours through them.

Our pipeline A7, end to end

A7 is the method we recommend, so know it by heart. It chains nine stages. The figure shows what goes in and comes out at each one, and the list links each stage to the page that teaches it.

  1. Render the CT

    Draw the grey CT surface from a virtual camera we choose, and keep the depth of every pixel. Our first test render was 1200 by 1200 px with a 20 degree field of view, from 560 mm in front of the face. See rendering and back projection.

  2. Detect landmarks on the render and the photo

    MediaPipe finds 478 points on the photo and on the render. The same index means the same spot on the face. We keep 22 rigid ones and leave out the eyelids, lips and outline. See face landmarks.

  3. Back project

    Each render landmark is a pixel with a known depth. Follow its ray to that depth and you land on a real 3D point of the CT. That gives 3D to 2D pairs with no hand clicking. This trick comes from Park et al..

  4. Fuse

    Three landmark sources vote on each point. A1 gives the single render, A2 gives the consensus of 40 renders (Paulsen et al.), and A4 snaps to the geometry of the surface. Their disagreement becomes a per landmark uncertainty, which weights the solve. This is method A5.

  5. Joint solve

    One Huber least squares fit sets three poses and one shared focal length for all three photos at once. That is 19 numbers. Least squares makes the sum of squared errors as small as possible, and the Huber version limits the pull of bad points. It starts from each photo's own A5 camera. That camera came from EPnP, a fast camera solver for point pairs, run inside RANSAC, which throws out bad pairs. A weak prior, a soft pull toward the learned focal estimates, is allowed but barely matters. The shared focal comes out at 4050 px. This is method A6.

  6. Dense refinement with the guard

    With the focal length held fixed, each photo's pose is refined with hundreds of DINOv2 patch matches, the FoundPose recipe. The new pose is kept only if the head outline and the nose, lip and eyelid edges both line up better. This guard is worth 1.47 dB on our cross view test, which scores a camera on a photo it was not fitted to (higher is better).

  7. Visibility and bake

    For each photo, find the triangles the camera sees. Drop those seen at a grazing angle, beyond a cosine of 0.35, which is about 70 degrees. Then sample the photo colour for every texel, one pixel of the texture image. See painting the surface.

  8. Polish

    Match each side photo's brightness and colour to the front photo, smooth away what is left of the seams, and fill the unseen skin with a tone that follows its neighbours. The step between photos fell from 8.40 to 6.03 grey levels.

  9. Export

    Write face.obj, face.mtl and face_texture.png, in the CT's millimetres and frame.

In our project

A7 scored 26.18 dB on the cross view test, the best of any method with a usable outline. Its three camera distances agree to 106.9 mm, the tightest in the landmark family. Read the full comparison on our methods and results.

Remember

The input is a grey CT mesh and three photos with no EXIF. The output is a textured OBJ in CT coordinates. Everything hard is finding \(R\), \(t\) and \(f\), and the focal length is the hardest part.

Start S3All 15 methodsA1 to A7, B1 to B4, C1 to C4

Our methods and results

We built 15 ways to find the camera and scored them all on the same case. This page explains each method in one paragraph, shows the numbers, teaches you how to read every metric, and says why we recommend A7.

The short version
  • All 15 methods make their own 3D to 2D matches, then hand them to the same camera solver.
  • There is no ground truth, so every score is a consistency check with its own bias.
  • Fit rewards agreeing with MediaPipe. Contour checks the face outline. Cross view checks a camera against a photo it was not fitted to.
  • Use A7. It scores 26.18 dB on cross view, keeps a 6.40 px outline on the front photo, and its three camera distances agree to 106.9 mm.
  • C4 scores higher on cross view, 26.39 dB, but its outline is 16.58 px off.

Read first The task and our pipeline

Four families, one camera solve

Every method makes 3D to 2D matches in its own way, each pairing a CT point with the photo pixel that shows it. All of them hand those matches to the same solver, so the comparison is about the matches, not the solver.

That shared solver is a PnP with focal length refinement. PnP finds a camera from point pairs. First RANSAC runs EPnP, a fast PnP solver, on random small sets of matches and, by default, drops matches more than 12 px off. Then a Huber least squares polishes the rotation, the translation and the log of the focal length together. A residual is the leftover error of one match after the fit. By default the Huber loss treats residuals up to 4 px as squared and larger ones as linear, so one bad match cannot drag the camera far.

  • Family A, landmarks. Find named face points on the CT and on the photo, then solve. Built on Park, Paulsen and Amberg.
  • Family B, dense image refiners. Start from a camera and improve it by comparing a render with the photo pixel by pixel or patch by patch. Built on Corsini and FoundPose.
  • Family C, rebuild then register. Rebuild a face from the photos, line it up with the CT in 3D, and carry the cameras across. Built on DUSt3R.
  • Family D, focal length evidence. Not a camera method. Two learned estimators read a focal length from each photo, and their answers serve as a check and as a weak prior.

Family A, landmarks

A1 Single render. Render the CT once, run MediaPipe on the render and on the photo, back project the render landmarks through the depth map, and solve on 22 rigid landmarks. This is what Cybermed tried. Fit 5.30 px, focal 8348 px, contour 9.39 px, cross view 25.18 dB. The rendered silhouette bulges outside the cheeks.

A2 Multi view consensus. Forty renders with different angles and lights. Each landmark becomes a cloud of 3D candidates. An inlier ball drops candidates far from the rest. A geometric median, the point with the smallest total distance to all candidates, collapses the cloud to one point, and the spread becomes its uncertainty. It drops the sliding jaw points by itself. The surviving central points still scatter 0.7 to 1.4 mm. Cross view 25.37 dB, but the distance spread is the widest of the A family at 238.5 mm.

A3 Template landmark transfer. Start from a template, a generic face mesh whose landmark vertices are already known. Place the MediaPipe canonical face on the CT with a similarity Procrustes fit, which finds the best rotation, shift and scale. Tighten with rigid ICP on stable regions, then bend it onto the CT with Amberg non rigid ICP. The eyes and lips get zero weight. The landmarks are then just known vertices of the fitted template.

ICT FaceKit, a second face template, ran the same way as a cross check. The fit residual was 0.02 to 0.07 mm on stable regions and 1.4 to 1.5 mm at the eyes and lips, which measures the expression mismatch. Cross view 23.96 dB, the worst of the A family, because its side focal lengths land far apart.

A4 Geometric snapping. No appearance at all. Find the face's symmetry plane, walk the midline profile for its extreme points (nose tip, subnasale, lips, chin), and use surface curvature (how sharply the skin bends) to place the eye corners and the nose wings. Each A2 landmark snaps to a feature found within a 6 mm disc. Contour 6.20 px, the best landmark outline. It also found that the scan clipped the nose tip flat, a patch about 6 by 11 mm.

A5 Fusion. Combine the A1, A2 and A4 candidates. Each landmark gets a sigma from how much they disagree, and the PnP weights each point by it. A leave one out table (solve again with each point removed) and a corruption test (push one point and watch the camera) show which point holds the answer. Cross view 25.46 dB, contour 6.39 px, focal 4147 px. Removing jaw landmark 172 or 136 makes the focal fall to about 2350 px. It runs in about half a second.

A6 Joint solve. A5's matches for all three photos go into one least squares with three poses and one shared focal length. The same camera took all three, so one focal is the right model. A5 had given three separate focals of 4147, 7811 and 2792 px. A6 gives one, 4050 px. Front fit 5.25 px, cross view 25.56 dB, distance spread 145.9 mm. The right photo pays for the shared focal with a 31.8 px outline. About five seconds.

A7 Joint solve plus guarded dense refinement. Keep A6's focal fixed. Refine each photo's pose with B3's DINOv2 matching. Keep the new pose only if the outline and the nose, lip and eyelid edges both get closer to the photo. Cross view 26.18 dB, distance spread 106.9 mm. Then the texture polish runs. It costs about twelve seconds per photo on top of A6.

Family B, dense image refiners

B1 Differentiable rendering. A differentiable renderer says how a score changes when you nudge the camera. Mitsuba renders the CT and gives the gradient of a silhouette score, then a normalised gradient field score, with respect to the pose. It moved only 0.03 degrees from its A1 start. The Metal backend could not differentiate the field of view, and the segmenter's mask edge is coarse, about 6 px, and sits a few mm inside the CT outline.

B2 Render and compare without gradients. The Corsini idea. Render the CT as surface direction (normals), depth and ambient occlusion (how hidden each spot is from light). Score each render against the photo with a gradient field measure plus a silhouette chamfer, the average distance between the two outlines. Search with CMA-ES then Powell, two methods that need no gradients. Contour 3.20 px and the best interior edge score, 9.07 px.

Mutual information alone drifted 2 degrees, because the photo is lit flat. Its basin, the set of starting cameras that lead to the right answer, is narrow. Started from A1 it lands somewhere else. 66 s.

B3 DINOv2 dense correspondence. The FoundPose recipe. Match DINOv2 patches between the photo and a render. DINOv2 is a network that turns each small image patch into a list of numbers that describes it. Lift the render side to 3D through the depth map, and run RANSAC PnP. It finds 180 to 260 matches per round with a 4.6 px inlier residual, about a third of a patch.

On the side photos the right chin group went from 40 to 4 px. It cannot recover from a 10 degree push, so it is a refiner, not a starter, and it overfits over rounds. Cross view 25.75 dB. 25 to 45 s per photo.

B4 Optical flow loop. Optical flow says, for every pixel of one image, where it moved to in another. Render a shaded CT, compute optical flow to the photo, lift each flow vector to a 3D match through the depth, and solve. The best front outline of all, 2.80 px and IoU 0.842 (overlap, see below). But its fit rises to 9.32 px, and on the side photos it drifts, 2 degrees on the left and 13 degrees and 238 mm on the right.

Family C, rebuild then register

C1 MapAnything. A DUSt3R successor turns the three photos into one shared cloud of 3D points. A similarity ICP fits the cloud to the CT, allowing a change of scale because the photo cloud has no true size. The cameras follow. Surface distance on stable regions 2.66 mm. One shared focal of 5311 px and a tight distance spread of 99.4 mm. The side cameras are poor, with 28 to 30 px of contour.

C2 Depth Pro. One network predicts a metric depth map from the front photo, a distance in real units for every pixel. Unproject it to 3D points by walking each pixel's ray out to its depth. Fit the points to the CT with similarity ICP. The depth came out 9 percent long. The camera is clearly worse, with the worst contour on the page, 24.77 px, and the worst cross view, 22.33 dB.

C3 3DDFA_V3. A 3D morphable model is an average face plus a few sliders that change its shape. Fit one to the photo, then register that model face to the CT. About 1 mm surface distance on stable regions, and it works on the side views too. Its three focals agree within a factor of 1.14. But the outline is 10.98 px off. Its 0.43 px fit is not comparable, because it measures how well the model fits its own landmarks.

C4 COLMAP plus triangulated landmarks. Classic structure from motion, which recovers 3D points and cameras together from several photos. SIFT, a classic feature detector, found only 44 points on skin. So a three view reconstruction from the landmarks carries the row, 424 points at 1.87 px. Its three focals agree within a factor of 1.05, the tightest of all, and it has the top cross view score, 26.39 dB. Its outline is 16.58 px off.

Family D, focal length evidence

This family checks the focal length from outside the landmarks. GeoCalib gave 4665, 4192 and 3800 px for the front, left and right photos. Depth Pro gave 3319, 4474 and 4391 px. These six values spread by a factor of 1.41, where the landmark PnP values spread by 2 to 2.8 across the same photos. With C3 and C4 they form four independent estimates that cluster at 3300 to 4700 px. A6 lands at 4050 px inside that cluster. Its result barely depends on the prior. It gave 4046 px with the prior off and 4050 px with it on.

How to read each number

There is no hand marked ground truth for this case, so no number here is an absolute accuracy. Each one is a consistency check with a bias you should know before you rank on it.

Fit, in px and mm

Fit is the reprojection error of the method's own matches. Project each 3D landmark through the solved camera and measure how far it lands from the photo landmark. Then take the root mean square.

\[ \text{fit} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lVert \pi(X_i) - x_i \rVert^2} \]
X_i
the 3D landmark on the CT
x_i
the matching photo landmark, in pixels
π
the projection through the solved camera
N
the number of matches

In words, square each arrow length, average the squares, and take the square root. It is a typical arrow length in pixels.

To turn pixels into millimetres at the face, multiply by depth over focal length, \( \text{mm} = \text{px} \times Z / f \). A6 fits to 5.25 px at \(f = 4050\) px and reports 1.28 mm, so its face depth is about \(1.28 \times 4050 / 5.25 \approx 987\) mm. A1 reports 5.30 px and 1.47 mm at \(f = 8348\) px, which puts the face about 2315 mm away. Both fit the front photo about equally well. They disagree on the distance by more than a metre, which is the focal and distance trade at work.

The catch is that fit rewards agreeing with MediaPipe, not being right. A method that copies MediaPipe's mistakes fits well. C3 shows it most clearly, 0.43 px fit with an outline 10.98 px off.

Contour, in px

Contour checks the one thing landmarks cannot fake, the edge of the face. Take the head outline of the CT rendered at the solved camera. A segmentation is a mask that marks which pixels are face skin. Take the face skin outline from a segmentation of the photo. Along the jaw and cheeks, measure the distance from one outline to the other and take the median. No landmark is involved, so a landmark method cannot game it. It only sees the front photo, and it only checks the edge of the face.

Silhouette IoU

IoU is intersection over union. Count the pixels inside both the rendered head and the photo's face mask, and divide by the pixels inside either one. 1 is a perfect overlap. It is coarse, because the photo mask edge is only good to about 6 px, so a few thousandths of difference mean little.

Cross view PSNR, in dB

This is the fairest single number we have. It tests a camera on a photo it was not fitted to. PSNR (peak signal to noise ratio) scores how close two images are, in decibels (dB), and higher is better.

Only skin pixels that came from the photo count, after removing any overall brightness and colour difference between the two shots. We repeat for front to left, front to right and left to front, and average.

\[ \text{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{255^2}{\text{MSE}}, \qquad \text{typical error} = \frac{255}{10^{\text{PSNR}/20}} \]
MSE
the mean of the squared grey level differences, on a 0 to 255 scale
255
the largest possible pixel value

In words, PSNR compares the error with the largest possible pixel value on a log scale. Every 6 dB up halves the typical error. The second formula reads PSNR back as that typical pixel error, the root mean square difference. For example, 25 dB gives \(255 / 10^{1.25} \approx 14\) grey levels.

PSNR dBTypical error, grey levels out of 255Where you see it
22about 20C2 at 22.33
25about 14A1 to A6, most of family B
26about 13A7 at 26.18, C4 at 26.39

The leading methods differ by only 0.1 to 0.3 dB, while the three directions differ from each other by up to 4 dB. So the ranking is consistent but not strong. The test also rewards cameras that agree with each other as much as cameras that are right. Methods that solve all three photos at once, such as C3 and C4, start ahead.

Distance spread, in mm

The subject turned her head and the camera stayed put, so the three solved camera distances should agree. The spread is how far apart they are, and smaller is better. Like cross view, it favours joint solves. C3 reaches 89.3 mm and C1 99.4 mm, while independently solved landmark methods sit at 151.1 to 238.5 mm.

The results, drawn to scale

Why A7, and why not C4

Look at the two charts together. A good camera must do two things. It must put the head outline where the photo has it, and it must agree with the cameras of the other photos. Contour checks the first. Cross view and distance spread check the second.

C4 wins cross view because its three cameras come out of one joint solve with one shared focal, so they cannot disagree much. But its outline is 16.58 px off, and its IoU of 0.690 is the lowest on the page. The faces it paints would line up with each other and still sit in the wrong place on the photo. B4 and B2 have the best outlines, but they are fragile or narrow, and B1 and B2 only ever ran on the front photo.

A7 is the only method in the top group on both axes. It got there by borrowing the right idea from each family. From C it took the joint solve with one shared focal, which became A6. From B it took dense DINOv2 refinement. And it wrapped the refinement in a guard, because a dense refiner has its own fixed point. It helps a camera that is worse than that point and hurts one that is better.

The guard in numbers

On the front photo the refinement made the outline worse, 6.40 to 7.80 px, so it was reverted. On the left photo it improved the outline, 6.39 to 3.40 px, but pushed the interior edges from 11.45 to 11.73 px. The cross view test scores that pose 1.9 dB worse, so a guard that only checked the outline would have let it through. On the right photo both checks improved and the outline went from 31.8 to 7.39 px. Without the guard A7 scores 24.71 dB. With it, 26.18 dB. The guard is worth 1.47 dB.

After the camera, the texture polish evened out the tones. The step between photos fell from 8.40 to 6.03 grey levels. The step between photo texels and filled texels fell from 11.20 to 6.08. The fine detail disagreement between views moved only from 5.72 to 5.12, which shows that nothing was blurred.

Limitations

Read before you quote a number
  • One case and no ground truth. Every number comes from one patient and measures consistency, not accuracy.
  • The focal length is weakly fixed. The fit stays flat over a factor of 3.7 to 6.8 in focal length. Using all three photos does not narrow it. A6's pooled plateau is a factor of 5.85. Three near frontal photos force one answer, but they do not pin it down.
  • Cross view mixes two things. It rewards camera agreement as much as correctness, and the leaders differ by only 0.1 to 0.3 dB. Read it next to contour and IoU.
  • Expression mismatch. The CT has closed eyes and lips, the photo has open eyes and a slight smile. Every method ignores the eyes, lips and chin when fitting, so seams show at the eyelids and lips.
  • Scan clipping. The nose tip is clipped flat, and the chin rest cut just below the chin point. These are properties of this scan and should be checked on a second case.
  • Thin coverage. From the front photo alone, about 17 percent of the surface gets photo colour, 7 percent is mirrored and 76 percent is filled skin tone. Adding the side photos lifts the photo share to 24.3 percent.
  • The cheapest real fix is on Cybermed's side. The original JPEGs with EXIF, the lens, or one tilted checkerboard shot at the same zoom would remove the focal length problem.

Which paper fed which method

PaperWhat we tookOur methods

Paulsen et al. 2018Many views, consensus per landmark, throw out the disagreeing onesA2, and through it A5 to A7
Amberg et al. 2007Non rigid ICP with a stiffness schedule and zero weights for bad regionsA3
Corsini et al. 2009Render geometric maps, score against the photo, search without gradientsB2, and the idea behind B1
FoundPose 2024DINOv2 patch matches lifted through render depth, then RANSAC PnPB3 and the refinement in A7

A4, B4, C2, C3 and C4 draw on other work that this guide does not cover as a paper page. They use the same building blocks, mainly ICP, PnP and RANSAC.

Remember

Fit rewards agreeing with MediaPipe, contour checks the outline, and cross view checks one camera against another photo. Rank on contour and cross view together. A7 is the only method near the top on both.

About 35 minutes

Building block K1Used in all 15 methods

Cameras and projection

A camera turns a 3D point into a pixel. This page builds that rule from nothing, one matrix at a time. At the end you can read \( u = K\,[R \mid t]\,X \) and say what every number in it means for our photo.

The short version
  • A camera first moves a 3D point into its own frame with a rotation \(R\) and a shift \(t\). These are the extrinsics.
  • Then it divides by depth and scales by the focal length \(f\). The matrix \(K\) holds \(f\) and the image centre. These are the intrinsics.
  • Homogeneous coordinates (one extra number) let you write both moves as one matrix product.
  • In our project the camera has seven unknowns, three for rotation, three for position and one focal length.
  • On a face, a longer lens further away looks almost the same, so the focal length is hard to pin down.

Why you need it

Our whole task comes down to one question. Where was the studio camera, relative to the CT head, when it took the photo? Once we know that, we can send a ray from the camera through every pixel and paint the colour onto the CT surface it hits.

In this project a camera is described by seven numbers. Three say which way it points. Three say where it stands. One says how much it zooms, the focal length. We fix the image centre and assume no lens distortion, so nothing else is unknown. Every one of our 15 methods ends by solving for these seven numbers. That solve is called PnP, and it only makes sense once you know how a camera maps points to pixels.

Points and coordinate frames

A point in 3D space is three numbers. Those numbers only mean something once you say which frame they are measured in. A frame is an origin plus three directions called axes. The same physical point, say the tip of the nose, has different numbers in different frames.

We use two frames all the time. The CT frame is the one the STL mesh file is written in. It is in millimetres. The subject's right is \(-X\), the front of the face (anterior) is \(-Y\), and the top of the head (superior) is \(+Z\). The camera frame follows the OpenCV convention. Its origin is the camera centre. Its \(x\) axis points right in the image, \(y\) points down in the image, and \(z\) points forward out of the lens into the scene.

The face in the drawings is the MediaPipe canonical face, a generic average face, with the CT style origin at the centre of the head model.

Rotation: what a 3 by 3 matrix does to a point

A rotation turns every point about the origin without stretching anything. You write it as a 3 by 3 matrix \(R\). To rotate a point \(X\) you multiply, \(X' = R X\). Each new coordinate is a weighted sum of the old ones.

Start with the simplest case, because every rotation is built from three of these. Turning by an angle \(\theta\) about the vertical \(Z\) axis leaves the height alone and mixes \(X\) and \(Y\).

A rotation about the vertical axis

\[ R_Z(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad X' = R_Z(\theta)\,X \]
θ
the angle of the turn, in radians or degrees
X
the point before the turn, a column of three numbers
X′
the same point after the turn

In words, the new \(X\) and \(Y\) are a blend of the old ones, set by the angle, and the height \(Z\) does not change.

Worked example. Take the outer corner of the subject's right eye on the canonical face, \(X = (-44.5,\,-31.7,\,26.6)\) mm in our CT style frame. Turn it by \(30^\circ\). Then \(\cos 30^\circ = 0.866\) and \(\sin 30^\circ = 0.5\).

\[ X'_1 = 0.866 \cdot (-44.5) - 0.5 \cdot (-31.7) = -22.6, \quad X'_2 = 0.5 \cdot (-44.5) + 0.866 \cdot (-31.7) = -49.7, \quad X'_3 = 26.6 \]

The height stays at 26.6 mm. The point swings toward the midline and forward. Its distance from the vertical axis is the same before and after, about 54.6 mm.

Two facts make a matrix a rotation. Its columns have length one and are at right angles to each other. Its determinant, a single number that says how the matrix scales volume and whether it flips space, is \(+1\). A determinant of \(-1\) would be a mirror, which turns a right face into a left face. That bug is silent and common.

A general rotation is built from three simple turns. Yaw turns about the vertical axis, like shaking your head no. Pitch turns about the left to right axis, like nodding yes. Roll turns about the front to back axis, like tilting an ear to your shoulder.

You multiply the three matrices together. The order matters, because turning then nodding is not the same as nodding then turning. A rotation always has exactly three degrees of freedom (numbers you can set freely), even though the matrix holds nine numbers.

Translation and the extrinsics

A rotation alone keeps the origin fixed, but a camera also stands somewhere. A translation is a shift. You add a vector \(t\) to every point. Rotation followed by translation is a rigid motion, \(X_{\text{cam}} = R X + t\). It has six degrees of freedom, three for \(R\) and three for \(t\).

For a camera, \(R\) and \(t\) are called the extrinsics. They take a point from the CT frame into the camera frame. Be careful with what \(t\) means. It is not where the camera stands. It is where the CT origin lands in camera coordinates. The camera centre in CT coordinates is \(C = -R^{\top} t\). You get it by asking which point lands at the camera origin, \(R C + t = 0\).

People often write the two together as one 3 by 4 matrix \([R \mid t]\), which is \(R\) with \(t\) glued on as a fourth column.

The pinhole model

The simplest camera is a dark box with a tiny hole in one wall. Light from each scene point passes through the hole in a straight line and lights up exactly one spot on the back wall. The picture comes out upside down. Real lenses gather more light, but for geometry they behave like this hole.

This is where the division by depth comes from. Look at one ray from the side. The point sits at height \(Y\) and depth \(Z\) in front of the hole. The image plane sits at distance \(f\) from the hole. The ray forms two similar triangles, one in the scene and one inside the camera. Their sides are in the same ratio.

Similar triangles give the projection

\[ \frac{y}{f} = \frac{Y}{Z} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = f\,\frac{Y}{Z}, \qquad x = f\,\frac{X}{Z} \]
X, Y, Z
the point in the camera frame, in millimetres, with Z the depth in front of the camera
f
the distance from the hole to the image plane, the focal length
x, y
where the ray crosses the image plane

In words, the image height is the real height divided by the depth, times \(f\). That one division is all of perspective. Far things are small because \(Z\) is large. Moving the face twice as far away halves every image coordinate.

Physically the image plane sits behind the hole and the picture is flipped. In the math we put a virtual image plane the same distance in front of the hole. The rays cross it at the same sizes, but the right way up. Everyone does this, and from here on so do we.

Focal length in pixels

The formula gives \(x\) in millimetres on the sensor, but photos are measured in pixels. A sensor is a grid of tiny light cells. If one pixel is \(p\) millimetres wide, then \(x\) mm is \(x / p\) pixels. The two scale factors combine into one number, the focal length in pixels, \(f_{\text{px}} = f_{\text{mm}} / p\).

So \(f_{\text{px}}\) mixes the lens and the sensor and any later resizing of the image. Our photos were cropped and resized to 1500 pixels wide, and the EXIF data (the settings a camera writes into the file) was stripped. That is why we cannot read the focal length off the file and have to estimate it.

A clean way to feel \(f_{\text{px}}\) is the field of view. Half the image width, seen from the camera centre, spans the angle \(\tan(\text{fov}/2) = (W/2)/f_{\text{px}}\). Our A6 focal of 4050 px on a 1500 px wide photo gives a horizontal field of view of about \(21^\circ\). A1's focal of 8348 px gives about \(10^\circ\), a longer lens. Our CT render camera used an \(18^\circ\) field of view on a 1400 px image, which is a focal of 4420 px.

On the physical side, an 85 mm studio lens on a full frame sensor, 36 mm wide, gives \(85 / 36 \times 1500 \approx 3540\) px if the crop kept the full sensor width. Tighter crops push the number up. Our research notes used this to set a studio prior of roughly 3500 to 9000 px.

The principal point

The formula \(x = fX/Z\) puts the optical axis, the line straight out of the lens centre, at \(x = 0\). Pixel coordinates start at the top left corner instead. So we add the pixel where the optical axis hits the image. That pixel is the principal point \((c_x, c_y)\). We fix it at the image centre. For the 1500 by 1234 front photo that is \((749.5,\,616.5)\), because OpenCV counts pixel centres from 0.

The intrinsic matrix K

Focal length and principal point describe the inside of the camera. They are called the intrinsics, and they live in one 3 by 3 matrix.

Intrinsics

\[ K = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & s & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{ours: } K = \begin{pmatrix} 4050 & 0 & 749.5 \\ 0 & 4050 & 616.5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]
f_x, f_y
focal length in pixels along each image axis. Square pixels make them equal, and we assume that
s
skew, nonzero only for slanted pixel grids. It is 0 for every modern camera
c_x, c_y
the principal point in pixels

In words, \(K\) scales camera coordinates by the focal length and then shifts them so pixel counting starts at the top left corner.

Homogeneous coordinates, from scratch

This trick is why every paper writes the camera as one matrix. The projection has two awkward parts. Translation is an addition, not a multiplication. Perspective is a division. Homogeneous coordinates turn both into plain matrix multiplication, so the whole camera becomes one matrix.

The trick is to add one extra number. A 2D point \((x, y)\) becomes \((x, y, 1)\). Then you declare that any multiple means the same point, so \((2x, 2y, 2)\) is also \((x, y)\). To go back you divide by the last number, \((a, b, w) \mapsto (a/w,\, b/w)\). Each 2D point is now a whole line of 3D vectors through the origin. The figure shows the same idea one dimension down, where the picture is flat and easy to see.

Two things follow. First, a translation becomes a matrix. With the extra 1, the product \([R \mid t]\,(X, Y, Z, 1)^{\top}\) equals \(RX + t\). The 1 multiplies the column \(t\) and adds it on. Second, perspective division gets postponed. You multiply everything through, then divide by the last coordinate once at the end.

The full projection

Now the whole camera fits on one line. Figure 5 follows one landmark through it, with real arithmetic from a synthetic camera set to our A6 numbers.

From a CT point to a pixel

\[ \begin{pmatrix} u' \\ v' \\ w \end{pmatrix} = K\,[R \mid t] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad u = \frac{u'}{w}, \quad v = \frac{v'}{w} \]
(X, Y, Z, 1)
a CT point in millimetres, made homogeneous
[R | t]
the extrinsics, moving the point into the camera frame
K
the intrinsics, turning millimetres at depth into pixels
w
the depth of the point in front of the camera
u, v
the pixel, after the perspective division

In words, move the point into the camera frame, scale it into pixels, then divide by its depth.

Worked example. A frontal camera in our CT frame looks along \(+Y\). Its rotation is \(R_0\), the matrix below. This is exactly the rotation of the virtual camera A1 renders with. The canonical nose tip sits at \(X = (0,\,-75.9,\,-4.6)\) mm. Put the head centre 977 mm in front of the camera, so \(t = (0, 0, 977)\).

\[ R_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad R_0 X + t = (0,\; 4.6,\; 901.1), \quad u = 4050 \cdot \tfrac{0}{901.1} + 749.5 = 749.5, \quad v = 4050 \cdot \tfrac{4.6}{901.1} + 616.5 = 637.3 \]

The second row of \(R_0\) says camera \(y\) is minus CT \(Z\). Up in the head becomes down in the image, since image \(y\) grows downward. The third row says camera depth is CT \(Y\). The nose tip is 76 mm closer to the camera than the head centre.

The same seven unknowns move every landmark at once. That is why 22 landmark pairs can pin them down.

Focal length and distance trade off

This fact shaped half our project. Zoom in and step back, and the face stays the same size in the picture. Only the depth cues change. Close up, the nose looks bigger relative to the ears, and far away the face looks flatter. On a face those cues are tiny.

Our research notes put a number on it. Scale the focal length by \(1 + e\) and move the camera back so the face plane keeps its size. A point at image offset \(u\) from the centre and depth offset \(d\) from the face plane then moves by about

Why zoom and distance look alike

\[ \Delta u \;\approx\; u \, e \, \frac{d}{Z} \]
u
the point's distance from the image centre, in pixels. On our front photo it is at most about 270 px
e
the relative change in focal length. e = 1 means twice the focal
d
how far the point sits in front of or behind the face plane, at most about 50 mm
Z
the camera distance, about 1200 mm in that note

In words, the zoom change only shows up through how far a point sticks out of the face plane, and that is small next to the camera distance. Put in those numbers. Doubling the focal moves the worst landmark by about 11 px and most landmarks by only a few. MediaPipe landmarks on our photo are already off by 2 to 5 px. So the fit can barely tell the two cameras apart.

In the bottom plot, the curves are real. They come from our focal sweeps. At each fixed focal length we re-solved the pose and recorded the fit error. The plateau is the range of focal lengths whose error is within 5 percent of the best. For A6's joint solve over three photos it runs from 2714 to 15884 px, a factor of 5.85. For A5 on the front photo alone it is a factor of 3.69. For A1 it is 4.30, and it touches the edge of the sweep.

A wider plateau with three photos sounds wrong. The three photos disagreed about which way the focal should move. The front photo's best value was 4304 px, the right photo wanted 2714 px, and the left photo ran to the end of the sweep. Pooling them flattened the curve. Three near frontal photos at one focal force one answer to the focal versus depth trade. They do not remove the trade.

In our project

The same fit error came out of very different cameras. A1 settled on 8348 px with the camera about 2057 mm from the face points. A6 settled on 4050 px with the front camera about 977 mm away. A1 fits its landmarks to 5.30 px and A6 to 5.25 px. The tiebreaker came from outside the fit. Two learned focal estimators, networks that guess the focal length from one photo, gave 4665, 4192 and 3800 px (GeoCalib) and 3319, 4474 and 4391 px (Depth Pro) on the three photos. Together with C3 and C4 they cluster at 3300 to 4700 px. A6's 4050 px lands inside that cluster without being told about it.

Our CT frame versus the OpenCV camera

Two conventions meet in every one of our camera solves, and mixing them up mirrors or flips the face. The table puts them side by side.

DirectionCT frame (the STL)OpenCV camera frame
Unitsmillimetresmillimetres for points, pixels after K
Rightsubject's right is −X+x is image right
Front and backanterior (face side) is −Y+z points forward, away from the lens
Up and downsuperior (head top) is +Z+y is image down
Origina corner of the CT scan volumethe camera centre

The CT frame matches the standard DICOM patient frame, called LPS. A camera in front of the face looks along \(+Y\), toward the back of the head. In a normal photo, image left shows the subject's right, which is \(-X\). So a frontal camera has camera \(x = +X\), camera \(y = -Z\) and camera \(z = +Y\). Those three facts are the three rows of \(R_0\) above.

The canonical face drawn on this site has its own axes, in centimetres, with \(+x\) the subject's left, \(+y\) up and \(+z\) out of the face. Converting it to the CT style frame is \(X = 10x\), \(Y = -10z\), \(Z = 10y\).

Variants that matter here

Full perspective

What we use. Divide by each point's own depth. Needed because the nose is about 100 mm closer to the camera than the ears.

Weak perspective

Divide every point by one average depth. It is a scaled orthographic view, as if the camera were infinitely far away and zoomed in. It works when the object is shallow compared with the distance, and it is exactly the limit our plateau slides toward at long focal lengths.

Lens distortion

Real lenses bend straight lines a little. OpenCV models it with extra coefficients. We set them all to zero, which is reasonable for a long portrait lens.

Free principal point

We fix \((c_x, c_y)\) at the image centre. Our photos are crops of a larger frame, so the true centre may be elsewhere. One face cannot pin it down, so freeing it would only add a degree of freedom to the plateau.

Where it shows up

Every method writes its answer as a camera, \(K\), \(R\) and \(t\), in the CT frame. The table lists the focal length each method settled on for the front photo, from our comparison table.

MethodFocal pxHow the focal was found
A18348Huber PnP with free focal on one render's landmarks
A25581same solver, multi view consensus landmarks
A54147same solver, fused and weighted landmarks
A6 A74050one focal shared by three photos in a joint least squares
B34893dense DINOv2 matches, then the same PnP
C33781chained from a 3D morphable model fit
C43906COLMAP over the three photos

The camera model also appears in places that do not solve for it. Rendering the CT (K3) uses a known virtual camera. Painting the texture (K12) projects every CT vertex into the photo with the solved camera. The cross view test bakes a texture from the front photo and renders it at a side camera. A wrong focal fits one photo and fails that test, which is why A7 scores 26.18 dB there and A1 only 25.18 dB.

Watch out

Image \(y\) points down. Forget it and the face comes out upside down.

A determinant of \(-1\) is a mirror. Our camera code checks \(\det R = 1\) for exactly this reason. A mirrored face can still fit the landmarks well, because faces are nearly symmetric.

\(t\) is not the camera position. The position is \(C = -R^{\top}t\).

Units must agree. The CT is in millimetres and the canonical face is in centimetres. A factor of ten in the points shows up as a factor of ten in the distance, never in the fit error.

Some libraries flip axes on you. Open3D's ready made ray helper gave us vertically flipped renders, so our code builds the rays by hand from the same \(K\) it projects with.

Remember

A pixel is \(K\,[R \mid t]\,X\) divided by its last number. Seven unknowns in our case.

Rotation and translation move the CT into the camera frame. \(K\) turns millimetres at depth into pixels.

On a face, focal length and distance nearly cancel, so our focal comes from evidence outside the fit.

About 25 minutes

Building block K2Used in A1 to A7, C4

Face landmarks

A landmark is a named point you can find on any face, like the tip of the nose. If you find the same named points on the photo and on the CT, you have pairs of matching points, and pairs are what a camera solve needs.

The short version
  • MediaPipe finds 478 numbered points on a face photo. The same number always means the same spot, so equal numbers make a matching pair.
  • To use it on the CT, we first draw a shaded picture of the CT and run the detector on that.
  • Only 22 rigid points go into the camera solve. Eyelids and lips changed with expression, and outline points slide when the view changes.
  • We measured the CT side points. Central points scatter 1 to 2 mm, while jaw and outline points slide 10 to 30 mm.

Why you need it

To solve for the camera with PnP, the standard solver that finds a camera from point pairs, we need pairs. Each pair is a 3D point on the CT surface and the pixel where that same spot of skin appears in the photo. A face has no printed markers, so we use the face's own features. The nose tip in the photo goes with the nose tip on the CT. The outer eye corner goes with the outer eye corner.

A detector finds these points for us. We use Google's MediaPipe Face Landmarker. It gives every point a fixed number, called its index, and the index means the same spot on every face. Index 4 is always the nose tip. So if we run it on the photo and on a picture of the CT, matching is free. We just pair equal indices.

The catch is that the CT has no colour. To run a photo detector on it we first draw a shaded picture of it, which is the job of rendering and back projection. Cybermed had tried this and found the CT side landmarks imprecise. This page explains why, with our own measurements.

What MediaPipe gives you

On a photo, MediaPipe returns 478 points. The first 468 cover the face as a dense mesh. The last 10, indices 468 to 477, outline the two irises. Each point has an \(x\) and \(y\) in the image and a \(z\) for relative depth. That \(z\) is a learned relief, not a measured distance. The model card, the short document that describes the model, says it was trained on synthetic data and is scaled to the face width.

The same 468 indices exist on MediaPipe's canonical face. That is a fixed average face mesh in centimetres, with 468 vertices and 898 triangles. Vertex \(i\) of the canonical face is landmark \(i\) of a detection. It is the face drawn on every page of this site.

Most of the 468 points are not anatomical landmarks. They are a dense grid that lets the network describe the whole face shape. Only some sit on features an anatomist would name, such as eye corners, the nose tip and mouth corners. Those are the ones worth trusting.

How a detector finds the points

You do not need to build a detector, but knowing its shape explains its failures. A landmark detector is a convolutional neural network, a CNN. A CNN is a stack of small learned filters. Each filter slides over the image and responds to a pattern.

Early layers respond to edges. Later layers combine edges into parts like an eye or a nostril. Each layer usually makes the image smaller and the description richer. At the end, the network turns that description into numbers.

For MediaPipe, the numbers are the coordinates of all 478 points. It works in two stages. A small detector first finds a box around the face. The landmark network then sees only that box, cut out with a margin of 25 percent and resized to 256 by 256 pixels. Its output is mapped back to the full photo. On our photo one call took 9 to 11 ms.

Other detectors produce a heatmap per landmark instead, an image that is bright where the landmark probably is. The brightest pixel is the answer. The hourglass network in Paulsen et al. works this way.

Two practical facts follow from this design. First, the detector needs the whole face in view. A close crop of only the mouth was not detected in our tests. Second, the network only knows what it was trained on. It has seen photos, mostly with open eyes. A grey render of a CT with closed eyes is unusual input, and nothing guarantees the points land on the same skin as they would on a photo.

The named points we use

You will hear these names in every conversation about the method. MediaPipe does not publish anatomical names for its indices. Our names come from its own connection sets, the TensorFlow.js annotation map and the canonical mesh coordinates. The table lists the ones this project uses.

IndexNameGroupIn the camera solve
4nose tip (pronasale), the most forward pointnoseyes
168sellion, the deepest point of the nose bridgenoseyes
6nose bridgenoseyes
2subnasale, where the nose meets the upper lipnoseyes
129, 358alar base, the sides of the nostrilsnoseyes
33, 263outer eye corners, right and lefteye cornersyes
133, 362inner eye corners, right and lefteye cornersyes
116, 345, 50, 280cheekbonescheekbonesyes
172, 397, 136, 365, 58, 288jaw, three on each sidejawyes, with a low weight
152, 199chin, menton and pogonionchinyes
61, 291mouth cornerslipsno
159, 145, 386, 374eyelid centres, upper and lowereyelidsno
234, 454face outline at the cheekoutlineno
468, 473iris centres, photo onlyirisno

Left and right always mean the subject's side. Index 33 is the outer corner of the subject's right eye. In a normal photo you face the person, so it appears on the image left. In our CT frame the subject's right is \(-X\). On our CT, index 33 back projected (lifted from the render to the 3D surface) to about \(x = 80\) mm and index 263 to about \(x = 171\) mm, which confirms the two conventions agree.

The 22 rigid landmarks, and what we leave out

We call a landmark rigid when it sits on bone or firm tissue and does not move when the expression changes. Our camera solve uses 22 of them in five groups. Nose has 6, eye corners 4, cheekbones 4, jaw 6 and chin 2. By default 86 indices are excluded. Three kinds of point are left out, each for its own reason.

  1. Eyelids

    The CT patient had their eyes closed. The photo subject has them open. The upper lid landmark sits on a different piece of skin in the two images, so pairing them pairs two different points.

  2. Lips

    The mouth was closed in the CT and slightly smiling in the photo. MediaPipe rated the photo's smile at 0.53 and 0.39 for the two sides, on a scale from 0 to 1.

  3. The face outline

    Outline points mark the edge of the face as seen from the camera. That edge is not a fixed spot on the skin. It moves when the head turns, as the next section shows.

The irises, indices 468 to 477, are left out too. A CT skin surface has no iris.

The detector itself noticed the difference. MediaPipe also gives blink scores, from 0 for open eyes to 1 for closed. On the CT render it reported 0.67 and 0.76. On the photo it reported 0.07 and 0.05. Our template method A3 measured the size of the mismatch directly. After bending the canonical face onto the CT, the leftover distance was 0.02 to 0.07 mm on stable regions and 1.4 to 1.5 mm at the eyes and lips.

Why outline points slide

This is the main reason Cybermed's first try failed. Look at the edge of a face on a photo. Your eye follows the line where the cheek turns away from you. Every point on that line is a place where your line of sight just grazes the skin. When the head turns, a different strip of skin becomes the grazing strip. So the outline landmark keeps its index, but it moves to a new spot on the skin.

That is fatal for a 3D to 2D pair. On the CT render, landmark 234 lands on whatever skin forms the edge in that render. On the photo, it lands on whatever forms the edge in the photo. If the two views are not identical, those are different spots on the skin, and the pair lies.

How precise are landmarks on a CT render?

This is the measurement behind our whole A family. We rendered the cleaned CT from 45 virtual cameras, with the head turned from \(-20^\circ\) to \(+20^\circ\), tilted from \(-10^\circ\) to \(+10^\circ\), and lit from three directions. A face was found in all 45 renders. Each landmark was lifted back to 3D, and we measured how far it scattered around its median position. The table gives the median and the 90th percentile, the value that 90 percent of cases stay below.

GroupLighting only, median / 90th pct mm9 near frontal rendersAll 45 renders
Nose1.7 / 2.41.5 / 2.62.1 / 5.3
Eye corners1.5 / 4.81.6 / 5.62.1 / 7.1
Eyelid centres1.1 / 4.31.4 / 3.82.0 / 5.4
Cheekbones0.9 / 9.82.5 / 9.62.6 / 9.6
Chin1.8 / 4.61.7 / 5.32.3 / 5.7
Lips0.7 / 3.11.4 / 3.31.8 / 3.6
Jaw3.9 / 10.88.3 / 15.09.8 / 33.9
Face outline sides2.1 / 51.826 / 4931 / 51

Three things stand out. With the camera fixed and only the light moved, central landmarks still move 1 to 2 mm typically and 5 to 10 mm in bad cases. The jaw and outline points slide 10 to 30 mm or more once the view changes. That is the sliding of Figure 4, measured on real data. And the jaw points sit in our 22 anyway. The next section explains that choice.

Variants that matter here

One render A1

Detect once on a frontal render and trust it. This is what Cybermed tried. It inherits all the scatter above.

Many renders A2

Detect on 40 renders with different angles and lights, keep the detections within a 3 mm ball of agreement, and take their geometric median, the point closest in total to all of them. The spread becomes an uncertainty. It drops the sliding jaw points by itself.

Template transfer A3

Bend the canonical face onto the CT surface with non rigid ICP, which slides and bends one surface onto another, and read off its vertices. No detector on the CT at all.

Geometry A4

Find points from the shape itself, such as the most forward point of the midline profile or a curvature peak. It found the nose tip clipped flat by the scan volume, a patch about 6 by 11 mm.

Other schemes

Park et al. used Dlib's 68 points and kept 10 stable ones. Paulsen et al. trained their own network for 73 landmarks. Google's own face geometry code uses a weighted rigid subset that also avoids lips and eyelids.

Where it shows up

Every method in our A family turns landmarks into the pairs for the camera solve. They differ only in how they get the 3D side. A5 fuses A1, A2 and A4. It gives each landmark a sigma, an uncertainty in mm, from how much those methods and A2's views disagree, and weights the camera solve by it. A6 and A7 reuse A5's pairs. C4 triangulates landmarks instead of using the CT. It finds each 3D point where the rays from the three photos meet.

The jaw group stayed in the solve, with a low weight of 0.3, and that turned out to matter. A5's leave one out test removes one landmark at a time and solves again. Removing either jaw point 172 or 136 collapsed the focal length from 4147 px to about 2350 px. So the points that hold our focal length are the least reliable ones. That is a large part of why the focal needed evidence from outside the fit, as the camera page explains.

Remember that the fit error (fit px) measures distance to where MediaPipe found the photo landmarks. It rewards agreeing with MediaPipe, not being right.

Watch out

Left and right are the subject's. Image left is the subject's right, which is \(-X\) in the CT frame.

Iris points 468 to 477 exist only on photo detections. The canonical face stops at 467.

A landmark can miss the CT entirely. Landmark 10, the top of the forehead, lifted back to infinity on our CT, because it sits above where the scan was cut off. A1's render missed 7 landmarks this way, and every miss must be dropped.

A detector that works on photos may still fail on a render. Always render the whole face, and check its blink scores. They tell you how the network read the eyes.

Remember

MediaPipe gives 478 numbered points on a photo, and the same 468 indices on the canonical face. Equal index means a matching pair.

Use only rigid points. Eyelids and lips changed with expression, and outline points slide with the view.

On our CT renders, central landmarks scatter 1 to 2 mm and jaw and outline points 10 to 30 mm.
