Building block K3Used in A1, A2, A5, A6, A7, B3, B4

Rendering, depth and back projection

A face detector only reads pictures. The CT is a surface. This page shows how we draw a picture of the CT, keep the distance to the surface at every pixel, and use that distance to lift any 2D point on the picture back onto the 3D surface.

The short version
  • To run a face detector on the CT, we draw a picture of it from a virtual camera. That picture is a render.
  • While drawing, we also store the distance to the surface at every pixel. That image of distances is the depth map.
  • Back projection turns a landmark pixel plus its depth back into a 3D point on the CT.
  • The CT has no colour, so the render is shaded by a light. Moving only the light moved our landmarks by 1 to 2 mm.

Read first Cameras and projection and Face landmarks

Why you need it

We want 3D landmarks on the CT with the same index numbers MediaPipe uses on the photo. MediaPipe takes an image, so we make one. We place a virtual camera in front of the CT and draw what it would see. That is a render. MediaPipe finds landmarks on the render, and each landmark is a pixel.

Because we drew the render ourselves, we know exactly which 3D surface point sits behind every pixel. Going from pixel back to surface point is called back projection.

This is the core of our method A1 and of Park et al. 2023. A2 does it 40 times. B3 and B4 use the same lift for dense matches instead of landmarks.

What rendering is

A camera, as the camera page explains, sends one ray of sight out through each pixel. Rendering runs that backwards. For every pixel you build its ray, find the first piece of surface the ray hits, and decide how bright that spot should look. This way of rendering is called ray casting. Graphics cards often do the same job the other way round, by projecting every triangle onto the image and keeping the nearest one per pixel. Both give the same picture and the same depth.

Our CT mesh has about 300,000 vertices. So for every pixel the core question is this. Does the ray hit this triangle, and if so, where?

Ray and triangle

A ray starts at a point \(o\), the camera centre, and goes in a direction \(d\). Every point on it is \(o + s\,d\) for some distance \(s \ge 0\). A triangle has three corners \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\).

Any point in the plane of the triangle can be written as a weighted mix of the corners. The weights are its barycentric coordinates. They always add up to 1. The point is inside the triangle exactly when all three weights are between 0 and 1. Each weight also has a neat meaning. It is the area of the small triangle opposite that corner, divided by the whole area.

The intersection, step by step

Set the ray equal to the mixed point and solve for the three unknowns \(s\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\).

\[ o + s\,d \;=\; (1-\beta-\gamma)\,A + \beta\,B + \gamma\,C \] \[ \Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{pmatrix} -d & B - A & C - A \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} s \\ \beta \\ \gamma \end{pmatrix} = o - A \]
o, d
the ray origin and direction
s
how far along the ray the hit is. Negative means behind the camera
β, γ
the barycentric weights of B and C. The weight of A is 1 − β − γ

In words, find how far along the ray you must go to land in the triangle's plane, and how much of each corner that landing point is made of. It is a 3 by 3 linear system. The Möller and Trumbore method, the standard fast ray and triangle test, solves it with a few cross products. The ray hits the triangle when \(s > 0\), \(\beta \ge 0\), \(\gamma \ge 0\) and \(\beta + \gamma \le 1\). Over all triangles, keep the hit with the smallest \(s\). That is the visible surface.

Worked example. A ray from \(o = (0,0,0)\) along \(d = (0,0,1)\). A triangle with \(A = (-1,-1,5)\), \(B = (3,-1,5)\), \(C = (-1,2,5)\). The plane is \(z = 5\), so \(s = 5\) and the hit is \((0,0,5)\). In the plane, \((0,0) = (-1,-1) + \beta\,(4,0) + \gamma\,(0,3)\), so \(\beta = 0.25\) and \(\gamma = 0.333\). The weight of \(A\) is \(0.417\). All three are positive, so it is a hit.

The weights do more than the inside test. They blend any value stored at the corners, such as depth, surface normals or texture coordinates, into its value at the hit point. The texture step uses the same trick, see K12.

The depth map

The depth map is what makes the lift possible. It is an image where each pixel stores a distance instead of a colour. For our renders it is the depth \(z\) of the hit point in the camera frame, in millimetres. Pixels whose ray misses the surface store nothing, or infinity.

There are two common kinds of depth, and mixing them up is a classic bug. z depth is measured along the camera's viewing axis. Ray length is measured along the pixel's own ray. They agree at the image centre and differ toward the edges. The formula below needs z depth.

In our project

A1 renders the CT at 1400 by 1400 pixels with an \(18^\circ\) field of view from 600 mm, which makes the focal length 4420 px. About 49 percent of its pixels hit the surface. Open3D's ray casting scene (Open3D is the 3D geometry library we used) cast a 1200 by 1200 image against the 600,000 triangle face mesh in about a second on the CPU.

Back projection, with the math

Projection takes a 3D point to a pixel and throws away the depth. Back projection puts it back. The pixel tells you the ray, and the depth map tells you how far along that ray the surface is.

From pixel and depth to a CT point

\[ X_{\text{cam}} = z \, K^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} z\,(u - c_x)/f \\ z\,(v - c_y)/f \\ z \end{pmatrix}, \qquad X = R^{\top}\,(X_{\text{cam}} - t) \]
u, v
the pixel where the detector put the landmark on the render
z
the depth map value at that pixel, in millimetres
K, f, c_x, c_y
the render camera's intrinsics, which we chose
R, t
the render camera's extrinsics, also chosen by us
X
the landmark on the CT surface, in the CT frame

In words, turn the pixel back into its ray, walk out along the ray to the stored depth, then move that point from the camera frame back into the CT frame. The first equation undoes the intrinsics \(K\) and scales by depth. The second undoes the extrinsics. Because \(R\) is a rotation, its inverse is its transpose.

Worked example with A1's render camera. It has \(f = 4420\) px, \(c_x = c_y = 699.5\), the frontal rotation \(R_0\) from the camera page, and \(t = (-122.7,\,103.4,\,557.5)\) mm. Suppose the detector puts a landmark at pixel \((760, 640)\) and the depth map reads 575 mm there.

\[ X_{\text{cam}} = \Big(575 \cdot \tfrac{60.5}{4420},\; 575 \cdot \tfrac{-59.5}{4420},\; 575\Big) = (7.9,\; -7.7,\; 575) \] \[ X_{\text{cam}} - t = (130.5,\; -111.1,\; 17.5), \qquad X = R_0^{\top}(X_{\text{cam}} - t) = (130.5,\; 17.5,\; 111.1) \text{ mm} \]

A CT \(Y\) of 17.5 mm is near the front of the face, since our nose tip sits near \(y = 20\). The pixel and depth in this example are made up. The camera numbers are A1's real ones.

  1. Render

    Ray cast the CT from a chosen camera. Keep the shaded image and the depth map.

  2. Detect

    Run MediaPipe on the shaded image. Each landmark is a pixel \((u, v)\).

  3. Read the depth

    Look up \(z\) at that pixel. No hit means the landmark is dropped.

  4. Lift

    Apply the formula to get \(X\) on the CT surface, in the CT frame.

  5. Pair

    The same index on the photo gives the matching pixel. Now you have a 3D to 2D pair for PnP.

Why the CT needs shading, and why light moves landmarks

A CT scanner measures how strongly each small block of tissue absorbs X rays. The skin surface is an isosurface, the boundary where that density crosses a threshold. So the surface has a shape but no colour. If you painted every hit pixel the same grey, the picture would be a flat silhouette. A detector could find nothing inside it.

Shading fixes that. The simplest rule is Lambert's, where a patch looks brighter the more directly it faces the light.

Lambert shading

\[ I = a + (1 - a)\,\max(0,\; n \cdot \ell) \]
I
the brightness of the pixel, from 0 to 1
n
the surface normal at the hit, a unit vector pointing out of the skin
ℓ
the unit direction toward the light
a
ambient light, a floor so that shadowed parts are not black. Our renders use 0.25

In words, a patch is brightest when it faces the light head on and gets darker as it turns away, but never darker than the ambient floor \(a\). Our renderer takes the absolute value of \(n \cdot \ell\) instead of the max, because the CT isosurface has normals that point the wrong way in places. The normal comes from the hit triangle, blended from its corners with the barycentric weights. If the light comes straight from the camera, a patch facing the camera gets \(n \cdot \ell = 1\) and full brightness. A patch tilted \(60^\circ\) away gets \(\cos 60^\circ = 0.5\).

This is why light matters for us. The detector reads brightness patterns. A light from the left makes the left cheek bright and puts a shadow beside the nose. A light from above changes both. The CNN sees a different picture and moves its points, even though the surface did not move at all. Figure 4 shows the effect with a toy detector that marks the brightest spot on the cheek. MediaPipe is far smarter, but it still reads the same pixels.

We measured this on the real CT with MediaPipe. With the camera fixed and only the light direction changed, central landmarks moved 1 to 2 mm typically and 5 to 10 mm in the worst cases. That is the main reason a single render is not enough, and the reason A2 renders 40 views under different lights and keeps only what they agree on. A2 uses three grey light directions plus a photo like variant.

Variants that matter here

Depth buffer lift

What A1 and A2 do. One render, one depth lookup per landmark. Exact for the render, fragile at grazing angles. A2 rejects any hit where the ray meets the surface at more than about \(78^\circ\) from the normal, a view cosine below 0.20.

Two views, one formula

Park et al. render each surface at two angles \(40^\circ\) apart, detect in both, and solve for the 3D point from the two 2D positions. They prove the error grows like one over the angle gap.

Many rays, consensus

Paulsen et al. render 100 views and turn every detection into a ray. The landmark is the point closest to all the good rays, found by least squares inside RANSAC, then snapped to the surface.

Dense lift

FoundPose lifts the centre of every matched image patch through the rendered depth. Our B3 does the same with DINOv2 patches, and B4 lifts optical flow vectors.

Where it shows up

A1 is the plain version. One frontal render, one detection, one lift, then PnP on the 22 rigid landmarks. It fits the photo to 5.30 px and scores 25.18 dB on the cross view test, the weakest of the methods that hold together on all three photos. Its rendered outline bulges outside the cheeks, the failure Cybermed reported. A2 repeats the lift over 40 renders and keeps a consensus. A5, A6 and A7 reuse those 3D points. B3 lifts 180 to 260 patch matches per round through the render depth.

Watch out

Check whether a depth map holds z depth or ray length. Feeding ray length into the z formula pushes edge points too far.

A landmark whose pixel has no surface behind it lifts to infinity. Our forehead landmark 10 did, because the scan was cut off above it. Drop such points.

The CT isosurface also contains the nasal cavity, sinuses and airway as separate inner shells. A camera outside never sees them, but a ray cast from inside the head would hit them. Keep the largest connected piece of the mesh, the biggest set of triangles joined by shared edges.

Near the silhouette a fraction of a pixel moves the depth by millimetres. Treat grazing hits as unreliable.

Open3D's ready made pinhole ray helper produced vertically flipped images for us. Build rays by hand from the same \(K\) you use to project.

Remember

A render gives a picture and a depth map. The picture feeds the detector, and the depth map lifts its answers.

Back projection is \(X = R^{\top}(z\,K^{-1}(u, v, 1)^{\top} - t)\).

The CT has no colour, so the render is shaded, and changing only the light moved our landmarks by 1 to 2 mm.

About 35 minutes

Building block K4Used in all 15 methods

PnP: camera from point pairs

You know where some points are in 3D and where they appear in the photo. PnP finds the camera that took the photo. It is the last step of every method we built.

The short version
  • A pair is a 3D point on the CT plus the pixel where that spot shows up in the photo.
  • PnP searches for the camera that makes every 3D point land on its own pixel.
  • The leftover gap per point is the reprojection error. Their RMS is our "fit px".
  • A fast linear method gives a first camera. A step by step optimiser then shrinks the gaps, with the focal length as an extra unknown.
  • A frontal face pins the focal length down badly. Two cameras with focal lengths a factor of two apart can fit equally well.

Read first Cameras and projection. Helpful Least squares.

Why you need it

Every one of our 15 methods produces pairs. A pair is a 3D point on the CT surface and the pixel where that same spot appears in the photo. A1 gets 22 pairs from landmarks, the named face points such as the nose tip that MediaPipe finds. B3 gets a few hundred pairs from image patches. The methods differ only in how they find pairs. The camera solve is the same for all of them.

PnP stands for Perspective n Point. Given \(n\) points with known 3D positions and known pixels, find the camera. Here the camera is seven numbers from the camera page. Three describe the rotation \(R\), which way the camera points. Three describe the translation \(t\), where the camera sits. The last is the focal length \(f\), how much the lens zooms.

The problem, by hand

Pick any camera. Push each 3D landmark through it and you get a predicted pixel. Compare it with the pixel the detector found in the photo. The gap between them is the reprojection error of that point. A good camera makes all the gaps small at once. Try it yourself first.

You probably found that turn and side shift look alike, and so do distance and face size. The solver has the same trouble.

Reprojection error

This is the number every camera solve tries to make small.

\[ \hat u_i = \pi\big(K\,(R X_i + t)\big), \qquad e_i = \hat u_i - u_i, \qquad E(R, t, f) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert e_i \rVert^2 \]

In words, project each 3D point to a pixel, measure how far it lands from its photo pixel, square and add up.

X_i
the 3D point of pair \(i\), in millimetres in the CT frame
u_i
its pixel in the photo
K
the intrinsic matrix, which holds \(f\) and the image centre
π
the perspective division, \((a, b, w) \mapsto (a/w,\, b/w)\)
û_i
where the camera predicts the point should appear
e_i
the error vector, in pixels
E
the total squared error. The RMS (root mean square) error is \(\sqrt{E/n}\)

Worked example. Suppose a camera predicts the nose tip at \((752.1,\,640.0)\) and the detector found it at \((749.5,\,637.3)\). Then \(e = (2.6,\,2.7)\) and \(\lVert e \rVert = \sqrt{2.6^2 + 2.7^2} = 3.75\) px. Do this for all 22 landmarks, square, average and take the root. That is the "fit px" column of our results table.

How many points do you need?

Each pair gives two equations, one for \(u\) and one for \(v\). A camera with known focal length has six unknowns, so three pairs look like enough. But the equations are not linear, and three points allow up to four cameras that fit exactly. This is the classic P3P problem. A fourth point picks the right one.

With the focal unknown you need at least four points, and the linear method below needs six. Every landmark is a few pixels off, so extra points help average the noise down. We use 22.

The direct linear transform

A solver needs a starting camera. The DLT gives one without any guess. It makes the problem linear by forgetting, for a moment, that \(R\) is a rotation. Combine everything into one 3 by 4 matrix \(P = K\,[R \mid t]\) with 12 entries. A point projects as \(u \simeq P X\), where \(\simeq\) means equal up to the scale that the division removes.

Two linear equations per pair

Write the rows of \(P\) as \(p_1^{\top}, p_2^{\top}, p_3^{\top}\). Projection says \(u = p_1^{\top}X / p_3^{\top}X\) and \(v = p_2^{\top}X / p_3^{\top}X\). Multiply out the fractions.

\[ p_1^{\top}X - u\,p_3^{\top}X = 0, \qquad p_2^{\top}X - v\,p_3^{\top}X = 0 \]

In words, each pair says "this 3D point must land on this pixel", written so that the unknowns appear without any division.

Both equations are linear in the 12 unknown entries of \(P\). Stack them for all \(n\) pairs into one tall matrix \(A\), with \(2n\) rows and 12 columns.

\[ A\,p = 0, \qquad \min_{\lVert p \rVert = 1} \lVert A\,p \rVert \]

In words, find the 12 numbers that break all the equations as little as possible, without letting them all shrink to zero.

p
the 12 entries of \(P\) written as one column
A
known numbers, built from the \(X_i\) and \(u_i\)
‖p‖ = 1
rules out the useless answer \(p = 0\). Any scale of \(P\) is the same camera

With perfect data some \(p\) gives exactly zero. With noisy data we take the \(p\) that \(A\) shrinks the most. The singular value decomposition (SVD) finds it. When \(K\) is known, you first turn pixels into normalised coordinates with \(K^{-1}\). The left 3 by 3 block of the answer is then a rotation times a scale. You snap it to the nearest true rotation and read off \(t\).

The DLT is quick and needs no starting guess. Its weakness is that \(\lVert A p \rVert\) is not a distance in pixels. So the DLT is only a starting point, and a nonlinear solve finishes the job.

EPnP in plain words

The first solve in our chain is OpenCV's EPnP, short for efficient PnP. It needs only four points and stays fast with many. It describes every 3D point as a weighted mix of four control points, \(X_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} c_j\), with weights that add up to 1. These are like the barycentric weights on the back projection page, one dimension up. Moving and turning the cloud does not change the weights.

So the unknowns are only the four control points in camera coordinates, 12 numbers. Each pair gives two linear equations in them. Solve, and every landmark is known in camera coordinates. A Procrustes alignment to the CT landmarks then gives \(R\) and \(t\).

Refining with nonlinear least squares

This step gets the error down to the noise level. We minimise the reprojection error \(E\) directly over the camera's own parameters. Rotation needs care. A 3 by 3 matrix has nine numbers but only three degrees of freedom. We write it as a rotation vector. Its direction is the axis to turn about and its length is the angle in radians.

Then the parameters are six numbers, or seven with \(\log f\). The least squares page explains the solvers. In short, Levenberg Marquardt (LM) asks how each error arrow would change if the camera moved a little. It takes the small step that shrinks the arrows most, keeps it if the error drops, and repeats.

Rotation vectors

A rotation vector \(\omega\) has length \(\theta = \lVert \omega \rVert\), the angle, and direction \(k = \omega / \theta\), the axis. The Rodrigues formula turns it into a matrix.

\[ R = I + \sin\theta\,[k]_\times + (1 - \cos\theta)\,[k]_\times^2, \qquad [k]_\times = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -k_3 & k_2 \\ k_3 & 0 & -k_1 \\ -k_2 & k_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \]

In words, three numbers that say "turn this far about this axis" become the 3 by 3 matrix that does that turn.

ω
three numbers, the rotation the solver adjusts
[k]×
the matrix that computes a cross product, \([k]_\times v = k \times v\)
I
the identity matrix

Worked example. Take \(\omega = (0, 0, \pi/2)\), a quarter turn about the \(z\) axis. Then \(\sin\theta = 1\) and \(\cos\theta = 0\). The formula gives \(R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), which sends \((1, 0, 0)\) to \((0, 1, 0)\). That is the quarter turn you expect.

Why not three Euler angles? At some poses two of them turn about the same axis, and a small step can mean a huge turn or none. A rotation vector avoids this near our rotations. OpenCV calls it rvec.

Estimating the focal length too

Our photos have no EXIF data, the camera settings saved in the file. So \(f\) is unknown and becomes a seventh parameter. We optimise \(\log f\) rather than \(f\). A step in \(\log f\) is a percentage change, so the same step size makes sense at 3000 px and at 9000 px.

The trouble is that a frontal face barely constrains \(f\). Zoom in and step back and almost every landmark stays put, as the dolly zoom showed. The only signal is the face's own depth, mainly the nose against the cheeks, and a few pixels of noise drown it. The fit error as a function of \(f\) has a long flat bottom, which we call the plateau.

The research notes put a rough number on it. With \(N\) landmarks and pixel noise \(\sigma\), the relative uncertainty of the focal length is about

\[ \frac{\sigma_f}{f} \;\approx\; \frac{\sigma}{\operatorname{rms}_i\!\big(u_i\,d_i / Z\big)\,\sqrt{N}} \]

In words, the focal is uncertain when the noise is large compared with how much the face's depth bends the image. More points help only by the square root of their number.

σ_f / f
the focal's uncertainty as a fraction of the focal
u_i
landmark \(i\)'s distance from the image centre, in pixels
d_i
its depth in front of or behind the face plane
Z
the camera distance

A test on the real CT mesh used 60 points with \(\operatorname{rms}(u\,d/Z)\) of about 1.1 px. One pixel of noise then gives about 12 percent uncertainty in \(f\), and three pixels about 35 percent. MediaPipe landmarks are 2 to 5 px off, and the CT side adds a systematic error on top. So expect the face alone to leave the focal uncertain by a factor of 1.5 to 2 either way.

On clean synthetic data a second view helps. Our real photos did not behave that way. A6 solved the three photos jointly with one shared focal. Its plateau came out wider than the front photo's alone, a factor of 5.85 against 3.69. The photos disagreed about which way the focal should move, so pooling them flattened the curve. The camera page shows the measured curves.

Our camera solve, step by step

All 15 methods end in the same chain of three solves, built on OpenCV and SciPy. The numbers in brackets are our settings.

  1. RANSAC with EPnP

    cv2.solvePnPRansac at a starting focal of 5000 px. It tries many small random subsets and keeps the camera most pairs agree with (12 px threshold, 2000 iterations, 0.999 confidence). Pairs that agree are inliers. The rest are outliers and get dropped. See RANSAC.

  2. Levenberg Marquardt on the inliers

    cv2.solvePnPRefineLM polishes the six pose numbers at the same focal.

  3. Huber least squares with the focal free

    scipy.optimize.least_squares over the rotation vector, \(t\) and \(\log f\). The Huber loss trusts errors beyond 4 px less. The principal point stays at the image centre, and \(f\) is bounded to 2000 to 12000 px. Each pair can carry a weight.

  4. Report

    The camera, the RMS error over the inliers, the focal, and a focal sweep that measures the plateau.

In our project

On the front photo A1 went through exactly this chain. It started with 22 pairs, and RANSAC kept 19 as inliers. The RMS error was 5.66 px after RANSAC, 5.61 px after the LM polish and 5.30 px after the Huber solve with a free focal. The focal settled at 8348 px with the camera about 2057 mm from the landmarks. Pairs carry group weights by default, 1.0 for nose and eye corners, 0.7 for cheekbones and chin, and 0.3 for the jaw, because the jaw points slide.

Variants that matter here

P3P and AP3P

Exactly four points, three to solve and one to pick. Ideal inside RANSAC.

EPnP

Four or more points, fast with many. Our first solve, inside RANSAC.

SQPnP

Three or more points and globally optimal. A good default for tens of noisy points.

Iterative LM

Starts from a DLT, then minimises pixels. Our second step.

With the focal

OpenCV's PnP assumes \(K\) is known. Freeing \(f\) needs your own least squares, as in our third step.

Several photos at once

A6 solves three poses and one shared focal together. See the joint solve.

Where it shows up

Every row of our results table is a PnP solve. The table gives the front photo fit and the focal each method settled on. Fit px rewards agreeing with MediaPipe, not being right. C3 and C4 fit their own matches, so their fit is not comparable.

MethodFit pxFit mmFocal pxWhere the pairs come from
A15.301.478348one render's landmarks
A26.431.395581consensus of 40 renders
A36.021.937298canonical face bent onto the CT
A46.731.474201geometric features of the CT
A55.911.464147fusion of A1, A2 and A4, weighted

Look at A1 and A6. Their fit errors differ by 0.05 px, while their focal lengths differ by a factor of two. That is the plateau at work. A5's leave one out test showed the same thing. Removing either jaw point 172 or 136 collapsed its focal from 4147 px to about 2350 px.

Watch out

Row \(i\) of the 3D and 2D arrays must be the same landmark. A wrong order gives a confident wrong camera and no error.

A tiny fit error does not mean a right camera. Check something the fit did not use, such as the face outline.

Watch for a focal sitting on its bound. Our code warns when it lands on 2000 or 12000 px, because then the bound set the value, not the data.

Faces are nearly symmetric. A mirrored or left right swapped set of pairs can still fit well. Check the handedness.

Units decide the translation. Feed centimetres instead of millimetres and every distance is ten times smaller, while the fit error stays the same.

Remember

PnP finds the camera that makes the 3D points land on their pixels, by minimising the reprojection error.

Linear methods like DLT and EPnP give a start. Levenberg Marquardt on pixels finishes, with \(\log f\) as a seventh parameter.

A frontal face constrains the focal badly, so equal fit errors can hide focal lengths a factor of two apart.

About 20 minutes

Building block K5Used in A1 to A7, A2's consensus, B3, Paulsen, FoundPose

RANSAC

Some of your point pairs are simply wrong. RANSAC finds the model that most pairs agree with, by fitting many tiny random subsets and counting votes. Then it fits properly on the pairs that voted yes.

The short version
  • Some pairs are plain wrong. These outliers pull a normal fit toward them.
  • RANSAC fits a model to a tiny random handful of pairs and counts how many pairs agree. It repeats, keeps the biggest crowd, and refits on it.
  • The number of tries grows fast with the share of outliers and the handful size.
  • Every one of our camera solves starts with RANSAC at a 12 px threshold.

Read first PnP. Helpful Least squares.

Why you need it

Our pairs come from detectors, and detectors make mistakes. A landmark can land on the wrong side of the nose. A jaw point can slide along the outline. In B3, which matches image patches between the photo and a CT render, a left cheek patch can match a right cheek patch. Such a pair is an outlier. It is not a bit off. It is wrong.

A plain least squares fit squares every error. One pair 50 px off counts as much as a hundred pairs 5 px off, so the fit bends toward it and spoils the good pairs. RANSAC, short for random sample consensus (Fischler and Bolles), removes outliers before the real fit.

The idea, on a line

Fit a line through 2D points where a third are junk. A line needs only two points. So pick two at random, draw the line, and count how many points lie close to it. Do that many times. A line through two good points collects a big crowd. A line through a junk point collects almost nobody. Keep the line with the biggest crowd. Then forget that line and fit a proper least squares line through its crowd.

  1. Sample

    Pick a minimal set at random. It is the smallest number of pairs that fixes the model. Two points for a line. Four pairs for the EPnP or P3P camera solvers. Six for the DLT.

  2. Fit

    Solve the model exactly from the minimal set, which is cheap.

  3. Score

    Measure every pair's error under that model. Pairs below the inlier threshold \(\tau\) are inliers. Count them.

  4. Repeat

    Do this \(N\) times and remember the model with the most inliers.

  5. Refit

    Fit the model properly on all inliers of the winner, then usually recount.

How many tries?

RANSAC only works if at least one sample is all good, so this decides how long it must run. Let \(w\) be the fraction of inliers and \(s\) the minimal set size. A random sample is all inliers with probability \(w^s\), and spoiled with probability \(1 - w^s\).

The iteration count

All \(N\) samples are contaminated with probability \((1 - w^s)^N\). You want that to be at most \(1 - p\), where \(p\) is the confidence you ask for. Take logs and solve for \(N\).

\[ (1 - w^s)^N \le 1 - p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log(1 - w^s)} \]

In words, draw enough samples that the chance of every single one being spoiled drops below the risk you accept.

p
the chance you want that at least one sample is clean, for example 0.99
w
the inlier fraction. 1 minus the outlier ratio
s
the minimal set size
N
the number of samples to draw, rounded up

Worked example. Half the pairs are outliers, so \(w = 0.5\). Use a four point solver, \(s = 4\), and ask for \(p = 0.99\). Then \(w^s = 0.0625\) and

\[ N = \frac{\log 0.01}{\log 0.9375} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.0645} = 71.4 \;\Rightarrow\; 72 \text{ samples.} \]

In words, 72 random handfuls of four give a 99 percent chance that at least one handful is clean.

Our case. A1 kept 19 of 22 pairs as inliers, so \(w = 19/22 = 0.864\). With \(s = 4\) and \(p = 0.999\), \(w^s = 0.556\) and \(N = \log 0.001 / \log 0.444 = 8.5\), so 9 samples would do. We ran 2000. That costs almost nothing for 22 pairs, and it protects the dense methods, which have far more outliers.

More outliers or a bigger minimal set both make \(w^s\) tiny and \(N\) huge. That is why RANSAC uses the smallest solver it can.

The inlier threshold

The threshold \(\tau\) decides how far off a pair may be and still vote, so a bad choice breaks RANSAC quietly. Too small, and good pairs with ordinary noise get thrown out. Too large, and outliers sneak in. A common rule is two or three times the typical error of a good pair.

Our camera solve uses \(\tau = 12\) px on a 1500 px wide photo. MediaPipe landmarks on our photo are off by 2 to 5 px, and the CT side landmarks add their own error, so 12 px keeps honest pairs and rejects gross mistakes. FoundPose uses 10 px.

RANSAC for PnP

Inside our camera solve, the model is the camera and the error is the reprojection error. Each sample of 3D to 2D pairs proposes a full camera. Below, five of our 22 synthetic pairs are wrong. Both inner eye corners are swapped left for right, two jaw points have slid, and one cheekbone is misplaced.

Notice what RANSAC cannot do. If several pairs are wrong in the same way, they agree with each other. Sliding jaw points all slide in a similar direction. RANSAC finds consensus, not truth.

Variants that matter here

A2 uses a RANSAC style consensus for each landmark, but without randomness. Each landmark is detected on 40 renders and lifted to 3D, which gives up to 40 candidate points. Every candidate is tried as the centre of a 3 mm ball, and the ball with the most members wins. With a few dozen candidates this exhaustive search is cheap and removes the luck.

The centre is then moved to the geometric median of the members. That is the point with the smallest summed distance to them, and unlike the average it ignores a few far points. Membership is refreshed and the median recomputed, up to three times. A landmark with fewer than 8 members out of 40 is dropped. The median distance of the members from the centre becomes that landmark's spread.

Paulsen et al.

Each landmark becomes up to 100 rays, one per rendered view. A RANSAC try fits a point to three random rays and scores the sum of squared ray distances. The final point is the least squares point of the inlier rays, snapped to the surface.

FoundPose

EPnP on minimal sets of 4 correspondences, up to 400 iterations, inlier threshold 10 px. The pose with the most inliers wins and is then refined.

Our dense methods

B3 matches 180 to 260 patches per round and runs RANSAC PnP on them. Its inlier residual is 4.6 px, about a third of a patch.

Trimming instead

A6's joint solve runs no RANSAC of its own. It reuses A5's inliers, solves with a Huber loss, drops pairs beyond 12 px, and solves once more. Huber counts large errors less, so it shrinks an outlier's pull but never to zero.

Where it shows up

Every method's camera solve starts with cv2.solvePnPRansac using EPnP, a 12 px threshold, 2000 iterations and a confidence of 0.999, at a starting focal of 5000 px. On the front photo A1 kept 19 of its 22 pairs. Two more ideas from this page live elsewhere in the pipeline. A2's ball consensus drops the sliding jaw points by itself, and A5 builds its per landmark weights partly from A2's spread.

Watch out

The threshold is in pixels, so it depends on image size. 12 px on a 1500 px photo is not 12 px on a 4000 px original.

A minimal set can be degenerate, for example six DLT points almost on one plane. It gives a wild model, so real code checks for it.

RANSAC runs at a fixed focal in our chain. A focal far off the truth pushes good pairs outside the threshold. Our 5000 px start sits near the middle of the plausible range.

It is random. Two runs can keep slightly different inliers. Fix the seed when you compare methods.

Remember

Fit tiny random minimal sets, count who agrees within a threshold, keep the biggest crowd, refit on it.

The number of tries is \(N = \log(1 - p) / \log(1 - w^s)\). It explodes with the outlier ratio and the set size.

RANSAC finds the largest consistent group, which is not always the truth.

About 40 minutes

Building block K6Used in all 15 methods, A5, A6, ICP, Procrustes, Park, Paulsen, FoundPose

Least squares and robust fitting

Most fitting problems in this project have more equations than unknowns and no exact answer. Least squares picks the answer whose errors, squared and added up, are smallest. This page goes from a straight line to our joint camera solve, and shows how to stop bad points from ruining it.

The short version
  • A residual is how far the model misses one measurement. Least squares minimises the sum of squared residuals.
  • For a line that is one small matrix solve. For a camera you improve a guess step by step, with Levenberg Marquardt.
  • Squares let one wild point drag the fit. The Huber loss counts big misses less, and weights say whom to trust.
  • Our A6 puts three photos into one solve with a single shared focal length.

Read first PnP. Helpful focal and distance tradeoff.

Why you need it

Our camera solve has seven unknowns (turn, position and focal length) and 22 landmark pairs. Each pair gives two equations, 44 in all. Noise means no camera satisfies all 44, and least squares is the rule for the best compromise. The same rule sits inside ICP (sliding one surface onto another), Procrustes alignment (lining up two point sets), Paulsen's ray intersection, Park's rigid fit and FoundPose's refinement. A6 is one least squares problem with 19 unknowns.

Fitting a line, from scratch

A line shows every idea of this page in the smallest problem. Start with points \((x_i, y_i)\) and a line \(y = a x + b\). For each point the residual is how far the line misses it vertically, \(r_i = a x_i + b - y_i\). We square the residuals, so signs cannot cancel, and add them up. That sum is the cost.

The sum of squares

\[ E(a, b) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a x_i + b - y_i)^2 \]

In words, the cost of a line is the total area of the squares built on its misses.

a, b
the unknowns, slope and intercept
r_i
the residual of point \(i\)
E
the cost. Least squares means the \(a, b\) that make \(E\) smallest

The normal equations

At the lowest point of \(E\), the slope of \(E\) is zero in every direction. So set both partial derivatives to zero.

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial a} = 2\sum_i x_i\,(a x_i + b - y_i) = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial E}{\partial b} = 2\sum_i (a x_i + b - y_i) = 0 \]

In words, nudging the slope or the intercept a little must not lower the cost any more. Both equations are linear in \(a\) and \(b\). Rearranged they are the normal equations.

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum x_i^2 & \sum x_i \\ \sum x_i & n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum x_i y_i \\ \sum y_i \end{pmatrix} \]

In words, two equations in two unknowns, built from five sums over the data.

In matrix form, stack one row \((x_i, 1)\) per point into \(A\), the unknowns into \(\theta = (a, b)\) and the targets into \(y\). The residuals are \(r = A\theta - y\) and the normal equations become

\[ A^{\top}A\,\theta = A^{\top}y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta = (A^{\top}A)^{-1}A^{\top}y \]

In words, squash the tall system of all measurements into a small square one, one row per unknown, and solve that.

A
the design matrix, one row per measurement and one column per unknown
AᵀA
a small square matrix, unknowns by unknowns
θ
the best fit unknowns

Worked example. Four points \((0,1), (1,2), (2,2), (3,4)\). Then \(n = 4\), \(\sum x = 6\), \(\sum x^2 = 14\), \(\sum y = 9\) and \(\sum xy = 18\).

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 14 & 6 \\ 6 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; a = \frac{18 \cdot 4 - 6 \cdot 9}{14 \cdot 4 - 6 \cdot 6} = 0.9, \quad b = \frac{14 \cdot 9 - 6 \cdot 18}{20} = 0.9 \]

The residuals are \(-0.1, -0.2, 0.7, -0.4\). They add up to zero, which the second normal equation guarantees. The cost is \(E = 0.01 + 0.04 + 0.49 + 0.16 = 0.70\). No other line does better.

Why squares?

This tells you when least squares is the right tool. Suppose each measurement has noise from a bell curve, a Gaussian, with spread \(\sigma\). The chance of residual \(r_i\) is proportional to \(e^{-r_i^2 / 2\sigma^2}\). The log of the chance of all of them is \(-\sum_i r_i^2 / 2\sigma^2\). So the most likely parameters are exactly the ones with the smallest \(\sum_i r_i^2\).

So least squares is the best guess when the noise is Gaussian and nothing else goes wrong. A landmark on the wrong side of the nose breaks that, and the Huber loss below exists for that case.

Nonlinear least squares

Our camera solve is nonlinear, so this is the part you need for it. The projection divides by depth and rotates by sines and cosines. So the residuals \(r(\theta)\) are curved functions of the camera parameters \(\theta\), and there is no formula for the minimum. You improve a guess step by step.

The trick is to pretend, near the current guess, that the problem is linear. The Jacobian \(J\) is the matrix of first derivatives. Entry \(J_{ij}\) says how much residual \(i\) changes when parameter \(j\) moves a little. For a small step \(\delta\),

Three ways to take a step

\[ r(\theta + \delta) \approx r(\theta) + J\,\delta \]

In words, near the current guess each residual changes in a straight line with a small step.

Gauss Newton minimises this linear model exactly. That is a normal equation again, with \(J\) in place of \(A\).

\[ J^{\top}J\,\delta = -J^{\top}r \]

In words, take the step that would be best if the straight line picture were exact.

Gradient descent just walks downhill. The gradient of \(\tfrac12\lVert r \rVert^2\) is \(J^{\top}r\), so

\[ \delta = -\alpha\,J^{\top}r \]

In words, take a small step in the direction that lowers the cost fastest.

Levenberg Marquardt blends the two with a damping number \(\lambda\).

\[ (J^{\top}J + \lambda\,\mathrm{diag}(J^{\top}J))\,\delta = -J^{\top}r \]

In words, a Gauss Newton step with a brake. The bigger \(\lambda\), the shorter and more cautious the step.

J
the Jacobian, residuals by parameters. With 22 pairs and a free focal it is 44 by 7
α
a step size for gradient descent
λ
the damping. Small λ gives the Gauss Newton step. Large λ gives a short step along the gradient

Levenberg Marquardt adapts \(\lambda\) as it goes. If a step lowers the cost, it keeps it and shrinks \(\lambda\). If the cost rises, it rejects the step and grows \(\lambda\). Gauss Newton alone can overshoot far from the answer. Gradient descent alone crawls along narrow valleys.

Gauss Newton on one unknown

Take a single residual \(r(\theta) = \theta^2 - 2\). Its zero is \(\sqrt 2\). The Jacobian is \(J = 2\theta\), and with one unknown the Gauss Newton step is \(\delta = -r/J\).

\[ \theta_0 = 1:\; r = -1,\; J = 2,\; \delta = 0.5 \qquad \theta_1 = 1.5:\; r = 0.25,\; J = 3,\; \delta = -0.0833 \] \[ \theta_2 = 1.4167:\; r = 0.0069,\; J = 2.833,\; \delta = -0.0025 \qquad \theta_3 = 1.41422 \]

The true value is 1.41421. The number of correct digits roughly doubles at every step. That is the speed Gauss Newton has near the answer.

That narrow valley is the plateau from the camera page, seen from above. Gradient descent only sees the steep direction across it, so it bounces between the walls. Gauss Newton uses the curvature in \(J^{\top}J\) and steps along the floor.

You can measure how narrow a valley is. The eigenvectors of \(J^{\top}J\) are special directions, and each eigenvalue is the cost's curvature along its direction. Near the minimum of Figure 2 the largest is about 7000 times the smallest. The flat direction is the focal and distance trade. Along it the data barely determine the answer, however well the solver converges.

Why squared error is ruined by outliers

This is the main weakness of least squares, and our detectors trigger it. An outlier is a measurement that is plain wrong, not just noisy. A residual of 2 px contributes 4. A residual of 50 px contributes 2500, as much as 625 points that are 2 px off. One wrong pair drags the whole fit toward itself.

The Huber loss and its weight

Replace the square \(r^2\) by a function \(\rho(r)\) that is a square near zero and a straight line far out. With a transition point \(\delta\), the Huber loss is

\[ \rho(r) = \begin{cases} \tfrac12 r^2 & |r| \le \delta \\ \delta\,(|r| - \tfrac12\delta) & |r| > \delta \end{cases} \qquad w(r) = \frac{\rho'(r)}{r} = \begin{cases} 1 & |r| \le \delta \\ \delta / |r| & |r| > \delta \end{cases} \]
δ
the transition point. Our camera solve uses 4 px
ρ
the loss of one residual
w
the weight that residual effectively gets in a weighted least squares

In words, small misses cost their square as before, while big misses cost only in proportion to their size. Equivalently, a residual beyond \(\delta\) gets its weight cut to \(\delta / |r|\), so its pull stays bounded. One way to solve it is iteratively reweighted least squares. Compute weights from the current residuals, solve a weighted least squares, and repeat.

Worked example. With \(\delta = 4\) px, a residual of 12 px gets weight \(4/12 = 0.33\). Its loss is \(4 \cdot (12 - 2) = 40\) instead of \(\tfrac12 \cdot 144 = 72\). A residual of 3 px keeps weight 1 and loss \(4.5\).

Huber never sets a weight to zero, so a very wrong pair still pulls a little. That is why RANSAC runs before the Huber solve, and why the joint solve trims pairs beyond 12 px and solves again.

Weighted least squares

Weights let you say in advance which points to trust, and A5 depends on them. Give each residual a weight \(w_i\) and minimise \(\sum_i w_i\,r_i^2\). The normal equations become \(A^{\top}WA\,\theta = A^{\top}Wy\), with the weights on the diagonal of \(W\). If each measurement has Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma_i\), the statistically best choice is \(w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2\). So a point twice as noisy counts a quarter as much.

In our project

A5 gives each landmark a sigma, its expected error, from two sources added in quadrature, \(\sigma^2 = \sigma_{A2}^2 + \sigma_{\text{methods}}^2\). The first is A2's scatter across 40 renders. The second is how far A1, A2 and A4 disagree about that landmark.

The weight is \(1/\sigma\), with sigma clipped to 0.5 to 20 mm so that no landmark dominates and none vanishes. It is multiplied by the group weight (nose and eye corners 1.0, cheekbones and chin 0.7, jaw 0.3) and scaled so the mean weight is 1. Keeping the mean at 1 keeps the weighted RMS comparable across methods. \(1/\sigma\) is gentler than the textbook \(1/\sigma^2\), because the sigmas are rough estimates.

The joint solve of A6

A5 solved each of the three photos on its own. The focal lengths came out at 4147, 7811 and 2792 px, a factor of 2.8 apart, although one camera took all three. The three camera to face distances disagreed by 1282 mm. That cannot be right, because the subject turned her head and the camera stayed put.

A6 fixes the model, not the data. It puts all three photos into one least squares problem. Each photo keeps its own pose, six numbers each, and all three share one focal. That makes 19 unknowns.

One focal for three photos

\[ \theta = \big(\,\omega_{\text{front}},\, t_{\text{front}},\; \omega_{\text{left}},\, t_{\text{left}},\; \omega_{\text{right}},\, t_{\text{right}},\; \log f\,\big) \] \[ r(\theta) = \Big(\, \sqrt{w_{ki}}\,\big(\pi(K_f\,(R_k X_{ki} + t_k)) - u_{ki}\big) \text{ for every photo } k \text{ and pair } i, \;\; \sqrt{\lambda_p}\,\frac{\log f - \log \mu}{\sigma_{\log}} \,\Big) \] \[ \min_{\theta}\; \sum_j \rho\big(r_j(\theta)\big) \]

In words, the unknowns are three poses and one focal. The residuals are every pixel error from every photo, each scaled by its trust, plus one gentle pull toward a typical focal. Minimise the Huber cost of all of them at once.

ω_k, t_k
the rotation vector and translation of photo \(k\)
log f
the shared focal, on a log scale, inside every \(K_f\)
w_ki
A5's per landmark weights. Each pair contributes two entries, one for \(u\) and one for \(v\)
ρ
the Huber loss at 4 px, which SciPy applies to every entry of \(r\)
μ, σ_log
a weak prior on the focal, a mild preference before seeing the data. μ = 4291 px is the median of the six learned estimates from GeoCalib and Depth Pro, two networks that guess the focal from a single image. σ_log = 0.45 is GeoCalib's typical uncertainty as a fraction
λ_p
the prior's weight, 1, so it counts like one extra measurement

The Jacobian has a block structure. Each photo's rows touch only its own pose columns and the focal column. That shared column is the only thing tying the three photos together.

On the same pairs and weights, the shared focal is 4050 px. The front photo fit improves from 5.91 to 5.25 px. The left and right fits get slightly worse, 6.98 to 7.40 px and 6.45 to 6.66 px. That is the honest cost of forcing one focal. The camera distance spread shrinks to 146 mm.

The prior turned out to be inert. Without it the solve lands at 4046 px, with it 4050 px, and at ten times the weight 4082 px. Started at 8000 px it still converges to 4050 px. Leaving one photo out gives 4046, 3617 and 4578 px.

Variants that matter here

Closed form

The best rotation between two point sets has a closed form through the SVD. See Procrustes.

Alternating

ICP alternates between choosing pairs and a closed form least squares fit on them.

Trust region with bounds

Our third camera step uses SciPy's least_squares with the trust region reflective method, a cousin of Levenberg Marquardt. It handles the focal bounds of 2000 to 12000 px.

Other robust losses

Cauchy bends down harder than Huber, and soft L1 is a smooth Huber. We stayed with Huber.

Where it shows up

Every camera in the comparison table comes out of a Huber least squares over the rotation vector, the translation and \(\log f\), with a 4 px transition. A5 adds the sigma weights. A6 and A7 run the joint version. A7 then holds A6's 4050 px fixed while B3's dense refinement moves the poses. Zoom and distance can mimic each other, and fixing one keeps the refinement from wandering along the valley of Figure 2.

Outside the camera solve, least squares is the inner step of A3's ICP stages, the ray intersection of Paulsen et al., the rigid fit of Park et al. and the up to 30 Levenberg Marquardt steps of FoundPose's featuremetric refinement.

Watch out

A least squares minimum is only as good as its model. Three photos forced to one focal fit worse individually, and that is correct.

Scale your parameters. A step of 1 means a lot in radians and nothing in millimetres. Optimising \(\log f\) helps.

Nonlinear least squares finds a nearby minimum, not the best one. Start close, which is what RANSAC and EPnP are for.

A flat valley means the data do not determine the answer along it. A converged solver does not make the focal known.

Remember

Least squares minimises the sum of squared residuals. For linear models that is one solve of the normal equations.

For a camera, linearise with the Jacobian and step. Levenberg Marquardt blends Gauss Newton with gradient descent through a damping \(\lambda\).

Huber weights bound the pull of outliers, weights encode trust, and A6 shares one focal across three photos in a single 19 unknown solve.

About 30 minutes

Building block K7Used in Park A3 C1 C2 C3 C4

Aligning point sets: Procrustes

You have the same landmarks measured twice, in two different coordinate frames. Procrustes finds the one rotation, translation and (if you allow it) scale that lays the first set on top of the second. It has an exact answer, and that answer comes out of a single SVD.

The short version
  • You have the same points twice, in two frames, and you know which point matches which.
  • Put the two middles together first. That settles the shift.
  • One 3 by 3 matrix built from the pairs, split by the SVD, gives the best rotation. One ratio gives the scale.
  • Always block mirror images, or the face can come out flipped left for right.
  • We use it to place the template face (A3) and photo reconstructions (C1 to C4) on the CT.

Helpful Least squares. Next ICP uses this as its inner step.

Why you need it

Many steps in our project start with two lists of points that should be the same points, in two frames. For example, the MediaPipe canonical face has a nose tip at vertex 4, and so does the CT. The canonical face is in centimetres at the origin. The CT is in millimetres, in the scanner frame, somewhere else entirely. First you must move one set onto the other.

This is the orthogonal Procrustes problem. With scale allowed the answer is called the Umeyama solution, and with scale fixed the Kabsch solution. They are the same recipe with one line switched on or off. Here is where it shows up for us.

  • A3 places the canonical face template on the CT with a similarity Procrustes fit on the rigid landmarks. This puts a 15 cm template on a real head of unknown size.
  • C1 to C4 rebuild a face from the photos, with unknown size and pose. A similarity Procrustes fit on landmark pairs first brings it near the CT.
  • Park et al. register a face scan to a CBCT by a rigid least squares fit on three or more landmark pairs, then polish with ICP.
  • Inside every round of ICP, the "solve" step is a Procrustes fit on the current pairs.

The intuition

Picture two transparent sheets, each with the same face drawn on it. One sheet is turned, shifted and printed a little smaller. Your job is to slide, turn and resize the second sheet until the dots line up.

You would put the middles together, then turn the sheet until the dots point the same way, then resize. That order is exactly the math.

Try it by hand below. The magenta lines join each pair of matching landmarks. Their root mean square (RMS) length is the error you are trying to shrink. Then press Solve to see the exact answer.

Step by step

  1. Pair the points

    Point \(p_i\) in the first set and \(q_i\) in the second must be the same anatomical spot. Procrustes never guesses pairs. Without pairs you need ICP.

  2. Centre both sets

    Subtract each set's mean (its centroid) from its points. Now both clouds sit around the origin and translation is out of the picture.

  3. Build the cross covariance matrix

    Multiply each centred pair together (a column times a row gives a 3 by 3 matrix) and add them up into one 3 by 3 matrix \(H\). It records how the directions in one set line up with the directions in the other.

  4. Take the SVD of \(H\) and read off the rotation

    The SVD splits \(H\) into rotate, stretch, rotate. The best rotation is built from the two rotation parts, with a fix that blocks mirrors.

  5. Read off the scale (similarity only)

    One division of two sums gives the scale.

  6. Put the translation back

    The translation is whatever moves the turned and scaled centroid onto the target centroid.

The math

Rigid and similarity transforms

First, the moves you are allowed to make. A rotation \(R\) is a 3 by 3 matrix that turns points about the origin. It keeps lengths and angles. Its columns are three unit vectors at right angles, so \(R^\top R = I\), and its determinant is \(+1\). With determinant \(-1\) it is a reflection instead, which turns a right hand into a left hand.

A rigid transform turns and shifts. It has 6 degrees of freedom (3 for the rotation, 3 for the shift). A similarity transform also scales by one number \(s\). It has 7 degrees of freedom.

\[ q \approx s\,R\,p + t \]

In words, turn each moving point, scale it, shift it, and it should land on its partner.

p
a point in the moving set, a column of 3 numbers
q
the matching point in the fixed set
R
a rotation matrix, 3 by 3
s
a single scale factor, fixed at 1 for a rigid fit
t
a translation, 3 numbers

Use rigid when both sets are in real units, such as a CT and a face scan in millimetres, as Park et al. do. Use similarity when one side has an unknown size, such as the canonical face or a reconstruction from photos.

What we minimise

This is a least squares problem.

\[ E(s,R,t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert s R p_i + t - q_i \rVert^2 \]

In words, add up the squared lengths of all the magenta lines in Figure 1. The best \(s, R, t\) make that total smallest.

Park et al. write the rigid version of exactly this equation, with \(J \ge 3\) landmark pairs. Three pairs that do not lie on one line are the minimum in 3D.

Step 1. Centring removes the translation

Take the derivative of \(E\) with respect to \(t\) and set it to zero. You get one line.

\[ t = \bar q - s R \bar p, \qquad \bar p = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i p_i, \quad \bar q = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i q_i \]

In words, the best translation always carries the moved centroid onto the target centroid. Put that back into \(E\) and the translation disappears. What is left only involves the centred points.

\[ p_i' = p_i - \bar p, \qquad q_i' = q_i - \bar q, \qquad E = \sum_i \lVert s R p_i' - q_i' \rVert^2 \]

In words, measure every point from its own set's middle, and the problem shrinks to turning and scaling only.

Step 2. The cross covariance matrix

Expand the square. The terms \(\lVert sRp_i'\rVert^2\) and \(\lVert q_i'\rVert^2\) do not depend on \(R\), because a rotation does not change length. Only the cross term depends on \(R\).

\[ E = s^2 \sum_i \lVert p_i'\rVert^2 + \sum_i \lVert q_i'\rVert^2 - 2s \sum_i q_i'^\top R\, p_i' \]

In words, the first two sums are fixed sizes of the two clouds. Only the last sum changes when you turn. So the best rotation makes \(\sum_i q_i'^\top R\, p_i'\) as large as possible. Each term is a dot product. It is large when the turned point \(R p_i'\) points the same way as its partner \(q_i'\). This sum can be written as a trace, using the cross covariance matrix \(H\).

\[ H = \sum_i p_i' \, q_i'^\top \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_i q_i'^\top R\, p_i' = \operatorname{tr}(R H) \]

In words, all you need from the 22 pairs is one 3 by 3 summary \(H\). The rotation that best agrees with \(H\) is the answer.

H
3 by 3. Entry \(H_{xy}\) adds up \(p'_x q'_y\) over all pairs. It says how much the x direction in one set moves together with the y direction in the other.
tr
the trace, the sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix

Step 3. SVD in plain words

The singular value decomposition says that any matrix \(A\) can be written as three simple moves done one after another.

\[ A = U \Sigma V^\top \]
V^T
a rotation (or rotation plus flip) that lines the input's special directions up with the axes
Σ
a diagonal matrix of singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3 \ge 0\) that stretches each axis
U
another rotation (or rotation plus flip) that turns the result into place

In words, every matrix is "rotate, stretch along the axes, rotate". A circle becomes an ellipse whose half axes have lengths \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) and point along the columns of \(U\). Figure 3 shows it.

Step 4. The Kabsch rotation

Take the SVD of the cross covariance, \(H = U\Sigma V^\top\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}(RH) = \operatorname{tr}(R U \Sigma V^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(V^\top R U\,\Sigma)\). The matrix \(M = V^\top R U\) is itself a rotation, so each diagonal entry of \(M\) is at most 1. The trace is \(\sum_k M_{kk}\sigma_k\), and that is largest when every \(M_{kk} = 1\), which means \(M = I\). Solve \(V^\top R U = I\) for \(R\).

\[ R = V U^\top \]

In words, undo the first turn of the SVD and apply the second turn, while ignoring the stretch.

There is one catch. \(V U^\top\) is always orthogonal, but its determinant can be \(-1\). Then it is a reflection, the mirror image of the face. This happens when one frame has a flipped axis, or when the points are nearly flat and noise tips the balance. The fix flips the axis with the smallest singular value, which costs the least.

\[ R = V\,D\,U^\top, \qquad D = \operatorname{diag}\big(1,\ 1,\ \det(V U^\top)\big) \]

In words, if the answer would be a mirror, flip its weakest axis back so it becomes a true rotation.

In 2D the same recipe collapses to one angle. With centred points, the best angle is

\[ \theta = \operatorname{atan2}\Big(\sum_i (p'_{ix} q'_{iy} - p'_{iy} q'_{ix}),\ \sum_i (p'_{ix} q'_{ix} + p'_{iy} q'_{iy})\Big) \]

In words, the top sum adds up cross products (how much each pair wants to turn). The bottom sum adds up dot products (how much they already agree).

Step 5. Umeyama's scale

With \(R\) fixed, \(E\) is a parabola in \(s\). Set its derivative to zero.

\[ s = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(D\Sigma)}{\sum_i \lVert p_i' \rVert^2} = \frac{\sum_i q_i'^\top R\,p_i'}{\sum_i \lVert p_i'\rVert^2} \]

In words, how far the target points reach along the turned source directions, divided by how far the source points reach. If the target is twice as big, every \(q_i'\) is about \(2Rp_i'\), and the ratio is 2.

Then the translation from step 1 finishes the job, \(t = \bar q - sR\bar p\).

A worked example in 2D

Three source points \(p_1 = (0,0)\), \(p_2 = (2,0)\), \(p_3 = (0,1)\). The target points are \(q_1 = (3,1)\), \(q_2 = (3,5)\), \(q_3 = (1,1)\). We secretly made them with a 90 degree turn, a scale of 2 and a shift of \((3,1)\). Let us recover that.

  1. Centroids. \(\bar p = (2/3,\ 1/3)\) and \(\bar q = (7/3,\ 7/3)\).
  2. Centred points. \(p' = (-2/3,-1/3),\ (4/3,-1/3),\ (-2/3,\ 2/3)\). \(q' = (2/3,-4/3),\ (2/3,\ 8/3),\ (-4/3,-4/3)\).
  3. Cross covariance. \(H_{xx} = 4/3\), \(H_{xy} = 16/3\), \(H_{yx} = -4/3\), \(H_{yy} = -4/3\).
  4. Angle. The cross sum is \(H_{xy} - H_{yx} = 20/3\). The dot sum is \(H_{xx} + H_{yy} = 0\). So \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(20/3,\ 0) = 90^\circ\).
  5. Scale. \(\sum \lVert p_i'\rVert^2 = 10/3\). The aligned dot sum is \(\sqrt{(20/3)^2 + 0^2} = 20/3\). So \(s = (20/3)/(10/3) = 2\).
  6. Translation. \(sR\bar p = 2\cdot(-1/3,\ 2/3) = (-2/3,\ 4/3)\). So \(t = (7/3 + 2/3,\ 7/3 - 4/3) = (3,\ 1)\).

All three hidden numbers come back exactly, because the data had no noise. With noise you get the least squares best guess and a residual that measures the noise.

Variants that matter here

Rigid or similarity

Allowing scale is not free. A free scale can soak up errors that have nothing to do with size. Our C1 notes record this.

The landmark Procrustes fit (13 pairs, 5.2 mm RMS residual on a face spanning about 120 mm) gives a scale good to a few percent. Every free scale that the later surface fitting produced was 6 to 13 percent smaller, and it made the camera two to three times worse. So C1 rejects a surface scale that differs from the landmark scale by more than 5 percent. The ICP page shows why surfaces tend to shrink.

Weighted Procrustes

Some landmarks are more trustworthy than others, and weights let the fit listen to them more. Use weighted centroids and \(H = \sum_i w_i p_i' q_i'^\top\), and everything else stays the same. MediaPipe's own pipeline does this. Its rigid basis gives the alar base (vertex 129) the largest weight, 0.121, and the nose tip (vertex 4) 0.071.

Outliers

This matters most for us because our CT landmarks include sliding points. Least squares listens to every pair equally, so one bad pair drags the whole answer. On CT renders the jaw and face outline landmarks slide 10 to 30 mm, because the outline of a surface is wherever it turns away from you, not a fixed spot on the skin. That is why A3 runs its Procrustes on the rigid subset only. Figure 6 lets you slide the jaw points and watch the fit tilt.

Where it shows up

Each row below starts with a Procrustes fit and then hands over to a surface method. NRICP is non rigid ICP, which bends the template instead of only moving it.

In code we call trimesh.registration.procrustes with reflection=False. Our tooling notes put the reason plainly. A reflection would silently mirror the face.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • Pairs must be right. Swap the left and right eye corners and Procrustes will happily turn the face to honour your mistake.
  • Never allow a reflection. A mirror fit can have a tiny residual and still be impossible. If the fixed fit has a large residual, check your axis conventions.
  • Units. The canonical face is in centimetres and the CT is in millimetres. A similarity fit absorbs that factor of 10 into \(s\). A rigid fit cannot, so convert first.
  • Scale is not symmetric. With noise, the scale from \(p\) to \(q\) is not exactly one over the reverse. Pick a direction.
  • Degenerate sets. Points on one line leave the turn about that line undefined. Nearly flat sets let a reflection sneak in.
Remember

Centre both sets, then the translation is just the difference of centroids.

The rotation is \(R = V D U^\top\) from the SVD of \(H = \sum p_i' q_i'^\top\), with \(D\) blocking mirrors.

Scale is one ratio, and you should only free it when one side truly has unknown size.

About 30 minutes

Building block K8Used in Park Amberg A3 A4 C1 C2 C3 C4

ICP: sliding surfaces together

Procrustes needs you to say which point matches which. Two surfaces never come with that list. Iterative Closest Point (ICP) guesses the pairs by taking the nearest point, solves the alignment for those guesses, and repeats. Each round the guesses get better and the surfaces slide into place.

The short version
  • Two surfaces have no list of matching points. ICP pairs every point with the nearest point on the other surface.
  • It fits the best rotation and shift to those guessed pairs, moves, and pairs again. The error never goes up.
  • It only finds the nearest answer, so it needs a good start from landmarks.
  • Point to plane ICP lets points slide along the surface and converges faster on smooth skin.
  • On faces, fit only the parts that do not change with expression, drop long pairs, and do not let the scale float freely.

Read first Procrustes. Helpful Least squares.

Why you need it

A CT skin surface has about 300,000 vertices. A face rebuilt from photos, or a template face, has different points in different places, with no named partners. Landmarks give a dozen rough pairs, enough for a first Procrustes fit. ICP uses the whole surface to get the last millimetres.

In our project ICP appears in four places.

  • A3 runs a trimmed rigid ICP from the canonical face template onto the CT, on the stable regions only (forehead, nasal bridge, zygoma). Then it hands over to Amberg's non rigid ICP, which bends the template.
  • A4 finds the face's symmetry plane, the plane that splits it into left and right halves, by mirroring the surface and running ICP between the surface and its mirror image.
  • C1 to C4 register a face rebuilt from the photos onto the CT. C1 and C2 let ICP change scale too, which turned out to be a trap.
  • Park et al. polish their landmark alignment with ICP around the landmarks.

The intuition

A curve is easier to watch than a surface. Hold two copies of a face profile, one turned and shifted. For each point on the moving copy, find the closest point on the fixed copy. Most pairs are wrong in detail, but on average they point the right way. Move the copy to fit those pairs. Now the closest points are better partners. Do it again.

Step by step

  1. Start close

    Get a rough pose from somewhere else, usually a landmark Procrustes fit. ICP will only fix what is left.

  2. Pair by closest point

    For every source point, find the nearest point on the target. A k d tree, a search structure that splits space into boxes, makes this fast on big meshes. These pairs are guesses.

  3. Throw out bad pairs

    Drop pairs that are too long, the worst fraction, or pairs on regions you know differ (eyes and lips).

  4. Solve the motion for these pairs

    Point to point ICP solves a Procrustes fit. Point to plane ICP solves a small linear system. Either way you get a rotation and a translation.

  5. Move the source and repeat

    Stop when the error stops falling or the motion gets tiny. A3 stops when the RMS changes by less than 0.005 mm, or after 40 rounds.

The math

Point to point

Given source points \(p_i\) and a target surface, ICP looks for the rigid motion that minimises

\[ E(R,t) = \sum_i \big\lVert R p_i + t - c(R p_i + t) \big\rVert^2 \]

In words, move every source point and measure its squared distance to the nearest spot on the target. Add them up.

c(x)
the closest point on the target to the point \(x\)
R, t
the rotation and translation being solved, see rigid transforms

This is hard because \(c\) depends on \(R\) and \(t\). ICP splits it into two easy half steps and alternates.

  1. Hold the motion fixed and update the pairs, \(q_i = c(Rp_i + t)\).
  2. Hold the pairs fixed and solve \(\min_{R,t} \sum_i \lVert Rp_i + t - q_i\rVert^2\). That is exactly the Kabsch problem, solved by one SVD.

Neither half step can make \(E\) larger. Re pairing picks the closest point, and the solve picks the best motion for those pairs. An error that never goes up and cannot go below zero must settle. So ICP always converges, but it can settle in the wrong place. It stops at the first spot where neither half step helps. That is a local minimum, a pose that is better than all nearby poses but not the best overall.

Now the same in 3D. The orange points are a third of the canonical face's vertices, moved away. Switch to the bad start to see a 3D local minimum.

Point to plane

C1, C2 and C3 finish with point to plane, and it is much faster near the answer. The closest point on a smooth surface is rarely the true partner. It is just somewhere on the same patch of surface. Point to point punishes the whole gap. Point to plane only punishes the part that sticks out of the surface. It uses the target normal \(n_i\) at each pair, the unit arrow that sticks straight out of the surface there.

\[ E(R,t) = \sum_i \big( (R p_i + t - q_i) \cdot n_i \big)^2 \]

In words, only count how far each moved point sits above or below the target's tangent plane. Distance along the surface is free.

There is no closed form, but for a small motion you can linearise. Write the small rotation as \(R \approx I + [\omega]_\times\), so \(Rp \approx p + \omega \times p\). Then each residual becomes linear in six unknowns.

\[ (p_i + \omega\times p_i + t - q_i)\cdot n_i = \underbrace{(p_i \times n_i)}_{a_i}\cdot \omega + n_i\cdot t - \underbrace{(q_i - p_i)\cdot n_i}_{b_i} \]

In words, for a small turn each pair's error is a plain weighted sum of the six unknowns, so all pairs together form one small linear least squares problem.

Stack \(x = (\omega, t)\), six numbers. Each pair gives one row \([\,a_i^\top\ \ n_i^\top\,]\). Solve the 6 by 6 normal equations \( \big(\sum_i g_i g_i^\top\big)\,x = \sum_i g_i b_i \) with \(g_i = (a_i, n_i)\). Turn \(\omega\) back into a proper rotation and repeat.

n_i
unit normal of the target surface at \(q_i\)
ω
a small rotation vector. Its direction is the axis and its length is the angle in radians
[ω]×
the matrix that does a cross product with \(\omega\)

Why it converges faster. In point to point, the wrong pairs along the surface keep pulling back when surfaces must slide. Point to plane ignores that pull and behaves like a Gauss Newton step, so a few rounds usually do on a smooth forehead.

A small worked example

Take a flat patch of target along the x axis, with normal \(n = (0,1)\). A source point sits at \(p = (0, 2)\) mm. Its closest target point is \(q = (0,0)\), but suppose the true partner was \(q^\ast = (1, 0)\). The point to point residual against \(q^\ast\) would be \(\sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = 2.24\) mm. Against the plane it is \((p - q)\cdot n = 2\) mm, whichever point on the patch you call \(q\). The 1 mm along the surface is simply not counted, and it is exactly the part you were unsure about.

Variants that matter here

Trimmed and robust ICP

Our surfaces never match everywhere, so this is the version we run. Plain ICP is least squares, so one long pair can drag everything. The CT has a chin rest fused under the chin and a cut at the neck. A rebuilt face has hair and shoulders. The expressions differ at the eyes and lips. Three tools deal with this.

  • A distance cutoff. Ignore any pair longer than a fixed distance. A3 uses 12 mm.
  • Trimming. Keep only the shortest fraction of the pairs each round. A3 keeps the 80th percentile, so it drops the worst 20 percent. This is Chetverikov's trimmed ICP.
  • A robust kernel. Replace the square with a function that grows more slowly for big residuals, and re weight each pair from its current residual (see robust least squares).
\[ \text{Huber: } w(r) = \begin{cases} 1 & |r|\le k \\ k/|r| & |r| > k \end{cases} \qquad \text{Tukey: } w(r) = \begin{cases} \big(1 - (r/k)^2\big)^2 & |r|\le k \\ 0 & |r| > k \end{cases} \]

In words, both give a pair full weight while its residual is small. Past \(k\), Huber fades the weight slowly and Tukey drops it to zero.

r
the residual of one pair in millimetres
k
the scale where a residual stops being normal. Huber keeps a small say for big residuals. Tukey gives them none at all.

The Open3D documentation recommends setting the Tukey \(k\) to the noise level. Our C1 and C2 use Tukey with \(k = 2\) mm in their point to plane stage.

Restricting to stable regions

The CT has the eyes and mouth closed and the photos show them open. So a rebuilt face and the CT differ at the eyes and lips, and ICP tilts the whole face to split the difference. The fix is to let ICP see only parts that do not change with expression. In our code these are the forehead, the nasal bridge and the zygoma (the cheekbones).

This is also the clinical habit. Aljawad and colleagues (2022) compared registration regions for face scans against CBCT, the dental cone beam CT. Forehead plus nasal bridge plus malar (cheekbone) areas gave 0.77 mm, against 0.93 mm for forehead and nose alone and 0.89 mm for malar alone. Jayaratne and colleagues (2012) excluded the periorbital and nasolabial regions, around the eyes and between nose and mouth.

A3 shows the size of the expression gap directly. After registration its residual is 0.02 to 0.07 mm on the stable regions and 1.4 to 1.5 mm on the eyes and lips.

Similarity ICP, and why scale hurt us

This section explains one of our clearest failures, so it is worth reading slowly. You can let ICP solve a scale too. The solve step becomes an Umeyama fit. This is tempting when one side has no known size, such as a point cloud from MapAnything (C1) or Depth Pro (C2). Open3D offers it only for point to point ICP (with_scaling=True). So C1 runs a similarity point to point stage first, then a robust point to plane stage with the scale frozen.

The trouble is that nearest point pairing has a built in bias toward shrinking. A rebuilt face covers things the CT does not have, like hair one to three centimetres outside the scalp. Every such point pairs with the CT surface inside it. The cheapest way to shorten all those pairs at once is to shrink the whole cloud, as Figure 7 shows.

We measured it on C1. With hair allowed into the similarity stage, the scale came out 15 percent small, the camera sat too close, and the CT projected too large. Restricting the source to points that already lay within 10 mm of the CT at the start (the mutual overlap) halved the camera error of that stage.

Even then, every free scale the surface fit produced was 6 to 13 percent smaller than the landmark scale, and it made the camera two to three times worse while improving its own surface fit. So C1 now rejects a free scale that differs from the landmark scale by more than 5 percent and reruns the stage rigidly. C2 shows the other face of the same problem. Depth Pro's depth came out 9 percent long (scale 0.914), and the similarity ICP absorbed a wrong focal length into scale and distance instead of fixing it.

Non rigid ICP

All of the above moves one shape as a whole, which is called rigid. Non rigid ICP gives every vertex of a template its own small transform and adds a stiffness term that keeps neighbours moving together. It is how A3 bends the canonical face onto the CT. It has its own page, Amberg et al. 2007.

Where it shows up

The table lists every ICP run in our methods. The surface numbers are distances between the two surfaces after the fit.

MethodSource to targetICP flavourResult
