Notice the pattern in family C. Good surface distances did not mean good cameras. C3 has the best surface fit of the family and still lands its outline 11 px off. A similarity ICP can fit the surface well with the wrong combination of scale and distance, and the photo only sees the result through the camera.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • It needs a good start. ICP only finds the nearest local minimum. Always start it from a landmark fit, never from nothing.
  • A low RMS is not proof. Figure 3 shows a wrong pose with a respectable residual. Check something ICP did not optimise, such as held out landmarks or the outline in the photo.
  • Partial overlap. Points with no partner on the other surface pull wrongly. Use a cutoff, trimming, an overlap mask or a robust kernel.
  • Sliding. On a nearly symmetric or cylinder like region, such as the sides of a face, surfaces slide along each other at almost no cost.
  • Free scale shrinks. Only let ICP change scale if nothing better is available, and check it against a landmark scale.
  • Normals. Point to plane needs consistent outward normals. A flipped patch pushes the wrong way.
Remember

ICP alternates two easy steps, pair by closest point and solve Procrustes, and the error can never go up.

It finds the nearest local minimum, so it needs a good start, and point to plane gets there faster on smooth skin.

Fit only the stable regions, drop or down weight long pairs, and do not trust a free scale.

About 25 minutes

Building block K9Used in B1 B2 Corsini

Searching without gradients

Some scores have no useful slope. You render the CT at a guessed camera, compare the picture with the photo, and get one number back. To improve the camera you must search, trying poses and keeping the better ones.

The short version
  • A render and compare score changes in tiny jumps as pixels flip, so it has no slope to follow. You search instead, with as few renders as you can.
  • A grid explodes with seven unknowns. Powell searches along lines and learns the valley direction. CMA-ES throws random darts from a cloud that moves, stretches and shrinks.
  • Every one of these finds only a nearby answer, so it must start from a good camera.
  • B2 uses CMA-ES then Powell. B1 instead made the renderer smooth and followed its slope with Adam.

Read first Nonlinear least squares. Helpful Comparing two images.

Why you need it

Our B family refines a camera by comparing images. B2 renders the CT as normals (the direction the skin faces), depth, and ambient occlusion (creases darkened). It scores the render against the photo with a gradient field measure plus an outline distance (see Comparing two images).

The score passes through a renderer, a pixel grid and a histogram, and none of those hands you a derivative. So B2 searches seven numbers directly (rotation, translation and log focal) with CMA-ES at 384 px and then Powell at 640 px. Corsini et al. search with NEWUOA, another derivative free method. B1 instead uses Mitsuba, a differentiable renderer that reports how the image changes with the camera, and follows that slope with Adam.

Searching is slow. B2 takes about 0.06 s per evaluation at 384 px and 0.14 s at 640 px, and 66 s in all. So the goal is a good answer with few evaluations.

Why there is no slope

This section explains why the usual solvers from the least squares page do not apply. A gradient is the slope of the score with respect to each unknown. If you have it, you can walk downhill. But a rendered score is made of pixels. Move the camera a tiny amount and most pixels do not change, then one flips from background to face. So the score is a staircase, with zero slope on every step.

You can make the renderer smooth, with soft edges, as Mitsuba does for B1. Or you give up on slopes and search, which is most of this page.

The landscape

Think of the score as a height over the space of unknowns. Each point is one camera, and its height is how badly the render matches. We want the lowest point. The figures below use two unknowns and the two features that hurt us in practice.

  • A narrow curved valley. The score changes slowly along the floor and fast across it. The focal length and the camera distance form such a valley.
  • A local minimum, a dip lower than its surroundings but not the lowest point. A search that falls in stops there.

Grid search

The grid is the baseline every smarter method tries to beat. It tries every combination, keeps the best, and maybe zooms in. It is easy to trust and hopeless in high dimensions. With 10 values for each of 7 unknowns you need \(10^7\) evaluations. At B2's 0.06 s each, that is about seven days.

Coordinate descent and Powell's method

B2 finishes with Powell, and Powell grows out of a simpler idea. Coordinate descent changes one unknown at a time. Hold the rest fixed, find the lowest point along the first axis, then the second, and so on, round and round. A 1D search is cheap. You bracket a minimum and shrink the bracket, for example by golden section, which cuts it by about 0.618 each time.

In a diagonal valley coordinate descent zigzags, because each axis move hits the wall after a short step. Powell's method fixes this. After a round of line searches, the total move of that round is a good direction. Search along it too, and keep it for the next round in place of an old one. After a few rounds the directions line up with the valley floor.

B2 uses Powell for its fine stage, after CMA-ES. It needs no gradient, respects the bounds, and suits the small, nearly independent adjustments left at that point. One Powell round over seven parameters is a full cycle of seven line searches, about 150 evaluations, or about 20 s at 640 px. So B2 allows it two rounds.

CMA-ES, throwing darts

B2 starts with CMA-ES, so this is the main search in our project. CMA-ES stands for Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. Imagine throwing darts at the landscape from a cloud shaped like an ellipse.

  1. Throw darts

    Draw a handful of random candidate points from the cloud. The cloud is a Gaussian, a bell shaped spread of random points, with a centre (the mean \(m\)), a shape (the covariance \(C\)), and an overall size (the step size \(\sigma\)).

  2. Score them and keep the best

    Evaluate the score at every dart. Rank them and keep the best half.

  3. Move the mean

    The new centre is a weighted average of the best darts, with the best getting the largest weight.

  4. Stretch the cloud

    Change \(C\) so the cloud grows longer where good darts were found. In a valley it turns to lie along the floor.

  5. Tighten or widen

    If the mean keeps moving the same way, widen \(\sigma\). If the moves cancel out, you are circling the minimum, so tighten.

  6. Repeat

    Stop when the cloud is small enough or the time runs out. B2 gives its CMA-ES stage 40 s.

The CMA-ES update

At generation \(g\) we sample \(\lambda\) candidates and sort them by score, best first.

\[ x_k = m + \sigma\, y_k, \qquad y_k \sim \mathcal N(0, C), \qquad k = 1,\dots,\lambda \] \[ m \leftarrow \sum_{i=1}^{\mu} w_i\, x_{i:\lambda}, \qquad w_1 \ge w_2 \ge \dots \ge w_\mu > 0, \quad \textstyle\sum w_i = 1 \]

In words, throw \(\lambda\) darts from the cloud, then move the centre to a weighted average of the best \(\mu\) darts. Here \(x_{i:\lambda}\) means the dart ranked \(i\) among the \(\lambda\).

The covariance learns from two sources. The evolution path \(p_c\) is a running average of recent mean moves. It remembers the direction you keep travelling. The rank \(\mu\) term uses the spread of this generation's good darts.

\[ C \leftarrow (1 - c_1 - c_\mu)\, C + c_1\, p_c p_c^\top + c_\mu \sum_{i=1}^{\mu} w_i\, y_{i:\lambda} y_{i:\lambda}^\top \]

In words, the new cloud shape is mostly the old shape, nudged toward the direction you keep travelling and toward where the good darts landed.

The step size follows a second path \(p_\sigma\), measured in units where the cloud is round. If that path is longer than a random walk would be, \(\sigma\) grows. If it is shorter, \(\sigma\) shrinks.

\[ \sigma \leftarrow \sigma \exp\!\Big( \frac{c_\sigma}{d_\sigma}\Big( \frac{\lVert p_\sigma \rVert}{E\lVert \mathcal N(0,I)\rVert} - 1 \Big) \Big) \]

In words, compare how far the centre has really travelled with how far a random walk would go. Grow the cloud if you travelled further, shrink it if less.

m
the mean, the current best guess of the answer
σ
the step size, the overall scale of the cloud
C
the covariance, the shape and orientation of the cloud
λ, μ
the number of darts per generation and the number kept
wi
recombination weights, larger for better ranks
c1, cμ, cσ, dσ
learning rates with standard default values that depend only on the dimension

CMA-ES never looks at the score values, only their ranking. So it does not care if the score is a staircase. That is why it suits a rendered score.

In B2 the starting cloud comes from the landmark solution it refines. The step sizes are 1 degree of rotation, 3 mm of translation and 0.05 in log focal. The bounds are 8 degrees, 30 mm and a focal between 2500 and 20000 px, five to ten times the expected error.

For contrast, gradient descent and Adam

B1 is our one gradient method, and this is how it moves. When you do have a gradient \(\nabla f\), the cheapest move is downhill. Gradient descent takes \(x \leftarrow x - \eta \nabla f(x)\) with a step size \(\eta\). In a narrow valley the gradient points mostly across the valley, so gradient descent bounces between the walls and creeps along the floor.

Adam keeps two running averages per unknown, of the gradient (momentum, which smooths the bouncing) and of the squared gradient (which scales each step).

\[ g = \nabla f(x),\quad m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1) g,\quad v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2) g^2,\quad x \leftarrow x - \eta\,\frac{\hat m}{\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon} \]

In words, step along the smoothed slope, divided by the typical size of that unknown's slope, so every unknown takes steps of a similar size. Here \(m\) is the gradient average, not the CMA-ES mean.

β1, β2
how long each average remembers, usually 0.9 and 0.999
m̂, v̂
the averages corrected for starting at zero
η
the learning rate

B1 runs Adam on the camera pose through Mitsuba, at about 0.03 s per step on the full CT head. It moved 0.03 degrees from its A1 start and stopped.

Two things went wrong, and neither was Adam's fault. The Metal backend (Mitsuba's mode for Apple GPUs) could not differentiate the field of view, so the focal length could not move. And the silhouette target was biased, because the segmenter's mask boundary is quantised to about 6 px and sits a few millimetres inside the CT outline. A gradient method follows the slope of the score you give it, including the slope of its mistakes.

Local minima and narrow basins

This is the limit that shaped how we used B2. A basin is the set of starting points from which a search ends in the same minimum. A narrow basin means you must start close. Every method here is local in practice. Even CMA-ES explores only about as far as its initial cloud. A large \(\sigma\) can jump out of a dip, at the cost of many more evaluations.

We saw this in B2. Started from A5's camera it reached a 3.2 px outline. Started from A1 instead, it landed somewhere else entirely. Corsini et al. report the same kind of behaviour for their mutual information search. From up to 50 pixels off, their normals plus ambient occlusion mix converged in 76 to 90 percent of runs on their stone capital test objects. They also start from a rough manual alignment.

Where it shows up

Three methods in this project search a camera by comparing images. Contour is the outline distance in pixels and IoU the overlap of the two face masks.

WhereSearchWhat it searchedOutcome
B2CMA-ES at 384 px, then Powell at 640 px7 numbers, rotation, translation, log focal, from A5contour 3.2 px, IoU 0.787, 66 s. From A1 it lands elsewhere
Corsini et al.NEWUOA, a quadratic model inside a trust regionthe same seven camera numbers, pose and focal, scored by mutual informationone tuning parameter, RHOBEG, set to 2.0 (about a tenth of the expected initial error)
B1Adam through Mitsubapose, from A1moved 0.03 degrees. The field of view could not be differentiated

NEWUOA fits a quadratic bowl to the scores it has seen, jumps to the bowl's minimum inside a trust region, and refits. Corsini et al. chose it because derivative estimates do poorly on mutual information near its minimum.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • Start close. These are refiners, not solvers. B2's basin is narrow, so it runs on top of a landmark camera.
  • Scale the unknowns. A step of 1 in degrees and a step of 1 in millimetres are not the same size. B2 searches the log of the focal so that a step means the same ratio everywhere.
  • Bound the weak directions. On one face the focal length is the weakest parameter. Without bounds the search wanders along the focal and depth valley for free.
  • The score must be right first. A search finds the minimum of the score you wrote. On our flat lit photo, mutual information alone drifted 2 degrees. The search worked fine. The score was wrong.
  • Budget the time. Count evaluations, not iterations. Powell can return worse than it started if cut off, so B2 keeps whichever of the CMA-ES and Powell answers scored better.
Remember

Render and compare scores are staircases, so you either smooth the renderer (B1) or search without slopes (B2).

Powell runs line searches and learns valley directions. CMA-ES throws darts from an ellipse that moves, stretches and shrinks, and only uses the ranking.

All of them are local. A good start matters more than a clever search.

About 35 minutes

Building block K10Used in B1 B2 B4 Corsini our evaluation

Comparing two images

To refine a camera, or to test one, you render the CT at that camera and compare the picture with the photo. The comparison gives one number. Which number you pick decides what "lined up" means. The wrong choice will pull a good camera somewhere bad.

The short version
  • A similarity measure takes two images and returns one score for how well they agree.
  • Pixel measures (SSD, NCC) need the same spot to have the same brightness in both images. A grey CT render and a colour photo break that.
  • Mutual information only asks whether one image's brightness predicts the other's. Gradient fields (NGF) compare edge directions. Outline measures (IoU, chamfer) compare shapes.
  • Mutual information drifted 2 degrees on our flat lit photo. Edges and outlines held up better.
  • Our fairest score is cross view PSNR. Paint the CT from the front photo, render it at a side camera and compare with the real side photo.

Read first Rendering, depth and back projection

Why you need it

A similarity measure is how a computer decides whether a camera is right. An image is a grid of numbers, for example 1.5 million grey values between 0 and 255. The measure takes two such grids and returns one score. Our project compares two very different pairs of images.

  • A render against a photo. A render is a picture of the CT surface that the computer draws from a chosen camera. The CT has no colour, so a render shows only shape. The photo shows skin colour, brows and lips. B1, B2 and Corsini et al. must score how well these two kinds of picture agree.
  • A photo against a photo. Our cross view test paints the CT with the front photo, renders it from a side camera, and compares that with the real side photo. Now both images show skin, and a simpler measure works.

The figures run on two synthetic images of the canonical face, a "photo" with skin, brows, eyes and lips and a grey shaded "render" of the bare surface.

Pixel differences and correlation

The simplest scores compare the images pixel by pixel. They only work when the same spot has about the same brightness in both.

Sum of squared differences

Subtract the two images pixel by pixel. Square each difference and add them up.

\[ \mathrm{SSD}(A,B) = \sum_{x} \big(A(x) - B(x)\big)^2, \qquad \mathrm{MSE} = \tfrac{1}{N}\,\mathrm{SSD} \]
x
a pixel position, summed over all \(N\) pixels in the comparison region
A(x), B(x)
the grey values of the two images at that pixel
MSE
the mean squared error, SSD divided by the number of pixels

In words, SSD adds up how far apart the two images are at every pixel. It is zero only for identical images. Make one image twice as bright and SSD explodes, even though nothing moved.

Normalised cross correlation

NCC removes each image's mean brightness and spread, then measures how well the two patterns rise and fall together.

\[ \mathrm{NCC}(A,B) = \frac{\sum_x (A(x) - \bar A)(B(x) - \bar B)}{\sqrt{\sum_x (A(x)-\bar A)^2\,\sum_x (B(x)-\bar B)^2}} \]
\(\bar A, \bar B\)
the mean grey value of each image

In words, NCC asks whether A is bright where B is bright and dark where B is dark, after ignoring overall brightness and contrast. It lies between \(-1\) and \(+1\). Any brightness change of the form \(B = aA + b\) with \(a > 0\) leaves it at exactly 1.

Worked example

Take four pixels, \(A = (10, 20, 30, 40)\) and \(B = 2A + 5 = (25, 45, 65, 85)\). SSD is \(15^2 + 25^2 + 35^2 + 45^2 = 4100\). That looks like a bad match. For NCC, subtract the means (25 and 55) to get \(A' = (-15,-5,5,15)\) and \(B' = (-30,-10,10,30)\). The top sum is \(450 + 50 + 50 + 450 = 1000\). The bottom is \(\sqrt{500 \cdot 2000} = 1000\). So NCC is exactly 1, a perfect match up to brightness.

Mutual information from scratch

Mutual information is the measure for two images that look different but show the same thing. A render and a photo can be perfectly aligned and still have unrelated brightness. The render's nose is bright where the light hits it, while the photo's nose has the same skin colour as the cheek. Correlation fails, because no straight line maps one brightness to the other. Mutual information (MI) only asks whether one image's value predicts the other's, by any rule at all. You build it in three steps.

Step 1. The joint histogram

Cut the brightness range into 16 bins and make a 16 by 16 table of zeros. At every pixel \(x\), find the bins of \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\) and add one to that cell. At the end, divide by the number of pixels.

This gives \(p(a,b)\), the fraction of pixels where A is in bin \(a\) and B in bin \(b\). Summing the table one way gives \(p(a)\), and the other way gives \(p(b)\). These marginals are the plain histograms of each image.

When the images are aligned, the counts pile up in a few cells. When they are misaligned, skin lands on brow and brow on background, so the counts smear across the table.

Step 2. Entropy

Entropy measures how spread out a distribution is, in bits. It is the average number of yes or no questions you would need to guess a value.

\[ H(A) = -\sum_a p(a)\log_2 p(a), \qquad H(A,B) = -\sum_{a,b} p(a,b)\log_2 p(a,b) \]

In words, entropy is small when a few bins hold almost everything and large when the counts are spread evenly. If every pixel had the same value, \(H = 0\), because there is nothing to guess. If the values spread evenly over 16 bins, \(H = \log_2 16 = 4\) bits. \(H(A,B)\) is the same idea for the whole joint table.

Step 3. Mutual information

\[ I(A;B) = H(A) + H(B) - H(A,B) \]

In words, MI is how many bits you save by describing the two images together instead of separately. If knowing A tells you a lot about B, the joint description \(H(A,B)\) is cheap and \(I\) is large. If they are unrelated, \(H(A,B) = H(A) + H(B)\) and \(I = 0\). Our code also reports the normalised form \(\mathrm{NMI} = 2I / (H(A) + H(B))\), which lies between 0 and 1.

Worked example

Take four pixels with two levels, \(A = (0,0,1,1)\) and \(B = (1,1,0,0)\). B is A with dark and light swapped. The joint histogram has two filled cells, (0,1) and (1,0), each with probability \(1/2\). So \(H(A) = H(B) = H(A,B) = 1\) bit and \(I = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1\) bit. Knowing A tells you B exactly, even though the rule is "flip it". Now shuffle B to \((1,0,1,0)\). All four cells get \(1/4\), so \(H(A,B) = 2\) bits and \(I = 0\). The correlation of the first pair is \(-1\), which SSD and NCC would call a terrible match.

Why MI works across modalities. A modality is a kind of image, such as a photo, a depth map or an X ray. MI never asks that bright matches bright. So Corsini et al. can render surface normals and ambient occlusion (how hidden each point is from open space) and maximise MI against a photo of an unpainted object. They use a 128 by 128 bin joint histogram. MI is also the standard measure for CT against MRI in medical registration.

Why it failed for us. MI needs the two images to vary for the same reasons. Our front photo is flat and evenly lit. Its variation comes from albedo, the skin's own colour (skin, brows, lips). The render has no albedo, so all its variation comes from shading. On the skin, the photo is nearly constant while the render varies a lot. The joint histogram has little to lock onto, and in B2 normalised MI on its own drifted 2 degrees. Corsini's test objects were carvings and statues, such as stone capitals and a bas relief, where shading is most of what a photo shows.

Normalised gradient fields

Edges are what a grey render and a colour photo share most reliably. An edge is where brightness changes fast. The outline of the face, the sides of the nose, the eye sockets and the line between the lips are edges in both images. Normalised gradient fields (NGF) compare edge directions and ignore edge strength.

\[ n_A(x) = \frac{\nabla A(x)}{\sqrt{\lVert \nabla A(x)\rVert^2 + \varepsilon^2}}, \qquad \mathrm{NGF}(A,B) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_x \big( n_A(x)\cdot n_B(x) \big)^2 \]
∇A(x)
the image gradient, a 2D arrow pointing uphill in brightness. In practice it is the difference of neighbouring pixels.
nA(x)
the gradient scaled to length about 1, so only its direction counts
ε
a small constant. Where the gradient is much weaker than \(\varepsilon\) (flat skin, noise), \(n\) shrinks to nearly zero and the pixel does not vote.
squared dot product
1 when the two edges are parallel, 0 when they cross at right angles. Squaring means a dark to light edge and a light to dark edge in the same place still agree.

In words, NGF is the average of how parallel the edges of the two images are, counting only places where there is an edge. A worked example. Say the photo gradient at a pixel is \((3, 4)\) and the render gradient is \((0, 2)\), with a tiny \(\varepsilon\). The unit arrows are \((0.6, 0.8)\) and \((0, 1)\). Their dot product is 0.8, and its square is 0.64. Flip the photo edge to \((-3,-4)\) and the score is still 0.64.

NGF comes from Haber and Modersitzki (MICCAI 2006). B1 and B2 use it, and our cross view test reports it, because a lighting change barely moves it.

Silhouette overlap and chamfer distance

The outline is the most dependable thing a render and a photo share, because it does not depend on light or colour. A mask is a black and white image that marks which pixels belong to the face. The render's mask is free, since every pixel that hits the surface is face. The photo's mask comes from a segmenter, a network that labels each pixel as face skin or not.

\[ \mathrm{IoU} = \frac{|M_r \cap M_p|}{|M_r \cup M_p|}, \qquad d_{\mathrm{ch}}(C_r, C_p) = \frac{1}{|C_r|}\sum_{u \in C_r} \min_{v\in C_p} \lVert u - v\rVert \]
Mr, Mp
the render and photo masks as sets of pixels
|·|
the number of pixels in a set
IoU
intersection over union, 1 for identical masks and 0 for no overlap
Cr, Cp
the outline pixels of each mask
dch
the chamfer distance. A symmetric version averages both directions.

In words, IoU is the shared area divided by the total area covered. The chamfer distance is the average gap, in pixels, from each render outline pixel to the nearest photo outline pixel. A worked example. Masks of 100 and 90 pixels that share 85 pixels cover \(100 + 90 - 85 = 105\) pixels together, so IoU is \(85/105 = 0.81\).

IoU is dominated by the big interior, so a few pixels of outline error barely move it. Chamfer speaks in pixels along the edge. Our "contour px" column is a chamfer measure, the median distance between the rendered head outline and the photo's face skin outline along the jaw and cheeks. It uses no landmarks, so a landmark method cannot game it.

B4 has the best outline on the front photo at 2.80 px and IoU 0.842. B2 reaches 3.20 px. The silhouette also sets a trap. B1's target was the MediaPipe selfie mask. Its boundary is quantised to about 6 px and sits a few millimetres inside the CT outline. Fitting the render's outline to that biased target dragged the pose in pitch (the up and down nod).

PSNR in decibels

PSNR is how we report the cross view test, so you need to read it as a pixel error. It is MSE put on a log scale.

\[ \mathrm{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{255^2}{\mathrm{MSE}} = 20\log_{10}\frac{255}{\mathrm{RMSE}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \mathrm{RMSE} = 255\cdot 10^{-\mathrm{PSNR}/20} \]
255
the largest possible grey value of an 8 bit image
RMSE
the root mean square pixel error in grey levels, the square root of MSE
dB
decibels, a log scale. Higher is better. Every 6 dB halves the typical error, and every 20 dB divides it by 10.

In words, PSNR says how many times smaller the typical pixel error is than the full brightness range, counted on a log scale. A worked example. An MSE of 196 means an RMSE of 14 grey levels. Then \(255/14 = 18.2\), \(\log_{10} 18.2 = 1.26\), and PSNR is \(20 \times 1.26 = 25.2\) dB.

PSNRtypical pixel error, out of 255where it appears
22 dBabout 20C2 22.33 dB
25 dBabout 14A1 25.18 dB, A6 25.56 dB
26 dBabout 13A7 26.18 dB, C4 26.39 dB

SSIM (structural similarity, Wang et al. 2004) compares local brightness, contrast and pattern inside a small sliding window. Our code uses an 11 by 11 Gaussian window (a soft round weighting) with sigma 1.5. On a smooth face it barely tells cameras apart, so we report it but do not rank on it.

Our cross view test, exactly

A camera can fit one photo well and still be wrong. A longer lens further away and a shorter lens closer in give almost the same front photo. The cross view test catches this by making the geometry carry the appearance from one view to another.

  1. Bake from the front

    Paint the CT with the front photo, through the method's front camera (see Painting the surface). Baking means writing photo colours into the CT's texture image.

  2. Render at a side camera

    Render that painted surface at the camera the same method found for each side photo.

  3. Compare with the real side photo

    If the front camera was wrong, the paint is in the wrong place and shows up shifted. If the side camera was wrong, even perfect paint lands on the wrong pixels. Either way the score drops.

  4. Only score what was measured

    Count only pixels inside the side photo's face skin mask, and only texels that came from the photo. A texel is one pixel of the texture image. Mirrored and inpainted texels are inventions, so they never count.

  5. Fit out the lighting

    The head turned between shots, so shading and exposure differ. Before PSNR and SSIM, fit a global gain and offset per colour channel between the two images and remove it. That difference says nothing about the pose.

Two more rules keep the test fair. The reverse direction (bake from a side photo, render at the front camera) is scored too. And B1 and B2 ran only on the front photo, so they borrow A5's side cameras. Their rows describe the pair, and the table marks them "borrowed".

The test has one known bias. It rewards the three cameras agreeing with each other as much as each one being right. C4 leads at 26.39 dB because its three cameras come from one joint solve with one shared focal length, yet its outline is 16.58 px off. A7 reaches 26.18 dB with a 6.40 px outline. The margins in the leading group are 0.1 to 0.3 dB, smaller than the spread of up to 4 dB between cross view directions. So read the dB column together with the contour column. A7's acceptance guard is worth 1.47 dB on this test. Without it A7 scores 24.71 dB.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • Same pose, same picture is circular. Bake a texture through camera X and render it back at camera X. It reproduces the photo whatever X is. B4 drove the flow between such a pair to 0.4 px, which sounds like a result and is not. Always compare at a different view.
  • MI needs shared structure. Check that the two images vary for the same reasons.
  • Masks can be biased. A segmenter mask that sits inside the true outline pulls a silhouette fit off. Look at its boundary first.
  • IoU hides outline error. Two masks can share 0.78 of their area and still disagree by several pixels all along the jaw. Use a chamfer distance for outlines.
  • Gain match before PSNR. Otherwise you are measuring exposure, not pose.
Remember

SSD needs equal brightness. NCC allows a straight line between brightnesses. MI allows any rule at all.

NGF compares edge directions and outlines compare shapes. Those survive between a grey render and a colour photo.

Our cross view test bakes from the front, renders at the side and scores photo sourced texels after gain matching. Read it next to the outline error.

Features, descriptors and DINOv2

To match a photo to a render you need a way to say "this patch here looks like that patch there". A descriptor turns a patch into a list of numbers, so that similar patches get similar lists. Hand made descriptors fail between a colour photo and a grey render. DINOv2's learned features do not, and that is what B3 and A7 are built on.

The short version
  • A camera solve needs pairs. Each pair is a photo pixel and the 3D point on the CT that it shows.
  • A descriptor is a list of numbers that describes a small image patch. Matching pairs up patches whose lists are close.
  • Hand made descriptors such as SIFT are built from brightness changes. Those differ between a colour photo and a grey render, so the matches come out wrong.
  • DINOv2 is a vision transformer trained without labels. Its patch features say which part of the object a patch shows, so the nose in the photo and the nose in the render get close vectors.
  • B3 and A7 match DINOv2 patches from photo to render, throw out wrong matches with RANSAC, lift the render side to 3D and solve the camera with PnP.

Read first PnP and RANSAC

Why you need it

Every camera solve in this project needs pairs, a pixel in the photo and the 3D point on the CT that it shows (see PnP). The A methods get about 22 pairs from a face landmark detector. That detector was trained on photos, so it is shaky on a grey CT render.

B3 takes a different route. It renders the CT and cuts both the photo and the render into small patches. It describes every patch with DINOv2 and pairs up patches whose descriptions agree. Each render patch knows its 3D point through the render's depth (see back projection). The result is hundreds of pairs, 180 to 260 per round in our runs, with an exact 3D side.

What a descriptor is

A feature (or keypoint) is a spot in an image worth describing, like an eye corner or the edge of a nostril. A descriptor is a vector of numbers that summarises the patch around that spot. The same thing should give close vectors, measured by straight line (Euclidean) distance or by the angle between them (cosine similarity). Different things should give vectors far apart.

The classic example is SIFT (Lowe 2004). It cuts the patch around a keypoint into a small grid of cells. In each cell it counts how much gradient points in each of a few directions. A gradient is the direction in which brightness rises fastest. The counts, laid end to end, are the descriptor. Because it is built from gradient directions, it ignores overall brightness changes. Figure 1 builds a small version with 2 by 2 cells and 8 directions, so 32 numbers.

Matching, the mutual check and the ratio test

Once every patch has a descriptor, you pair them up. The simplest matcher pairs each descriptor in image 1 with its nearest neighbour, the closest descriptor in image 2. Many of these pairs are wrong. Two cheap filters remove a lot of them.

  • Mutual nearest neighbour. Keep a pair only if A's nearest neighbour is B and B's nearest neighbour is also A. A patch on plain skin often has many near equal partners, and the mutual check usually drops such ties.
  • Ratio test. Divide the best match's distance by the second best. If the ratio is close to 1, the match is ambiguous, so drop it. On a dense grid the second best is usually just the next patch over. So B3 compares against the best descriptor outside a small neighbourhood, with a threshold of 0.92.

Neural network features

Learned features fixed the photo against render problem, so it helps to know roughly how a network makes them. A neural network is a long chain of simple steps, each with adjustable numbers called weights. Training adjusts the weights so the output does something useful. Stop the chain partway and the numbers there describe the input, often better than any hand made recipe.

Convolutional networks, briefly

A convolution slides a small grid of weights (a kernel, often 3 by 3) over the image. At each position it multiplies the weights by the pixels under them and adds up. The result is a new image called a feature map. A kernel like \([-1,0,1]\) in each row responds to vertical edges.

A convolutional network (CNN) stacks many such layers, with a simple bend between them (such as setting negative values to zero). Early layers find edges. Deeper layers combine them into corners, textures and parts. Each output sees only a local window of the input, which grows a little with every layer.

Transformers and vision transformers, from scratch

DINOv2 is not a CNN but a transformer. A transformer works on a list of vectors called tokens. It was invented for text, where each token is a word piece. The vision transformer (ViT) applies it to images with one trick.

  1. Cut the image into patches

    DINOv2 uses patches of 14 by 14 pixels. An image of 224 by 224 pixels becomes a 16 by 16 grid, 256 patches.

  2. Turn each patch into a token

    Flatten the patch's pixels (14 × 14 × 3 = 588 numbers) and multiply by a learned matrix to get one vector. Add a learned position code, so the network knows where the patch came from.

  3. Let every patch look at every other patch

    This is attention. Each token asks a question (its query). Every token offers a label (its key). The token then collects a weighted mix of everyone's content (their values), weighted by how well each key answers its question. A patch on the nose tip can pull in information from the eyes and the chin in a single step. A CNN would need many layers to see that far.

  4. Repeat

    A block is attention plus a small network applied to each token on its own. ViT-B stacks 12 blocks and ViT-L stacks 24.

  5. Read out one vector per patch

    After any block, each patch has a vector that describes it in the context of the whole image. These are the patch features.

Attention in one line

\[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt d}\Big)\,V, \qquad Q = XW_Q,\ K = XW_K,\ V = XW_V \]
X
the tokens, one row per patch
WQ, WK, WV
learned matrices that make the queries, keys and values
QKT
a table of dot products, how well each patch's query matches each patch's key
√d
the square root of the vector length \(d\). Dividing by it keeps the numbers in a sensible range.
softmax
turns each row into positive weights that sum to 1, \(\mathrm{softmax}(z)_j = e^{z_j}/\sum_k e^{z_k}\)

In words, each patch scores every other patch by how well it answers its question, turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and takes that weighted average of their contents. A worked example with two tokens and \(d = 4\). Say a query gives dot products 2 and 0 with the two keys. Divide by \(\sqrt 4 = 2\) to get 1 and 0. Softmax gives \(e^1/(e^1 + e^0) = 2.72/3.72 = 0.73\) and 0.27. If the values are \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), the output is \((0.73, 0.27)\), mostly the first token's content.

Self supervised learning and DINOv2

How a network is trained decides what its features care about. Self supervised learning needs no labels such as "this image is a cat". DINO and its successor DINOv2 train a student network to give the same output as a teacher network when the two see different crops and colour changes of the same image. The teacher is a slowly updated average of the student.

To agree across crops and colour changes, the network has to describe what is in a patch and where it sits on the object, and ignore the lighting of the moment. Nobody told it about faces, and it still gives the nose tip in two images close vectors.

Why it bridges a colour photo and a grey render. The training already varied colour, brightness and contrast heavily, so the features learned not to depend on them. What is left is shape and part identity, which a photo and a render of the same face share. FoundPose adds one observation. Features from the last blocks are very semantic (they know "nose" but not exactly where), and the first blocks keep position but lose meaning. An intermediate block is the useful middle. B3 takes block 9 of the 12 in ViT-B/14. FoundPose used block 18 of the 24 in ViT-L/14, also three quarters of the way up. In FoundPose's own test, block 18 scored 37.2 AR against 23.5 for the last block and 7.6 for SIFT descriptors.

Seeing features with PCA. A DINOv2 patch feature has hundreds of numbers. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the three directions along which the features vary most. Map those three numbers to red, green and blue and paint each patch. Similar features get similar colours.

From patch matches to a camera

Matching features is only the start, because the matches still contain mistakes. A face makes some mistakes very likely. The left and right cheek look alike, so a patch on one cheek can match its mirror twin. RANSAC removes them. It fits a model to a few random matches, counts how many others agree, and keeps the model with the most support.

B3 lifts each render patch to 3D through the render depth. Then it runs RANSAC with EPnP as the model, an 8 px threshold and 10000 iterations. EPnP is a fast PnP solver. Last, a PnP that down weights bad matches and also solves the focal length runs on the survivors.

WhereFeaturesHow they are usedNumbers
FoundPoseDINOv2 ViT-L/14, intermediate block, reduced by PCArender templates, retrieve by bag of words, match, PnP RANSAC, featuremetric refinement37.2 AR (average recall, roughly the share of poses judged correct) on the BOP benchmark before refinement, against 27.6 for the best trained rival. 1.7 s per image

The C4 row shows the classic descriptor's limit. Bare skin has little texture, so SIFT found only 44 points on it across three photos. The landmark version of C4 had to carry the row instead. The B3 row shows the learned features' limit. They are good at polishing a nearly right camera, but they cannot find one from scratch. B3 does not come back from a 10 degree, 100 mm push away from the answer. With too many rounds it drifts, because it starts fitting its own mistakes (it overfits). A7's guard exists because of this.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • Patch size limits precision. One DINOv2 patch is 14 pixels. B3 sizes its crop so a patch covers about 9 photo pixels and estimates the best spot inside a patch. Still its inlier residual is 4.6 px.
  • Symmetry. Mirror twin matches are common on a face. B3 rejects any solution whose rotation differs from the starting camera by more than a set angle.
  • Different things, same place. The CT's eyes are shut and the photo's are open. Any match on the eyes or lips is between two different things, so B3 masks them out on the photo side.
  • Same pose, same picture. A painted re render at the current pose matches the photo by construction. B3's optional LoFTR stage (another learned matcher) on a painted render added nothing for that reason.
  • Licences. DINOv2 weights are Apache licensed, which allows commercial use. FoundPose's code is CC BY-NC, which forbids it, so B3 re implements the recipe rather than using that code.
Remember

A descriptor is a vector per patch. Match by nearest neighbour, then keep mutual matches that pass a ratio test.

A ViT cuts the image into 14 pixel patches, lets every patch attend to every other, and outputs one vector per patch.

DINOv2 learned without labels to ignore colour and lighting. That is why its features match a photo to a grey render.

About 30 minutes

Building block K12Used in A1 to A7 B1 to B4 C1 to C4 cross view test

Painting the surface

Once you know the camera, you can paint the photo onto the CT. Every method in this project ends this way. The surface is unwrapped into a flat image. Each pixel of that image is traced to its spot on the skin and from there to the photo. Whatever the camera could not see is filled in. The result is three files, an OBJ, an MTL and a PNG.

The short version
  • Once the camera is known, the photo is painted onto the CT surface. Every method ends this way.
  • The surface is cut into flat pieces (charts) and packed into one square image, the texture. UV coordinates link each triangle to its spot in that image.
  • For every texture pixel, find its 3D point, check that the camera really sees it, and copy the photo colour from where it projects.
  • Skin no photo sees is filled by mirroring across the face midline, then by inpainting. A fill mask records which is which.
  • With three photos, colours are blended by view angle and the tone steps between photos are levelled. The output is face.obj, face.mtl and face_texture.png.

Read first Cameras and projection and Rendering, depth and back projection

Why you need it

The deliverable for Cybermed is a textured mesh in the original CT coordinates. The camera methods decide where the photo lands. The texturing decides what a reviewer actually sees. It also feeds our evaluation. The cross view test bakes a texture from the front photo and renders it at a side camera. So a mistake in the bake would look like a mistake in the camera.

Texturing is routine, but it has a dozen places to go quietly wrong. This page goes through them in order.

Meshes, texture images and UV coordinates

A mesh is a list of 3D points (vertices) and a list of triangles, each naming three vertices. The CT skin surface has about 300,000 vertices. A mesh has no colour of its own. To give it detailed colour you attach a texture, an ordinary image, and tell each triangle which part of the image to show.

That link is the UV coordinates. Each triangle corner gets a 2D position \((u, v)\) in the texture, with both numbers between 0 and 1. Inside the triangle, the colour comes from the matching point of the matching triangle in the image. Making UV coordinates is called unwrapping. Think of peeling the skin off the face and pressing it flat.

A curved surface cannot lie flat in one piece without tearing or stretching. So the unwrapper cuts it into pieces called charts. It flattens each chart with little stretch and packs them into the square, like pattern pieces on a sheet of fabric. The edges where charts were cut are seams.

We use xatlas for this. It runs on a decimated copy of the surface, meaning a copy with fewer triangles. Unwrapping 150,000 faces takes about a minute, so the result is cached. On our CT it makes 4371 charts after a Taubin smoothing pass (a gentle smoothing that does not shrink the surface), down from 5674 without it. That is about 500 texels per chart in a 2048 by 2048 texture. A texel is one pixel of the texture image.

Texture baking

Baking is the step that actually puts photo colour into the texture. It fills the texture texel by texel. The direction matters. You do not push photo pixels onto the surface. You pull. For every texel you ask three questions in a row.

  1. Which surface point is this texel?

    Find the chart triangle that contains the texel's centre in UV space. Find its barycentric coordinates there, three weights that say how close the point is to each corner and sum to 1. Apply the same weights to the triangle's 3D corners to get the 3D point. Our code builds a flat copy of the mesh with every vertex moved to \((u, v, 0)\) and shoots one ray per texel at it, which returns the triangle and the weights.

  2. Can the camera see that point?

    Three tests, described next.

  3. Which photo pixel shows it?

    Project the 3D point with the camera (see projection) and read the photo there, with bilinear sampling.

Visibility tests

Without these tests the photo would paint skin it never saw, such as the cheek behind the nose. A texel may take a photo colour only if the camera really saw its point. Our code uses three tests, and each one catches something the others miss.

  • Facing the camera. The triangle's outward normal (the direction it faces) must point toward the camera. Our code does not trust the CT's normals blindly. It checks their sign against the triangles the ray cast actually hit, and flips them all if the surface came out facing inward.
  • Not hidden. The nose hides part of the far cheek, and the chin hides the neck. Facing the camera is not enough. Our code renders a depth map from the camera, an image that stores the distance to the surface at each pixel. A triangle is accepted only when its depth agrees with the depth map at its pixel, within 1 mm.
  • Inside the skin mask. Near the outline, a surface point can project just outside the face in the photo, onto hair or the studio backdrop. Our code shrinks the rendered surface mask by 2 px. It also gates by the photo's segmentation mask, an image that marks which pixels are face skin. Gating by the mask removed all backdrop and hair from our texture.

The facing test and the grazing cutoff

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{n\cdot(C - c)}{\lVert C - c\rVert} \;>\; 0.35 \]
C
the camera centre
c
the centre of the triangle
n
the triangle's outward unit normal
θ
the angle between the normal and the direction to the camera

In words, the triangle must face the camera within about 70 degrees, not just face it at all. A worked example. If the normal points straight at the camera, \(\cos\theta = 1\) and the triangle passes. At 60 degrees, \(\cos\theta = 0.5\) and it still passes. At 75 degrees, \(\cos\theta = 0.26\) and it fails.

Why not just require \(\cos\theta > 0\)? A triangle seen almost edge on is visible, but one photo pixel gets smeared over several millimetres of skin. At a cutoff of 0.2 (78 degrees) the band near the outline still received badly stretched pixels. In a multi view bake, the weight also fades smoothly to zero over a band of 0.25 above the cutoff. So a stretched sample never outvotes a head on one.

Bilinear sampling

A projected point almost never lands on a pixel centre. Bilinear sampling blends the four nearest pixels, each weighted by how close the point is to it.

\[ c = (1-f_x)(1-f_y)\,c_{00} + f_x(1-f_y)\,c_{10} + (1-f_x)f_y\,c_{01} + f_x f_y\,c_{11} \]
c00 … c11
the colours of the four pixel centres around the point (top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right)
fx, fy
how far the point sits across and down between those centres, each from 0 to 1

In words, the colour is a mix of the four neighbours, and the closest neighbour gets the most say. A worked example. Take grey values 100, 200, 100 and 200 and a point with \(f_x = 0.25\) and \(f_y = 0.5\). The weights are 0.375, 0.125, 0.375 and 0.125, and the colour is \(37.5 + 25 + 37.5 + 25 = 125\).

This is smoother than taking the nearest pixel. It is also why the 2 px mask margin exists. The four pixel blend reaches one pixel past the point, so a point on the outline can pull in backdrop colour as a white smear.

Mirror fill and inpainting

A frontal photo sees only part of the head. Something has to go in the rest, and it should be honest about being invented. Our code fills in two stages.

  1. Mirror

    The face is roughly symmetric. For an empty texel, reflect its 3D point across the midline and look there instead. If the camera sees the mirrored point, take its colour. Our midline is the median x of the rigid landmarks, which is more reliable than the centre of the scan's bounding box. The mirrored point goes through the same visibility tests and skin mask. Otherwise the mirrored far cheek would pick up backdrop and hair.

  2. Inpaint

    Whatever is still empty is filled by growing colour inward from the edges of the known region. Our code uses OpenCV's Telea inpainting, a standard hole filling method. Very large regions (the scalp, the neck) are filled from a smooth skin tone field instead, so the back of the head does not become a smear.

A fill mask is written next to the texture, the same size. It records for every texel whether it came from a photo, a mirror or inpainting. A reviewer can then see which skin was measured and which was invented. With the front photo alone, about 17 percent of the surface is photo sourced, 7 percent mirrored and 76 percent inpainted. Most of the head is outside any frontal view.

Multi view blending and seams

Using all three photos covers more skin, but it brings its own problem. Many texels are seen by more than one photo. With A6's cameras, 66.8 percent of the photo sourced texels are reached by more than one photo. The bake blends them with view angle weights. Each photo's weight at a texel is its faded cosine, so a head on view counts most. The weights are normalised to sum to 1 at each texel. Blending all three photos lifts photo coverage from 16.5 to 24.3 percent and lowers the inpainted share from 76.5 to 72.2 percent.

We found two easy bugs here. The bake read the raw cosine instead of the faded weight that feathers a seam, and the blend weights were not normalised per texel.

The three photos were taken with the head turned under fixed studio light, and their exposure and white balance (colour tint) differ. Where one photo takes over from another, the skin tone jumps. That jump is a seam in the colour, even where the geometry is continuous. A second seam appears where photo texels meet invented ones.

Our texture polish

The polish removes those tone jumps without blurring the skin. It follows the order Brown and Lowe used for panorama stitching. First fix each photo globally, then fix what is left locally. It makes four changes.

  1. Per photo gain and offset

    For each side photo and each colour channel, fit one gain and one offset that best match it to the front photo. The fit is done in linear light (brightness values before the camera's gamma curve) on the texels both photos see. This removes the exposure and white balance difference.

  2. A smooth correction field

    What is left is a slowly varying difference, from light falling differently on a turned head. Solve a smooth additive correction for it. It is solved on the mesh vertex graph (vertices joined by triangle edges), not on the texture's pixel grid, so it stays continuous across every chart cut. Its smoothing length is 12 mm, so it can describe lighting but not skin detail.

  3. The front photo owns the features

    The eyes, brows, nostrils and lips are where the three photos do not show the same thing. So only the front photo paints them.

  4. A skin tone field for the fill

    Instead of one median colour, unseen skin takes the tone of the nearest seen skin, through a smooth field over the surface. Mirrored texels are levelled onto the same field.

Why the vertex graph. Two texels that touch on the skin are usually far apart in the texture image, because xatlas cut the surface into 4371 charts. A smoothing solve on the pixel grid would level each chart on its own and put a fresh step at every chart edge. On the mesh, neighbours stay neighbours. Each vertex value is an area weighted mean of a few hundred texels, and the field is much coarser than the vertex spacing.

Measured on A7's cameras, grey levels out of 255beforeafter polish
Tonal step between the photographs, mean8.406.03
Tonal step between the photographs, median4.393.04
Tonal step between the photographs, 90th percentile21.4516.28
Step between photo texels and fill texels, mean11.206.08
Step between photo texels and fill texels, median6.833.55
View disagreement on the same texels9.478.17
View disagreement after high pass (the "nothing got blurred" check)5.725.12

The last row is the safety check. A high pass keeps only the fine detail. If the polish had blurred skin detail, the fine detail disagreement between views would have changed a lot. It barely moved.

We also swept the smoothing length at 30, 15, 12, 8 and 4 mm. The seam step read 6.45, 6.16, 6.03, 5.69 and 4.74 grey levels. The high frequency disagreement stayed at 3.3 grey levels at every setting, so the field never carried detail. We chose 12 mm because below that the field starts to describe the registration error (about 1 mm of skin here) rather than the lighting. Bake plus fill went from 7.4 s to 11.9 s at 2048.

Ghosting (a doubled, blurry look where two photos disagree on position) was not the problem. Where views overlap they disagree by about 7 grey levels at the median, the same for A5's cameras as for A6's. Each photo is sampled through its own camera, so a per photo focal error is absorbed by that photo's own pose.

OBJ, MTL and PNG, and the V convention

The output is a folder of plain files that every 3D viewer reads.

face.obj           v x y z           vertex positions, CT frame, millimetres
                   vt u v            one texture coordinate per vertex
                   f a/a b/b c/c     triangles, vertex and vt indices (1 based)
face.mtl           newmtl face_texture
                   Kd 1 1 1          so a viewer does not darken the map
                   Ks 0 0 0          no specular highlight
                   map_Kd face_texture.png
face_texture.png   the baked texture, 8 bit RGB
face_fillmask.png  photo, mirrored or inpainted, per texel

The bottom left V convention. This one detail can turn the whole texture upside down. An image array starts at the top row, so row 0 is the top of the picture. OBJ texture coordinates start at the bottom left, so \(v = 0\) is the bottom row. Our code keeps \(v = 0\) at the top everywhere inside, like a numpy array, and flips exactly once, at export, writing \(1 - v\).

Flipping both the coordinates and the image is the usual cause of an upside down texture, so the round trip is tested on a synthetic square. Every export is also reloaded and compared with the input mesh to within 0.0001 mm, and rendered at the estimated camera to check the face landed on the face.

Where it shows up

Every method ends here, because a camera is only useful once the photo is painted through it. The cross view test reuses the bake. The side photos join the bake only once the cameras agree, so A6's joint solve and A7's refinement matter for the final look as much as for the numbers. A multi view bake goes to its own folder, so the cross view test never sees a texture that already holds the side photos.

Pitfalls

Watch out
  • Same view, perfect score. A texture baked through a camera reproduces the photo when rendered back through that same camera, whatever the camera is. Never judge a camera that way.
  • The outline. Grazing texels are stretched and bilinear sampling bleeds backdrop. Use a cosine cutoff, a mask margin and the segmentation mask.
  • Normals. A CT surface can come out facing inward. Check the sign against what the camera actually hit.
  • Invented skin. Most of the head is inpainted. Write the fill mask so nobody mistakes it for measurement.
  • The V flip. Flip once, at export, and test the round trip.
  • Expression. The CT's eyes and lips are closed and the photo's are open. The texture is projected as is, so the eyelids and the lip line are where a reviewer will see a seam.
Remember

Unwrap into charts. Then for every texel go texel to 3D point to photo pixel, and keep it only if the point faces the camera, is not hidden and is inside the skin mask.

Fill the rest by mirroring then inpainting, and record which is which in a fill mask.

Blend views by angle, then level the seams with a per photo gain and a smooth field on the mesh. Flip V once at export.

About 50 minutes

Paper P1arXiv 2305.10132, 2023Used in A1 and the base of family A

Automatic 3D Registration of Dental CBCT and Face Scan Data using 2D Projection Images

Hyoung Suk Park, Chang Min Hyun, Sang-Hwy Lee, Jin Keun Seo and Kiwan Jeon. National Institute for Mathematical Sciences (Daejeon) and Yonsei University (Seoul). arXiv preprint, version 3, July 2023.

Finding landmarks on a bare 3D surface is hard. Finding them on a picture of a face is a solved problem. This paper draws the 3D surface as pictures, runs an off the shelf 2D face detector on them, and lifts the 2D points back to 3D with a short formula. It is the idea our whole landmark family is built on.

The short version
  • Park lines up two 3D scans of one head, a dental CT and a colour face scan, with no training data.
  • It draws each surface as two grey pictures, lets a ready made 2D face detector mark ten landmarks, and turns each pair of 2D marks into one 3D point with a short formula.
  • Ten 3D landmark pairs give a first rotation and shift. ICP then polishes the fit on the parts of the face that do not move.
  • We kept the "render the CT, detect on the picture" idea for our method A1. We read depth from our own render and solve a camera with PnP, because our second input is a photo, not a surface.

Read first Face landmarks, Rendering, depth and back projection and ICP.

In one minute

A dental clinic has two scans of one patient. The CBCT gives bone, teeth and skin. A face scanner gives a second skin surface with colour, in its own coordinates. Park and colleagues render each surface as two shaded grey images and run Dlib, a free 2D face landmark detector, on them. A closed form formula turns each pair of 2D detections into one 3D landmark.

Ten landmark pairs give a first rigid alignment, meaning a rotation and a shift with no stretching. ICP then polishes it on the parts of the face that do not move. The mean surface error on three dental CBCT cases was 0.74 mm.

Where this sits in our project

This is A1, our baseline, and the start of every family A method (A2 to A7). We kept the core trick of detecting landmarks on a render of the CT skin.

We changed four things. We use MediaPipe (478 points) instead of Dlib (68 points). We read each landmark's 3D point from the render's depth map instead of using their two view formula. Our other side is a photo, not a second surface, so we solve a camera with PnP instead of a 3D rigid fit. PnP finds the camera position, direction and focal length from pairs of 3D points and their 2D spots in the photo. And there is no ICP, because a photo has no surface to slide on.

A1 scored a fit of 5.30 px (1.47 mm at face depth), a contour distance of 9.39 px and 25.18 dB cross view. Fit is the landmark error, contour is the outline error, and cross view checks the camera against the side photos (higher is better). Its focal length came out at 8348 px, far outside the 3300 to 4700 px range that four independent estimates agree on. That gap is why we built A2 to A7.

The problem they solve

Dentists and jaw surgeons plan treatment on one 3D model of bone, teeth and face. The bone comes from a cone beam CT (CBCT), a small X-ray CT built for the head. The coloured skin comes from a face scanner, a camera rig that measures the surface. Each machine uses its own coordinate system, so the face scan floats next to the CT, turned and shifted.

The fix is a rigid transformation. That is a rotation plus a shift, with no stretching. It has six numbers, three angles and three distances. Find the right six numbers and the face scan lands on the CT skin.

Two things make this hard. The surfaces do not quite match, because in a dental CBCT the patient often closes the eyes and bites on a plastic stick. And paired CT and face data is too rare and protected to train a network on. Their answer is to reuse a detector already trained on ordinary face photos.

The method step by step

  1. Make surfaces

    The CT volume is a 3D grid of density values. They keep the boundary where the density crosses the skin level, a threshold of -500 HU (Hounsfield units, the CT density scale). Marching cubes, a standard algorithm, turns that boundary into a triangle mesh. The face scanner already gives a surface. Call the face scan \(X\) and the CT skin \(Y\).

  2. Render two projection images of each surface

    Turn the surface by an angle \(\varphi\) about the vertical axis. Project it straight onto a flat plane and shade it with a point light. Do this at two angles, \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\). That gives four grey pictures in total, 1024 by 1024 pixels each.

  3. Detect 2D landmarks

    Dlib, a free library trained on ordinary photos, finds the face in each picture and places 68 points on it. From the 68 they keep 10 that change least between a CT session and a face scan session.

  4. Lift to 3D

    For each landmark, the two detections and the two known angles give its 3D position through Theorem II.1. Now both surfaces have the same ten named 3D points.

  5. Rigid fit

    Least squares finds the rotation and shift that bring the ten face scan points closest to the ten CT points.

  6. ICP on sub-surfaces

    Starting from that fit, ICP pairs every point of a stable patch with its nearest point on the other surface, refits, and repeats. The patches sit around the landmarks and leave out the lips and eyes.

The rest of this section explains each stage from the basics, in pipeline order.

Stage 2. The projection image

A CT skin surface has no colour, but a face detector was trained on photos. So the authors draw the surface the way light would show it, bright where the skin faces the light and dark where it turns away. That is enough for a detector to see a face.

From a surface to a grey picture

First you need a normal. At each point on a surface, the normal \(n\) is the unit vector that sticks straight out of the skin. On the tip of the nose it points forward. On the side of the nose it points sideways.

Second you need the dot product. For two unit vectors \(a\) and \(b\), \(a \cdot b = \cos\) of the angle between them. It is 1 when they point the same way, 0 when they are at right angles, and negative when they point apart.

Now the picture. After turning the surface by \(\varphi\), they put an image plane \(\Pi\) in front of it. For each pixel \((s, z)\) on that plane they shoot a line straight back toward the face and keep the first surface point it hits. That is equation (3) of the paper.

\[ x^{\varphi}(s,z) = \underset{x \,\in\, \ell(s,z)\, \cap\, X^{\varphi}}{\arg\min} \;\lVert x - (s, d, z) \rVert \]

In words, among all the skin points that lie on this pixel's line, pick the one nearest to the image plane. That is the point the pixel shows.

The pixel brightness is how directly that point faces the light, equation (4).

\[ I_{\varphi}(s,z) = \max\!\left( \frac{n\big(x^{\varphi}(s,z)\big) \cdot \big(q - x^{\varphi}(s,z)\big)}{\lVert q - x^{\varphi}(s,z) \rVert},\; 0 \right) \]

In words, a pixel is bright when the skin it shows faces the lamp and dark when the skin turns away.

X^φ
the surface after turning it by the angle \(\varphi\) about the vertical axis
(s, d, z)
a pixel on the image plane. \(s\) is sideways, \(z\) is height, and \(d\) is a depth far enough out that the plane sits in front of the face
ℓ(s, z)
the straight line through that pixel, parallel to the viewing direction
q
the position of a point light
n(x)
the unit normal of the surface at \(x\)
max(·, 0)
clips negative values, so skin facing away from the light is black rather than "negative bright"

Two words matter here. The lines \(\ell\) are all parallel, so this is an orthographic projection. A real camera is a pinhole. Its rays fan out from one point, so far things look smaller. In an orthographic picture nothing shrinks with distance, which makes Stage 4 much simpler.

The fraction in (4) is the cosine between the normal and the direction to the light. This is the classic Lambert shading model.

A worked example. Take a skin point at \(x = (0, 0, 0)\) with normal \(n = (0, 0, 1)\) and a light at \(q = (3, 0, 4)\). The direction to the light is \((3, 0, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0, 0.8)\). The dot product with \(n\) is 0.8, so the pixel is 80 percent bright. Move the light behind the head to \(q = (0, 0, -5)\) and the dot product becomes -1. The max clips it to 0, a black pixel.

Watch out

The shading changes with the light, and the detector's answer changes with the shading. On our CT we measured that MediaPipe moves central landmarks by 1 to 2 mm when only the light direction changes. In bad cases it moves them 5 to 10 mm. Park picks one light and keeps it fixed for both surfaces.

Stage 4. Two 2D points give one 3D point

This is the paper's main new piece. One image cannot tell you how deep a point sits, because the projection threw depth away. Two images from two angles can, for the same reason two eyes judge depth better than one.

The turn is about the vertical axis, so a landmark's height is the same in both images. The only work is in the flat top view. There a landmark sits at distance \(L\) from the axis and at angle \(\theta\). Turning the head by \(\varphi\) swings it to angle \(\theta + \varphi\), and the image records only its sideways position.

Theorem II.1 in plain steps

The paper writes the landmark in polar form, with \(y\) pointing toward the image plane, equation (5).

\[ x_j = (x_j, y_j, z_j) = (-L\sin\theta,\; L\cos\theta,\; z_j) \]

In words, instead of sideways and depth, describe the point by its distance \(L\) from the axis and its angle \(\theta\). The height \(z_j\) stays as it is.

After a turn by \(\varphi_i\), the sideways image coordinate is the first entry of the turned point.

\[ x^{\varphi_i}_j = -L \sin(\theta + \varphi_i), \qquad i = 1, 2 \]

In words, turning the head adds \(\varphi_i\) to the angle, and the picture records only the sideways part. We get two such readings, one per picture, and two unknowns, \(L\) and \(\theta\).

Write \(\theta_1 = \theta + \varphi_1\). The second reading is the first angle minus the gap, so a sine subtraction rule splits it into two pieces (equation 9).

\[ x^{\varphi_2}_j = -L\sin\big(\theta_1 - (\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)\big) = x^{\varphi_1}_j \cos(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2) + L\cos\theta_1 \,\sin(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2) \]

In words, the second reading equals a known piece built from the first reading plus one unknown piece, \(L\cos\theta_1\), times a known number.

Everything in it is known except \(L\cos\theta_1\). Solve for it (equation 10).

\[ L\cos\theta_1 = \frac{x^{\varphi_2}_j - x^{\varphi_1}_j \cos(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)}{\sin(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)} \]

In words, this is the depth of the turned point, computed from the two readings. Note the division by the sine of the angle gap. It comes back below.

You also know \(L\sin\theta_1 = -x^{\varphi_1}_j\) straight from the first reading. Two legs of a right triangle give the hypotenuse and the angle (equations 6 and 7).

\[ L = \sqrt{\frac{\big(x^{\varphi_2}_j - x^{\varphi_1}_j\cos(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)\big)^2}{\sin^2(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)} + \big(x^{\varphi_1}_j\big)^2}, \qquad \theta = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-x^{\varphi_1}_j}{L}\right) - \varphi_1 \]

In words, the depth and the first reading are the two legs of a right triangle. Pythagoras gives the distance \(L\), and the sine gives the angle.

L
distance of the landmark from the vertical rotation axis, seen from above
θ
its angle in the top view, measured so that \(\theta = 0\) points straight at the image plane
φ₁, φ₂
the two turn angles. The paper uses \(\varphi_2 = -\varphi_1\)
x^φ
the sideways coordinate of the Dlib detection in the image made at angle \(\varphi\)

The same thing as a 2 by 2 system. If you prefer linear algebra, write the point in the top view as \((x, z)\), sideways and depth. Turning by \(\varphi\) is a rotation matrix, and the image keeps the first row of the result, \(u = x\cos\varphi + z\sin\varphi\). Two images give two equations in two unknowns.

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \cos\varphi_1 & \sin\varphi_1 \\ \cos\varphi_2 & \sin\varphi_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix} \]

In words, each picture gives one equation, and two equations pin down the two unknowns. The determinant of that matrix is \(\sin(\varphi_2 - \varphi_1)\). Park's formula is the solution of this system written in polar form. Our animation code solves the system directly, and the two agree.

A worked example. Put a landmark at \(x = 2.00\) cm and \(y = 7.00\) cm in the top view. Then \(L = \sqrt{4 + 49} = 7.280\) and \(\theta = -15.9^\circ\). With \(\varphi_1 = 20^\circ\) the first image reads \(x^{\varphi_1} = -7.280 \sin(4.05^\circ) = -0.515\). With \(\varphi_2 = -20^\circ\) the second reads \(x^{\varphi_2} = 4.274\). The gap is 40°, where cos is 0.766 and sin is 0.643. So \(L\cos\theta_1 = (4.274 + 0.515 \times 0.766)/0.643 = 7.262\). Then \(L = \sqrt{7.262^2 + 0.515^2} = 7.280\) and \(\theta = 4.05^\circ - 20^\circ = -15.9^\circ\). You get back exactly the point you started with.

Why the two angles must be about 40 degrees apart

Look at the denominator \(\sin(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2)\) in equation (10). When the two angles are close, the sine is tiny. Any error in the detection gets divided by a tiny number. The paper's Corollary II.1 says exactly this. For a small gap \(\epsilon\), the error in \(L\) grows like \(\epsilon^{-1}\) times the detection error.

Corollary II.1

\[ |L - \hat L| = \epsilon^{-1}\,\Big|\,|\hat x^{\varphi_2}_j - \hat x^{\varphi_1}_j| - |x^{\varphi_2}_j - x^{\varphi_1}_j|\,\Big| + O(1), \qquad \epsilon = |\varphi_1 - \varphi_2| \to 0 \]
L̂, x̂
the true values. Plain \(L\) and \(x\) are the estimates from detected points
O(1)
a term that stays bounded as \(\epsilon\) shrinks

In words, when the two angles are close, a small slip of the detector becomes a large error in depth. In numbers, the factor \(1/\sin(\text{gap})\) is 1.56 at 40° and 5.76 at 10°. So a detector slip that costs about 1.6 mm of depth at 40° costs nearly 6 mm at 10°. In Figure 4 you can see why. The two viewing lines get closer to parallel, and a small shift of one line slides the crossing a long way.

The other end fails for a different reason. Turn the face too far and the detector itself starts to miss, because a face seen nearly side on does not look like the faces it was trained on. The authors found large errors for gaps of 20° or less and 60° or more.

On the CBCT images Dlib stopped finding the face beyond a gap of 70°. They chose a gap of \(2\pi/9\), which is 40°, with \(\varphi_2 = -\varphi_1\).

Stage 5. The rigid fit from landmark pairs

Now each surface has ten named 3D points. Point \(j\) on the face scan should land on point \(j\) on the CT. You want the single rotation and shift that does this best for all ten at once.

Least squares for a rotation and a shift

A rotation matrix \(R\) is a 3 by 3 matrix whose columns are three unit vectors at right angles. Multiplying a point by \(R\) turns it about the origin without changing any length. Adding a vector \(t\) shifts it. So the transform is \(T(x) = Rx + t\).

The fit is the least squares problem of equation (2). Least squares means you square every leftover distance and add them up, then pick the transform that makes that sum smallest.

\[ T = \underset{T}{\arg\min} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \lVert T x_j - y_j \rVert^2, \qquad J \ge 3 \]

In words, move the face scan landmarks with one rotation and one shift so that, added over all pairs, the squared gaps to their CT partners are as small as possible.

x_j
landmark \(j\) on the face scan \(X\)
y_j
the same landmark on the CT skin \(Y\)
J
the number of landmark pairs. Ten in the paper. You need at least three that are not on one line, because the transform has six unknowns and each pair gives three equations

This problem has an exact answer with no iterations, found by centring both point sets and decomposing a 3 by 3 matrix. The Procrustes page walks through it. Our animations use Horn's quaternion version.

A small check. Take \(p_1 = (0,0,0)\), \(p_2 = (1,0,0)\), \(p_3 = (0,1,0)\) and targets \(q_1 = (5,0,0)\), \(q_2 = (5,1,0)\), \(q_3 = (4,0,0)\). A turn of 90° about the vertical \(z\) axis sends \((1,0,0)\) to \((0,1,0)\) and \((0,1,0)\) to \((-1,0,0)\). Adding \(t = (5,0,0)\) lands all three exactly. The sum of squares is zero.

Figure 2, step 6, shows the limit of this stage. The ten lifted landmarks each carry some error, so the landmark fit is only close. In the paper the lifted 3D landmarks were 4.6 to 7.9 mm off the hand marked positions, depending on the subject and the surface. That is why a second stage exists.

Stage 6. ICP on stable sub-surfaces

The landmark fit is only close, so it needs a polish. ICP (iterative closest point) does not need named points. It guesses the pairs. Each point on one surface is paired with the nearest point on the other. Then the same least squares fit runs on those guessed pairs, the surface moves, and the guessing starts again.

The ICP loop, equations (16) and (17)

\[ T^{(k)} = \underset{T}{\arg\min}\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \big\lVert T\big(T^{(k-1)} x_i\big) - y_{j^*} \big\rVert^2, \qquad y_{j^*} = \underset{y_j \in Y_{sub}}{\arg\min}\; \lVert T^{(k-1)} x_i - y_j \rVert^2 \]

In words, the right half pairs each face scan point with its nearest CT point. The left half finds the rotation and shift that best closes those pairs. Round \(k\) starts from where round \(k-1\) left the scan.

T^(0)
the landmark fit from Stage 5
x_i
one of the \(N\) points of the face scan sub-surface \(X_{sub}\)
y_j*
its nearest point on the CT sub-surface \(Y_{sub}\) under the current transform

The paper writes the update in the form of Go-ICP. The idea is the plain ICP loop. Each round cannot make the sum of squares worse, because both the pairing step and the fitting step only lower it. That is why ICP settles.

It settles on the nearest minimum, though, so it needs a good start. Here the start is the landmark fit.

The sub-surfaces \(X_{sub}\) and \(Y_{sub}\) are patches cut around the landmarks, on the forehead, nose and cheeks. The lips and closed eyes are left out. If they were in, ICP would pull the face scan's open mouth toward the CT's bite stick mouth and tilt everything.

How they score it

The scores decide how to read the results table, so they matter.

Three error measures

For landmarks, a root mean square distance to hand placed points (equation 18).

\[ E_{poi} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J} \lVert k_j - \hat k_j \rVert^2} \]

In words, square each landmark's distance \(\lVert k_j - \hat k_j \rVert\) from its hand placed position \(\hat k_j\), average, and take the square root. For two landmarks 3 mm and 4 mm off, that is \(\sqrt{(9 + 16)/2} = 3.54\) mm.

For surfaces, two distances from each moved face scan point to the nearest CT point. The supremum is the worst one, the mean is the average (equations 19 and 20).

\[ E_{sup} = \sup_{x \in T(X_{sub})} \; \inf_{y \in Y_{sub}} \lVert x - y \rVert, \qquad E_{mean} = \frac{1}{|X_{sub}|}\sum_{x \in T(X_{sub})} \; \inf_{y \in Y_{sub}} \lVert x - y \rVert \]

In words, for every point of the moved face scan, find the distance to the nearest CT point. \(E_{sup}\) reports the largest of these distances and \(E_{mean}\) the average.

inf
the smallest value, here the distance to the nearest CT point
sup
the largest value, here the worst point of the face scan
|X_sub|
the number of points in the sub-surface

Note what \(E_{mean}\) measures. It is how close the two surfaces lie, not whether matching anatomy sits on matching anatomy. A surface can slide along itself and keep a small \(E_{mean}\). For the colour maps in their figures they also use a signed version, positive on one side of the CT skin and negative on the other (equation 21).

What they measured

The data was small. Three dental CBCT scans came from a RAYSCAN Studio scanner (0.3 mm voxels, 20 by 20 cm field of view) with face scans from a RayFace 200. For a second test they collected 20 hospital multi detector CT (MDCT) scans with matching face scans. The MDCT table reports ten subjects.

The lifted 3D landmarks were not precise on their own. Against hand placed points the average error over three subjects was 6.07 mm on the CBCT surface and 5.35 mm on the face scan. The final number is good because ICP cleans up after them.

Dental CBCT, 3 subjects (Table I)E_sup mmE_mean mm
CPD then ICP41.54 ± 4.0512.75 ± 3.73
FPFH then ICP8.26 ± 1.781.81 ± 0.32
Proposed, landmarks only7.56 ± 0.692.57 ± 0.78
Proposed, landmarks then ICP4.15 ± 0.850.74 ± 0.18
Hospital MDCT, ten subjects (Table II)E_sup mmE_mean mm
Manual alignment by a surgeon with more than 20 years of experience, then ICP2.29 ± 0.700.42 ± 0.12
CPD then ICP30.35 ± 17.379.01 ± 5.82
FPFH then ICP3.18 ± 1.260.70 ± 0.46
Proposed, landmarks only7.69 ± 3.603.10 ± 2.12
