CPD and FPFH are two standard automatic ways to get a rough alignment without landmarks. Both were followed by the same ICP. The landmark start gave the best final fit on both datasets. On MDCT it matched or beat the expert's manual start. The per subject CBCT means were 0.51, 0.76 and 0.95 mm.

Weak points

  • The dental result rests on three people. The MDCT result rests on ten.
  • The landmarks are 5 to 6 mm off on average. The final accuracy comes from ICP, and ICP only works from a start that is already close.
  • \(E_{mean}\) rewards surfaces lying on top of each other. It does not prove that the nose tip landed on the nose tip.
  • The CT must show the nose and brows. Many dental CBCT scans have a smaller field of view.
  • The fit is rigid. The mouth and jaw move between sessions, and the authors list non rigid matching near the mouth as future work. That future work is roughly the Amberg paper.
  • The light, the angles and the ten chosen points are all fixed by hand.

How we used it

Our task looks like Park's, but our second input is a frontal studio photograph, not a surface. That one change breaks the second half of their pipeline, so we kept the first half and rebuilt the rest.

What we kept

We kept the trick of reusing a 2D face detector on a rendered picture of a colourless surface. Nothing is trained. The detector's numbering does the matching for free, since landmark 4 is the nose tip on the render and on the photo. We also kept their rule that only stable landmarks go into the solve. Park keeps 10 of Dlib's 68. We keep 22 of MediaPipe's 478 on the nose, eye corners, cheekbones, jaw and chin, and leave out eyelids, lips and the face outline.

What we changed and why

StagePark et al.Ours, A1Why
DetectorDlib, 68 pointsMediaPipe Face Landmarker, 478 pointsSame numbering on render and photo, and a denser rigid subset
2D to 3DTwo renders and Theorem II.1One render, read the depth mapWe own the renderer, so the depth of every pixel is known. No triangulation, and no \(1/\sin\) error growth
Other sideA second 3D surfaceA 2D photoThat is the task
AlignmentRigid 3D to 3D fit, 6 numbersPnP, 3D to 2D, 6 pose numbers plus the focal lengthA photo has no depth. The photo had no EXIF, so the focal length is unknown too
RefinementICP on stable patchesNone in A1No second surface to slide against. Later methods refine with dense image matches instead

When we render the CT we also keep, for every pixel, the distance along its ray to the surface. A landmark at pixel \((u, v)\) with stored depth \(d\) sits at the 3D point \(d\,K^{-1}[u, v, 1]^\top\) in the render camera's frame, where \(K\) is the render camera's intrinsic matrix. Our code does the same thing by casting the pixel's ray against the mesh. The back projection page has the details. Any landmark whose ray misses the mesh is dropped. On our CT, 7 render landmarks missed, mostly at the top of the forehead where the scan is cut off.

The camera solve then runs in three stages. First, RANSAC with EPnP finds a pose and an inlier set at a starting focal length. EPnP is a fast direct PnP formula. RANSAC runs it on small random subsets and keeps the answer most landmarks agree with, the inliers. Second, Levenberg-Marquardt refines the pose by shrinking the squared errors step by step, as in Figure 6.

Third, a final least squares over rotation, translation and the log of the focal length uses a Huber loss of 4 px. Huber counts small errors squared and large ones only linearly, which stops a few bad points from dominating. On the front photo RANSAC kept 19 of the 22 landmarks.

What A1 got

Read the A1 row with the measures in mind. The fit of 5.30 px is the second best of the family, but fit only says the landmarks agree with MediaPipe's photo landmarks.

The landmark free measures tell a different story. The rendered outline sits 9.39 px from the photo's face outline, the worst of the family. The cross view score of 25.18 dB is the weakest of the methods that hold together on all three photos. Only A3, whose side focal lengths land far apart, scores lower.

The focal length of 8348 px is about twice what four independent estimates say. Its focal plateau, the range of focal lengths that fit almost equally well, spans a factor of 4.30. So the solve could not pin the focal length down.

The cause is the single render. MediaPipe's answer on one render is one draw from a noisy process. Central landmarks move 1 to 2 mm with the light alone, and the jaw points slide 10 to 30 mm along the outline as the view changes. MediaPipe also reads the CT eyes as closed (blink scores 0.76 and 0.61 on the render), which moves the eye corner points it reports.

Every later family A method attacks one of these. A2 averages over 40 renders (see Paulsen). A3 stops detecting on the CT and fits a template instead (see Amberg). A4 snaps points to curvature features. A5 to A7 combine them, share one focal length over three photos and refine with dense matches.

Remember

Park turns 3D landmark detection into 2D detection on rendered pictures, with no training.

Two views recover depth, but the error grows like one over the sine of the angle gap, so they use 40°.

We kept the render and detect idea, read depth from our own depth map, and solved a camera with PnP because our other side is a photo.

If they ask you

"Why not use Park's method directly?"

Park registers two 3D surfaces. Our second input is a 2D photo with no depth, so their rigid 3D fit and their ICP have nothing to work on. We kept their first half, render and detect, and replaced the second half with a camera solve.

"Why one render and a depth map instead of two views?"

We render the CT ourselves, so we already know the depth at every pixel. Two views would add a triangulation whose error grows as the views get closer, and need the detector to agree with itself across views, which it does not reliably do.

"What did your version of it score?"

A1 fits the landmarks to 5.30 px, about 1.47 mm at face depth, but its outline is 9.4 px off and its focal length came out near 8300 px against a 3300 to 4700 px consensus. That told us one render is not enough, and the rest of family A fixes that.

Building blocks used

Face landmarks · Cameras and projection · Rendering, depth and back projection · Least squares · Procrustes alignment · ICP · PnP · RANSAC

About 45 minutes

Paper P2ACCV 2018Used in A2 and through it A5

Multi-view Consensus CNN for 3D Facial Landmark Placement

Rasmus R. Paulsen, Kristine Aavild Juhl, Thilde Marie Haspang, Thomas Hansen, Melanie Ganz and Gudmundur Einarsson. Technical University of Denmark and Copenhagen. ACCV 2018, arXiv 1910.06007.

One rendered view of a face can fool a landmark detector. A hundred views rarely fool it the same way. This paper renders a 3D face from many angles, detects landmarks in every view, and keeps the 3D point that most views agree on.

The short version
  • A landmark detector on one rendered view of a face can be wrong. Many views are rarely wrong in the same way.
  • Paulsen renders a 3D face from 100 random directions, runs a 2D network in each view, and turns each 2D guess into a 3D ray.
  • RANSAC throws out the rays that disagree. Least squares finds the point closest to the rest, and that point is snapped to the skin.
  • Our A2 does the same with MediaPipe on 40 renders of the CT. It uses 3D points on the mesh instead of rays, a 3 mm ball and a geometric median, and keeps each landmark's spread as its uncertainty.

Read first Park et al. (our A1), RANSAC and Rendering, depth and back projection.

In one minute

Look at a 3D face from 100 random directions. In each view a 2D network marks each landmark, which says the landmark lies somewhere on one line of sight. A hundred views give up to a hundred lines, and some are wrong.

RANSAC throws those out. Least squares then finds the point closest to the remaining lines, and that point is moved onto the surface. The method scored 2.42 mm mean error on the BU-3DFE benchmark, against 2.88 mm for the best earlier method. It also worked on a colourless MR skin surface when fed depth and curvature pictures.

Where this sits in our project

This is A2. We kept the consensus idea. Render many views, detect in each one, and only trust what the views agree on.

We changed three things. We did not train a network. We run MediaPipe on 40 renders of the CT with varied angles and lights. Each detection is back projected onto the mesh, which means its pixel's line of sight is followed until it hits the CT surface. So it becomes a 3D point instead of a ray. And the consensus is an inlier ball plus a geometric median per landmark, with the spread of the cloud kept as that landmark's uncertainty.

A2 dropped three sliding jaw points by itself, with no hand written list. The 19 rigid landmarks it kept scatter 0.74 to 2.05 mm across views. On the front photo A2 scored a fit of 1.39 mm, a contour of 8.40 px and 25.37 dB cross view, all better than A1. Its spread values became the per landmark weights in A5.

The problem they solve

Doctors measure faces by marking landmarks on 3D scans. A landmark is a named anatomical point that exists on every face, such as the outer corner of the eye (exocanthion, Ex) or the point under the nose (subnasale, Sn). Marking them by hand is slow, and two experts put them in slightly different places. In 2018, deep networks had become very good at 2D landmarks in photos. 3D scans had not caught up, because a mesh is not a grid of pixels and an ordinary convolutional network cannot read it directly.

The authors' answer is to turn the 3D problem back into many 2D problems. The input is a face surface. The output is a set of 3D landmark positions in millimetres, ideally sitting on the surface.

The method step by step

  1. Render from 100 random views

    Put the scan near the origin. Place a virtual camera at 100 random positions around it, each one aimed at the origin. The projection is orthographic, so nothing shrinks with distance. Store each camera so the projection can be undone later.

  2. Draw several pictures per view

    A plain grey shaded view (they call it geometry), a depth map, a mean curvature map and, if the scan has texture, the colour image. Each is 256 by 256 pixels.

  3. Run one network on all views

    A two stack hourglass network, a CNN that shrinks the picture and then grows it back, reads the stacked pictures and outputs one heatmap per landmark. The brightest pixel of a heatmap is the 2D guess. Guesses with a peak below 0.5 are ignored.

  4. Turn guesses into rays

    The stored camera turns each 2D guess into a 3D line. For one landmark this gives up to 100 lines.

  5. Find where the rays agree

    RANSAC starts from three random rays at a time and keeps the point most rays pass near. Least squares on those inlier rays gives the final point.

  6. Snap to the surface

    The point is moved to the closest point on the scan, found with an octree search. An octree splits space into nested boxes so the nearest point is found fast.

Stage 1 and 2. Many views, several kinds of picture

Why render at all? A convolutional network (CNN) is a stack of small learned filters that slide over a grid of pixels. A mesh has no grid, so rendering gives the network what it was built for. The authors note that rendering many views beat the alternative of filling a coarse 3D voxel grid, which runs out of memory fast.

The kinds of picture matter for us. A depth map stores at each pixel how far the surface is from the camera. Theirs is the OpenGL z-buffer, with the clipping planes pulled tight around the scan so the precision is good.

A curvature map shades each point by how sharply the surface bends there, so the nose tip and the eye sockets stand out. They estimate curvature by fitting a small sphere to the neighbours within 10 mm of each vertex, which is less noisy than using only the vertices joined to it. Depth and curvature need no colour. That is what lets the method run on CT and MR skin, which have none.

The camera positions are random rather than a fixed grid. The authors believe this also acts as extra data augmentation in training. The pose of the head is not assumed to be known. They only need the rough direction the face points.

Stage 3. Heatmaps

The network's output decides how a guess and its confidence are read. A network could output two numbers per landmark, the pixel coordinates. Pose and face networks found it works better to output a whole image per landmark instead, called a heatmap. Bright pixels mean "the landmark is probably here". The guess is the brightest pixel, and the brightness tells you how sure the network is.

What the network is trained to draw

For training, each true landmark is turned into a target heatmap. It is a Gaussian bump centred on the landmark's projected 2D position \(u^*\).

\[ H(u) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert u - u^* \rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \]

In words, the target picture is 1 at the true landmark and fades smoothly to 0 as you move away from it.

u
a pixel position \((x, y)\) in the 256 by 256 heatmap
u*
where the true landmark projects in this view
σ
the width of the bump in pixels

At the landmark the value is 1. One \(\sigma\) away it is \(e^{-1/2} \approx 0.61\). Two \(\sigma\) away it is \(e^{-2} \approx 0.14\). The network learns to reproduce these bumps with a cross entropy loss. At test time the guess is the pixel with the largest value.

\[ \hat u = \underset{u}{\arg\max}\; \hat H(u), \qquad \text{kept only if } \hat H(\hat u) \ge 0.5 \]

In words, the guess \(\hat u\) is the brightest pixel of the predicted heatmap \(\hat H\). It is used only if that pixel is at least half as bright as a perfect peak.

The hourglass network shrinks the 256 by 256 input to 128 by 128 inside, then upsamples the heatmap back to 256 by 256 so the peak can be placed finely. Two hourglasses run in a row, and both outputs are scored in training, which the paper calls intermediate supervision. The peak is a whole pixel. The authors list sub-pixel peak finding as future work.

Why many views fix single view mistakes

This is the core idea of the paper. A single view can be wrong in two ways. Its guess can be a little off, which is noise. Or it can be badly off, because the landmark is hidden, seen at a grazing angle, or confused with a look alike. With one view you cannot tell which case you are in.

With many views, small errors point in different directions in 3D, because every view's image plane faces a different way. Averaging them shrinks the noise. Bad guesses are rare and disagree with each other, so they do not line up with the crowd. A consensus step can spot and drop them.

Stage 4. From a 2D guess to a 3D ray

To combine views you need them in 3D. Each view was made by a camera that the authors stored. Undoing a projection cannot give a point, because the projection threw depth away. It gives a line, called a ray. Every 3D point on that ray projects to the same pixel.

A ray from an orthographic view

Write a ray as a start point \(a\) and a unit direction \(n\). The points on it are \(a + s\,n\) for any number \(s\).

\[ r(s) = a + s\,n, \qquad \lVert n \rVert = 1 \]

In words, start at \(a\) and walk any distance \(s\) along \(n\). Every place you can reach is on the ray. With \(a = (0, 0, 0)\) and \(n = (0, 0, 1)\), the value \(s = 5\) gives the point \((0, 0, 5)\).

In an orthographic view every ray has the same direction, the viewing direction. Only the start point changes with the pixel. If the view's image plane has unit axes \(e_x\) and \(e_y\) and centre \(o\), then pixel \((x, y)\) gives \(a = o + x\,e_x + y\,e_y\) (after scaling pixels to millimetres) and \(n\) is the viewing direction. The paper does this with the inverse of each view's stored camera matrix. For a real pinhole camera the rays fan out from the camera centre instead, but the next step works the same.

Stage 5a. The point closest to many rays

In practice the rays never meet in one point. So the paper asks for the point with the smallest sum of squared distances to all of them. This is a least squares problem with a closed form answer.

From one distance to the paper's equation (1)

Distance from a point to one ray. Take the vector from the ray's start to the point, \(d = p - a\). Split it into a part along the ray and a part across it. The part along the ray has length \(d \cdot n\). By Pythagoras, the part across it, which is the distance you want, satisfies the formula below.

\[ \text{dist}^2(p, \text{ray}) = d^\top d - (d^\top n)^2 = (p - a)^\top (I - n n^\top)(p - a). \]

In words, the squared distance to the ray is the squared length of \(d\) minus the squared part of \(d\) that runs along the ray.

The matrix \(I - n n^\top\) removes the component along \(n\). It is a projection matrix onto the plane at right angles to the ray. You can check it on a flat example. A ray through \(a = (0, 0)\) along \(n = (1, 0)\) and a point \(p = (3, 4)\) give \(d^\top d = 25\) and \((d^\top n)^2 = 9\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{16} = 4\). That is the height of \(p\) above the \(x\) axis, as it should be.

Sum over all rays. This is equation (1) of the paper.

\[ \sum_i d_i^2 = \sum_i \Big[ (p - a_i)^\top (p - a_i) - \big((p - a_i)^\top n_i\big)^2 \Big] \]

In words, add up the squared distances from the point \(p\) to every ray \(i\). The best \(p\) makes this total smallest.

Set the gradient to zero. Each term is a bowl shaped quadratic in \(p\), and so is their sum. The bottom of the bowl is where the gradient is zero.

\[ \nabla_p \sum_i d_i^2 = 2 \sum_i (I - n_i n_i^\top)(p - a_i) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\Big[\sum_i (I - n_i n_i^\top)\Big]}_{S'} \, p = \underbrace{\sum_i (I - n_i n_i^\top)\, a_i}_{C'} \]

In words, the bottom of the bowl is where a 3 by 3 matrix \(S'\) times the point equals a vector \(C'\), both built only from the rays. One small linear solve gives the point.

The paper writes \(S = \sum_i (n_i n_i^\top - I)\) and \(C = \sum_i (n_i n_i^\top - I) a_i\), which are \(-S'\) and \(-C'\). The signs cancel, and \(p = S^{+} C\).

a_i, n_i
start point and unit direction of ray \(i\)
I
the 3 by 3 identity matrix
S⁺
the pseudo inverse of \(S\). It equals the ordinary inverse when \(S\) is invertible, and still gives a sensible answer when it is not, for example when all rays are parallel and the depth along them is undetermined

A worked example. In 2D, take ray 1 through \((0, 1)\) along \((1, 0)\) and ray 2 through \((2, 0)\) along \((0, 1)\). Then \(I - n_1 n_1^\top = \mathrm{diag}(0, 1)\) and \(I - n_2 n_2^\top = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0)\). Their sum \(S'\) is the identity. And \(C' = \mathrm{diag}(0,1)(0,1)^\top + \mathrm{diag}(1,0)(2,0)^\top = (2, 1)\). So \(p = (2, 1)\), which is exactly where the two lines cross. With a third noisy ray the answer moves to a compromise between all three.

This is the same kind of system as Park's two view formula. Two rays from views that are nearly parallel give an \(S'\) that is close to singular, and the answer becomes unstable along the rays. Many views from many directions make \(S'\) well conditioned.

Stage 5b. RANSAC over rays

RANSAC (random sample consensus) protects least squares from wild data. Pick the smallest random sample that defines an answer. Measure how much of the rest agrees with it. Repeat many times and keep the sample with the most agreement. Then fit again on everything that agreed.

Two rays already define a closest point, but the paper starts each try from three random rays.

A ray counts as an inlier when its distance to the candidate point is below a threshold. The paper does not state its threshold value. The try with the most inliers wins, and the final point is the least squares fit on its inliers.

The final point may float a little in front of or behind the skin, because rays only constrain it in their own directions. So the last step moves it to the closest point on the scan.

What they measured

Two datasets. DTU-3D has 601 uncropped face scans (with ears, neck and shoulders) from a Canfield Vectra M3 scanner, each with 73 hand placed landmarks. They trained on 541 and validated on 60. BU-3DFE has 100 people with seven expressions each, 2500 textured scans with 83 landmarks. They trained on 2000 scans (80 people) and validated on 500 (20 people), with colour renders only. All error numbers are 3D distances in millimetres to the hand placed points.

The new method beats every earlier method on every landmark except one. Grewe's subnasale was better, 1.97 against 2.52 mm. Note that the means average over different sets of landmarks, so they are not a strict like for like comparison.

  • DTU-3D. Many landmarks land within about 2 mm, close to what an experienced human achieves. The chin and eyebrows are worst. Human annotators disagree by about 6 mm on the chin, so part of that error is in the labels.
  • Which pictures. Colour renders did best. Depth plus curvature did nearly as well. Depth alone was poor around the chin. Adding all channels together did not help.
  • MR skin. On one noisy MR skin surface with depth plus curvature, eye and nose landmarks were off by 2 to 3 mm. The chin was worse.
  • Number of views. Going from 25 to 100 views lowered the error by less than a millimetre.
  • Speed. About 20 seconds for 100 renderings on one GPU, with no effort spent on speed.

Weak points

  • It needs a trained network and labelled 3D scans for training. A new scan type needs new training data.
  • Smooth regions stay uncertain. On the chin and brows every view sees little detail, and a guess can slide along the surface instead of crossing other rays cleanly.
  • The 2D guess is a whole pixel, so precision is tied to the heatmap resolution.
  • The CT and MR claim rests on one MR scan.
  • Expressions are part of BU-3DFE, but closed eyes against open eyes, our exact problem, is not tested.

How we used it

Our first method, A1, trusted one render. Before building A2 we measured what that costs. We rendered the CT 45 times (yaw -20° to 20°, pitch -10° to 10°, three light directions), ran MediaPipe on each, back projected, and measured how far each landmark scattered around its median.

So one render is one draw from a noisy process. Paulsen's paper is the published answer to exactly that, and A2 follows its shape.

What we kept

Render the surface many times. Detect in every view. Combine the detections with a consensus that ignores views which disagree. Snap the answer to the surface. Paulsen's ablation also set our view count. They saw under a millimetre of gain from 25 to 100 views, so we use 40.

What we changed and why

PartPaulsen et al.Ours, A2Why
DetectorOwn hourglass CNN, trained on 3D scansMediaPipe, pretrained on photosWe have one patient and no labelled CT faces to train on
Views100 random, orthographic40 on a fixed low discrepancy pattern over yaw -25° to 25° and pitch -15° to 15°, 900 by 900, pinholeThe views stay near frontal, like the photo. A fixed pattern gives the same views on every run
What variesViewpointViewpoint and lighting. Three grey light setups and one photo like skin render, cycled over the viewsWe measured that lighting alone moves MediaPipe's answer
2D to 3DA ray per detectionA point per detection, by casting its ray onto the meshWe have the exact surface, so the ray's hit point is the 3D candidate
ConsensusRANSAC on rays, least squaresBiggest 3 mm ball, geometric median, three refreshesPoints instead of rays, and a median resists strays inside the ball
UncertaintyNot keptThe median distance of the inliers becomes \(\sigma\) per landmarkPnP can weight each landmark by \(1/\sigma\)

Why points and not rays? Our 40 views span only 50° of yaw. Rays from such close views cross at shallow angles, which is the same instability Park's corollary describes.

We also have something Paulsen's method does not use, the exact mesh we rendered. A ray cast from the render camera through the detected pixel hits the mesh at one point, so the depth is known and nothing needs triangulating. The back projection page covers the details. We reject a hit when the surface there is nearly edge on to the view (the cosine between normal and ray below 0.20), because a tiny pixel error there moves the hit by millimetres.

The consensus step below is what turns 40 noisy detections into one point and one uncertainty per landmark.

The consensus per landmark

Landmark \(j\) now has a cloud of candidate 3D points \(x_1, \dots, x_K\), one from each view where MediaPipe found the face and the ray hit the mesh. \(K\) is at most 40.

1. The biggest ball. For every candidate \(x_i\), count how many candidates lie within \(\rho = 3\) mm of it. Keep the \(x_i\) with the largest count. This is RANSAC with a sample size of one, run over every possible sample, so there is no randomness at all.

\[ i^* = \underset{i}{\arg\max}\; \big|\{k : \lVert x_k - x_i \rVert \le \rho\}\big| \]

In words, the seed \(x_{i^*}\) is the candidate with the most neighbours within 3 mm.

2. The geometric median of the members. The geometric median is the point with the smallest sum of distances (not squared distances) to the members.

\[ m = \underset{y}{\arg\min} \sum_{k \in \text{in}} \lVert x_k - y \rVert \]

In words, \(m\) is the point whose total distance to all ball members is smallest.

3. Refresh. Recentre the ball on \(m\), recount the members, recompute \(m\). Up to three times, or until the members stop changing.

4. Keep or drop. If fewer than 8 candidates are inside the ball, drop the landmark. Otherwise its uncertainty is the median distance of the members from \(m\), with a floor of 0.5 mm, and its PnP weight is \(1/\sigma\).

\[ \sigma_j = \max\big(0.5\ \text{mm},\; \mathrm{median}_{k \in \text{in}} \lVert x_k - m \rVert\big) \]

In words, the uncertainty is the typical distance of the members from the median, but never below 0.5 mm. If members sit 0.3, 0.9 and 1.2 mm from \(m\), then \(\sigma = 0.9\) mm and the weight \(1/\sigma\) is about 1.1.

The geometric median and Weiszfeld's algorithm

Why a median and not a mean? The answer decides how far one stray view can move a landmark. The mean minimises the sum of squared distances. Squaring makes a far point very loud. A point 10 mm away counts 100 times as much as one 1 mm away. The geometric median minimises plain distances, so the far point counts only 10 times as much. In one dimension the geometric median is the ordinary median. For the numbers 0, 1, 2 and 10 the mean is 3.25 but any value between 1 and 2 minimises the sum of distances.

Weiszfeld's update

The sum of distances has no closed form minimum in 2D or 3D. Set its gradient to zero anyway.

\[ \nabla_y \sum_k \lVert x_k - y \rVert = -\sum_k \frac{x_k - y}{\lVert x_k - y \rVert} = 0 \]

In words, at the median the unit arrows from \(y\) toward every candidate cancel out. Each candidate pulls with the same strength, however far away it is.

Write \(w_k = 1/\lVert x_k - y \rVert\) and solve for the \(y\) that appears outside the weights. That gives a weighted mean, with weights that depend on the current guess.

\[ y^{(t+1)} = \frac{\sum_k w_k^{(t)}\, x_k}{\sum_k w_k^{(t)}}, \qquad w_k^{(t)} = \frac{1}{\lVert x_k - y^{(t)} \rVert} \]

In words, the next guess is a weighted average of the candidates. Each weight is one over that candidate's distance from the current guess.

y^(t)
the guess after \(t\) rounds. We start from the coordinate wise median
w_k
the weight of candidate \(k\). Near points get a big say, far points a small one

This is iteratively reweighted least squares. Each round is a weighted average, and the weights are refreshed from the new guess. If a candidate sits exactly on the guess its weight would be infinite, so that candidate is skipped for the round. Our code runs up to 64 rounds and stops when a step moves less than \(10^{-7}\) mm.

A worked example. Take the 1D points 0, 1, 2 and 10, and start at \(y = 3.25\), the mean. The weights are \(1/3.25, 1/2.25, 1/1.25, 1/6.75\), about 0.31, 0.44, 0.80 and 0.15. The new guess is \((0 + 0.44 + 1.60 + 1.48)/1.70 = 2.07\). One round has already pulled the guess most of the way from 3.25 toward the median interval of 1 to 2, because the far point at 10 got the smallest weight.

What A2 got

All 40 renders contained a face. Of the 468 mesh landmarks, 434 passed the consensus and 34 were dropped. The median spread over the kept ones was 1.28 mm. On the 22 rigid landmarks used for the camera, three jaw points were dropped for having too few inlier views, 397, 58 and 288. Jaw point 172 survived with exactly 8 of its 26 candidates, right at the limit. The camera was solved on the remaining 19.

Compared with A1, every landmark free measure improved. The outline moved closer (8.40 against 9.39 px), the silhouette overlap rose, and cross view went from 25.18 to 25.37 dB. The focal length dropped from 8348 to 5581 px, toward the 3300 to 4700 px range the independent estimates agree on.

The fit in pixels got worse, 6.43 against 5.30 px. Fit only measures agreement with MediaPipe's photo landmarks, so the landmark free measures are the ones to trust here.

The camera distance spread across the three photos also got worse, 238.5 mm, because A2 still solves each photo's focal length on its own. A6 fixes that by sharing one focal length.

The central landmarks that survive still scatter 0.7 to 1.4 mm across views. That is the honest uncertainty of running a photo detector on a CT render, and A2 is what measured it.

Watch out

A consensus removes disagreement, not bias. If MediaPipe puts the eye corner in the same wrong place in every render, because the CT eyes are closed, all 40 candidates agree and the ball keeps them. The closed eye bias is the reason A3 and A4 exist.

Remember

Many views turn one fragile detection into a vote, and RANSAC drops the views that disagree.

The point closest to many rays solves \(\big[\sum (I - nn^\top)\big] p = \sum (I - nn^\top) a\).

A2 uses points on the mesh instead of rays, a 3 mm ball and a geometric median, and keeps the spread as \(\sigma\).

If they ask you

"How is A2 different from your single render method?"

It renders the CT 40 times with different angles and lights, runs MediaPipe on every render, and only keeps a landmark if at least 8 views put it within 3 mm of each other. The spread becomes a weight in the camera solve.

"Why a geometric median and not an average?"

An average lets one bad view pull the answer by its squared distance. The median weights each view by one over its distance, so a stray that slipped into the ball hardly moves it.

"Did multi view fix the jaw problem?"

It exposed it. The jaw points slide along the outline from view to view, so they never form a tight cluster. Three of the six rigid jaw points were dropped automatically, with no hand written list.

Building blocks used

Face landmarks · Cameras and projection · Rendering, depth and back projection · Least squares and robust fitting · RANSAC · PnP

About 55 minutes

Paper P3CVPR 2007Used in A3

Optimal Step Nonrigid ICP Algorithms for Surface Registration

Brian Amberg, Sami Romdhani and Thomas Vetter. University of Basel. IEEE CVPR 2007.

You have a clean generic face mesh and a messy scan of one person. This paper bends the generic mesh onto the scan, smoothly, filling holes, starting stiff and slowly letting go. Its key finding is that every step of the bending is one exact linear solve.

The short version
  • Non-rigid ICP bends a generic template mesh onto a scan, so every template vertex finds its partner on the scan.
  • Each vertex gets its own small affine map. A stiffness weight \(\alpha\) asks neighbouring maps to stay alike.
  • With the closest points frozen, the best maps come from one sparse linear solve. Repeat, and lower \(\alpha\) from stiff to soft.
  • Vertices with no trustworthy match get weight zero and are carried by their neighbours.
  • Our A3 bends the MediaPipe face onto the CT, with the eyes and lips at weight zero, and reads the landmarks off the bent template.

Read first ICP, Procrustes alignment and Least squares.

In one minute

Give every template vertex its own small affine map, and ask three things of the maps. Each moved vertex should land on the scan. Neighbouring vertices should have similar maps, weighted by a stiffness \(\alpha\). A few known landmarks should go to known places. Start with \(\alpha\) very high, so the template moves as one block, and lower it step by step so smaller regions can bend on their own.

At each stiffness, alternate two moves. Find the closest scan point for every vertex, then solve one sparse linear system for the best maps. Vertices with no good match get weight zero and follow their neighbours. On 24 real faces the method beat a general purpose optimiser on the same cost.

Where this sits in our project

This is A3. Instead of detecting landmarks on the CT, we bend a template whose landmark vertices are known by construction onto the CT skin, then read the landmarks off. The primary template is the MediaPipe canonical face, where vertex \(i\) is MediaPipe landmark \(i\). ICT FaceKit, a second public face model, is registered the same way as a cross check.

The CT has the eyes and lips closed and the templates do not. So we set the distance weight of the eye and lip vertices to zero, which is the paper's own trick for missing data. They follow their neighbours instead of being dragged onto the wrong tissue.

The fit is tight where it should be. The residual is 0.02 to 0.07 mm on the stable regions and 1.4 to 1.5 mm on the eyes and lips. That second number is a direct measurement of the expression mismatch. As a camera method A3 scored a fit of 6.02 px, a contour of 8.40 px and 23.96 dB cross view.

The problem they solve

Registration means finding which point of one surface corresponds to which point of another. A rigid registration only allows a rotation and a shift, six numbers for the whole surface. That is enough when both surfaces are the same object, like a CT skin and a face scan of the same person on the same day (see Park). It is not enough when the shapes differ. A generic face and a real person differ in nose length, jaw width and a thousand small ways. You need a non-rigid registration, where different parts can move differently.

The paper's goal is dense registration. Every template vertex gets a partner on the scan, not just a handful of landmarks. This is how morphable face models are built. Register one template onto hundreds of scans, and vertex 1000 means "this spot on the left cheek" on all of them.

Two things make it hard. Real scans have holes, often more than half the head missing. And the right amount of bending differs from place to place. Too stiff and the template cannot follow the scan. Too soft and it collapses onto the nearest scan points in a crumpled mess.

The method step by step

  1. Template and target

    The template \(S = (V, E)\) is a mesh with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. The target \(T\) can be any surface where you can ask "what is the closest point to here".

  2. One affine map per vertex

    Vertex \(i\) gets a 3 by 4 matrix \(X_i\), twelve numbers. The moved vertex is \(X_i v_i\).

  3. A cost with three terms

    Distance to the target, stiffness between neighbours, and a landmark term. Weighted by 1, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

  4. Fix the correspondences, solve exactly

    With each vertex's closest target point frozen, the cost is quadratic in the unknowns. Its minimum is the solution of one sparse linear system.

  5. Inner loop

    Find new closest points from the moved template, solve again. Stop when the maps stop changing.

  6. Outer loop

    Lower \(\alpha\) and run the inner loop again. Lower the landmark weight \(\beta\) along the way.

  7. Handle missing data

    A vertex whose closest point is on the border of the scan, whose normal disagrees, or whose match lies behind the template gets weight zero.

  8. Finish

    Push each vertex onto the target along its normal. The scan is now described with the template's triangles.

One affine map per vertex

Homogeneous coordinates and the 3 by 4 matrix

A rotation and a stretch can be written as a 3 by 3 matrix times a point. A shift cannot. It is an addition. The trick is to add a fourth coordinate that is always 1, the homogeneous coordinate. Then a single 3 by 4 matrix does both.

\[ X_i v_i = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} & t_1 \\ a_{21} & a_{22} & a_{23} & t_2 \\ a_{31} & a_{32} & a_{33} & t_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}x + a_{12}y + a_{13}z + t_1 \\ \cdots \\ \cdots \end{bmatrix} \]

In words, the trailing 1 picks up the last column \((t_1, t_2, t_3)\), so one matrix product both reshapes the point and shifts it.

The left 3 by 3 block rotates, scales and shears. The last column shifts. This kind of map is called affine. Straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel.

A worked example. Let the left block be the identity and the last column \((2, 0, 0)\). Then \(X_i (1, 1, 0, 1)^\top = (3, 1, 0)\). The vertex moved 2 to the right and nothing else happened.

Twelve numbers per vertex looks wasteful, since a new position needs only three. The authors choose twelve for one reason. With twelve, the moved vertex \(X_i v_i\) is linear in the unknowns, and the stiffness between neighbours can compare whole maps, including their rotation. Both terms then become squares of linear expressions, so the cost has an exact minimum. With three numbers per vertex and a regulariser that favours rotations, the cost could not be solved directly.

The cost and its three terms

The cost says what a good bend is. Everything else in the paper is a way to minimise it.

Equations (2) to (5)

Distance. Each moved vertex should be close to the target.

\[ E_d(X) = \sum_{v_i \in V} w_i \,\mathrm{dist}^2\big(T,\; X_i v_i\big) \]

In words, add up the squared gap between every moved vertex and the target surface, each scaled by how much that vertex's match is trusted.

Stiffness. The maps of the two ends of each edge should be similar.

\[ E_s(X) = \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E} \big\lVert (X_i - X_j)\, G \big\rVert_F^2, \qquad G = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, 1, \gamma) \]

In words, for every edge of the mesh, measure how different the two end vertices' maps are, entry by entry, and add the squares.

Landmarks. A few known template vertices should reach known target positions.

\[ E_l(X) = \sum_{(v_i,\, l) \in L} \lVert X_i v_i - l \rVert^2 \]

In words, each landmark vertex should land on its known target point \(l\).

Total.

\[ E(X) = E_d(X) + \alpha\, E_s(X) + \beta\, E_l(X) \]

In words, fit the surface, stay smooth, and hit the landmarks, with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) setting how much the second and third wishes count.

dist(T, p)
the distance from point \(p\) to its closest point on the target surface
w_i
the reliability of vertex \(i\)'s match. 1 normally, 0 when no valid match exists
‖·‖_F
the Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of all squared entries. For \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\) it is \(\sqrt{1+4+0+4} = 3\)
G
a 4 by 4 diagonal matrix. \(\gamma\) weighs differences in the shift part against differences in the rotation and stretch part. The paper sets \(\gamma = 1\) and scales the data into the cube \([-1, 1]^3\)
α
the stiffness weight. High means the template acts like a solid plate. Low means it acts like cloth
β
the landmark weight. It is faded out toward the end, because hand placed landmarks are noisy

Note what the stiffness does not punish. If every vertex has the same map, \(E_s = 0\), whatever that map is. A global rotation, scaling or shear of the whole template is free. Only differences between neighbours cost, so the stiffest steps can still recover the pose and size of the template.

Without landmarks the cost has a silly global minimum, the whole template shrunk onto one point of the target. The paper shows that the correct local minimum is still found from a wide range of starts, and the landmark term helps it get there.

Fixed correspondences turn it into one linear system

This section is the heart of the paper, the reason each step is exact. The distance term contains \(\mathrm{dist}(T, \cdot)\), which is not a nice function. ICP's old trick removes it. Freeze, for this step, the closest target point \(u_i\) of every moved vertex. Then \(\mathrm{dist}^2(T, X_i v_i)\) becomes \(\lVert X_i v_i - u_i \rVert^2\), a plain squared distance to a fixed point. Every term is now a square of something linear in the unknowns. The rest is bookkeeping, and it is clearest on the smallest example.

Built from two vertices

Work in 2D so the matrices stay small. Then each map is 2 by 3 and a vertex is \(v = (x, y, 1)\). Take two vertices joined by one edge, \(v_1 = (0, 0)\) and \(v_2 = (1, 0)\).

Stack the unknowns. Put the transposed maps on top of each other. That gives a 6 by 2 matrix \(X\). Its first column produces new \(x\) coordinates, its second column new \(y\) coordinates.

\[ X = \begin{bmatrix} X_1^\top \\ X_2^\top \end{bmatrix} \quad (6 \times 2) \]

In words, all unknowns of all vertices sit in one tall matrix, three rows per vertex.

The distance term. Build a matrix \(D\) whose row \(i\) holds \(v_i^\top\) in the three columns of vertex \(i\) and zeros elsewhere. Then row \(i\) of \(DX\) is \(v_i^\top X_i^\top = (X_i v_i)^\top\), the moved vertex. With \(U\) holding the frozen targets \(u_i\) as rows, the distance term is \(\lVert W(DX - U) \rVert_F^2\) (equation 9).

\[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \mathrm{diag}(w_1, w_2) \]

In words, row 1 holds \(v_1 = (0, 0, 1)\) in vertex 1's columns and row 2 holds \(v_2 = (1, 0, 1)\) in vertex 2's columns. Multiplying by \(X\) moves each vertex with its own map.

The stiffness term. The node-arc incidence matrix \(M\) has one row per edge and one column per vertex. Edge \(r\) from vertex \(i\) to vertex \(j\) puts \(-1\) in column \(i\) and \(+1\) in column \(j\). Here there is one edge, so \(M = [-1 \;\; 1]\). The Kronecker product \(M \otimes G\) replaces every entry \(m\) of \(M\) by the block \(m\,G\). So \(M \otimes G = [-G \;\; G]\), and \((M \otimes G)X = G(X_2^\top - X_1^\top)\). Its squared Frobenius norm is exactly the stiffness of that edge (equation 10).

Stack the two terms. Put \(\alpha\) times the stiffness rows on top of the weighted distance rows (equation 12). With \(\gamma = 1\) and \(w_1 = w_2 = 1\) the whole problem is the one below.

\[ \bar E(X) = \Bigg\lVert \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -\alpha & 0 & 0 & \alpha & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\alpha & 0 & 0 & \alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\alpha & 0 & 0 & \alpha \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} X \;-\; \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ u_1^\top \\ u_2^\top \end{bmatrix}}_{B} \Bigg\rVert_F^2 . \]

In words, the first three rows of \(A\) measure how much the two maps differ, and the last two rows move the vertices so they can be compared with their targets in \(B\).

Solve. A sum of squares \(\lVert AX - B \rVert_F^2\) is smallest where its gradient \(2A^\top(AX - B)\) is zero. That gives the normal equations.

\[ A^\top A\, X = A^\top B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X = (A^\top A)^{-1} A^\top B \]

In words, multiply both sides by \(A^\top\) to get a square system, then solve it.

This is the optimal step of the title. For fixed correspondences and a fixed stiffness, it is the exact minimum, found in one solve. The two columns of \(X\) share the same matrix \(A^\top A\), so one factorisation serves both.

But this tiny example is singular. \(A\) has 5 rows and 6 columns, so \(A^\top A\) cannot be inverted. You can see which direction is missing. Both vertices have \(y = 0\), so nothing in the data says what a map does to the \(y\) direction. Changing the coefficient that multiplies \(y\), in every map by the same amount, changes no residual.

The paper's well-posedness proof (Section 4.3) says exactly this. The stiffness rows force all maps to agree on any such hidden change, and the data rows then require \(v_i^\top a = 0\) for every vertex. That has only the zero solution unless all vertices lie on one line (in 2D) or one plane (in 3D). Add a third vertex off the line and the system becomes solvable. A face mesh is never flat, so \(A^\top A\) is invertible for any \(\alpha > 0\).

The general form. For \(n\) vertices in 3D, \(X\) is \(4n \times 3\), \(D\) is \(n \times 4n\), and \(M \otimes G\) is \(4m \times 4n\). With landmarks the stack gets a third block of rows taken from \(D\).

\[ \bar E(X) = \left\lVert \begin{bmatrix} \alpha\, M \otimes G \\ W D \\ \beta\, D_L \end{bmatrix} X - \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ W U \\ \beta\, U_L \end{bmatrix} \right\rVert_F^2 \]

In words, the same three wishes as before, stiffness, surface and landmarks, each as a block of rows in one big sum of squares.

The paper prints \(U_L\) without the \(\beta\). Scaling both sides makes the third block a weighted landmark cost, and our code builds it that way. Almost every entry of \(A\) is zero, so \(A^\top A\) is sparse. The paper solves it with the UMFPACK sparse solver.

Two loops and the stiffness schedule

One exact solve is not the whole method. Two loops wrap around it.

The algorithm, as printed in Section 4.1

  1. Initialise \(X^0\), for example every map the identity.
  2. Go through the stiffness values \(\alpha_1 > \alpha_2 > \dots > \alpha_n\) in order. For each \(\alpha_i\), repeat the two steps below until \(\lVert X^j - X^{j-1} \rVert < \epsilon\).
    1. Find preliminary correspondences for the moved template \(V(X^{j-1})\).
    2. Set \(X^j\) to the optimal deformation for those correspondences and \(\alpha_i\).

The outer loop is the schedule. At the start \(\alpha\) is so large that all maps are nearly equal, so the template moves as one affine block and global alignment comes first. Each later \(\alpha\) allows more local bending. The paper lowered \(\alpha\) in 100 equal steps. Starting too high costs only extra steps, never quality. Going too low hurts, because the conditioning of \(A\) suffers and the solution becomes unstable.

The inner loop is ICP. Because of the stiffness, vertices do not jump straight to their closest points. They may slide along the target, and the next closest point search sees them in a better place.

If every vertex has a match and no weights change, the residual can only fall. Solving lowers it, and a new closest point search cannot find anything farther away. The same argument proves rigid ICP converges.

Missing data and weights

Real scans have holes, and the template should not be pulled into them. This mechanism is also what A3 reuses for the closed eyes. The paper drops a correspondence, setting \(w_i = 0\), in three cases.

  1. The closest point \(u_i\) lies on a border of the target mesh. A vertex over a hole would otherwise be pulled to the hole's edge.
  2. The angle between the template normal at \(X_i v_i\) and the target normal at \(u_i\) is above a fixed threshold. The two points face different ways, so they are probably not the same part of the face.
  3. The segment from \(X_i v_i\) to \(u_i\) passes through the deformed template. This removes matches through stacked layers, like the folds of an ear.

A vertex with \(w_i = 0\) has no distance term at all. It still sits in the stiffness term, so it moves wherever keeps its map closest to its neighbours' maps. That fills holes smoothly with the template's own shape.

Weights have a side effect, which the paper's Figure 4 shows. As the template aligns, vertices that had no match find one and their weight goes from 0 to 1. The residual then jumps up even though the fit got better.

A general purpose optimiser such as L-BFGS-B assumes the cost should keep falling and stalls. The optimal step scheme does not care. It simply re-solves with the new weights. Convergence is checked by whether the maps stopped changing, not by the cost.

Why affine stiffness and not translation stiffness

Why go to the trouble of affine maps? The paper also builds N-ICP-T, the same algorithm with only a translation per vertex. Its stiffness punishes neighbouring vertices that move by different amounts. It is faster, with three unknowns per vertex. But a rotation of the whole template moves every vertex by a different amount, so N-ICP-T punishes rotation. The affine version does not. In the paper's synthetic test N-ICP-T fails at the very first step, recovering the global rigid motion.

What they measured

  • Synthetic. An embossed cube as template. Target one is the same cube moved rigidly with a large region missing. Target two is also bent. N-ICP-A recovered the rigid motion exactly and filled the hole smoothly in both. Allen and colleagues' 2003 method, which hands the same kind of cost to the L-BFGS-B optimiser, failed to find the optimum. N-ICP-T failed already at the global rigid motion.
  • Real faces. Structured light scans of 24 people aged 20 to 40. Fourteen landmarks were placed by hand, eight of them on the ears because the ear scans are fragmented. The faces were aligned rigidly on the landmarks first, then registered with each method. Stiffness was lowered in 100 equal steps for all methods.

There is no ground truth for dense correspondence on real faces, so they used two indirect measures. First, remove the rigid pose and compare the normals at corresponding points across all pairs of registered faces. If the side of the nose were mapped onto a cheek, the normals would disagree. Second, rebuild each face as a convex blend of all the others and measure the distance between corresponding vertices. Consistent registrations make faces easier to rebuild from each other.

Measure (24 faces)N-ICP-AN-ICP-TAllen '03
Mean angle between corresponding normals5.6°6.8°7.9°
Rebuild error from the other faces1710 µm1740 µm2040 µm

Lower is better for both. The affine optimal step method wins on both, and the gap to the general optimiser is larger than the gap to the translation version.

Weak points

  • It still needs a reasonable start. The face experiments began with a rigid alignment on 14 hand placed landmarks.
  • The stiffness values depend on the mesh size and the units. The paper gives no absolute \(\alpha\) values, only the advice to start high and stop before the system becomes unstable.
  • The evaluation has no millimetre accuracy against hand marked anatomy. The two measures are about consistency.
  • It uses shape only. The authors note that colour could help at places like the eye corners, but did not use it.
  • A closest point is not a corresponding point. Where the target's shape differs from the template's, such as closed eyes against open ones, the closest point is the wrong tissue. Weights can switch those regions off, but someone has to know which regions they are.

How we used it

A1 and A2 detect landmarks on renders of the CT. Both inherit the detector's scatter and its confusion about the closed eyes. A3 asks a different question. Instead of finding the landmark on the CT, bend a face whose landmarks are already known onto the CT, and see where they end up. Nothing is detected on the CT at all. What comes in instead is the template's shape prior.

The A3 chain

  1. Template

    The MediaPipe canonical face, 468 vertices, scaled from centimetres to millimetres and rotated into the CT frame. Its vertex \(i\) is MediaPipe landmark \(i\), the same index the photo detector uses. The second template is the face area of ICT FaceKit, 6706 vertices, with 68 landmark vertices in the iBUG numbering.

  2. Similarity Procrustes

    A rotation, shift and one scale from the template's landmark vertices to A2's consensus points, on the 19 rigid landmarks A2 kept. The fitted scale was 0.911, and the landmarks still sat a median 4.66 mm apart. That is the shape difference the next stages must remove.

  3. Trimmed rigid ICP on stable regions

    Only the forehead, nasal bridge and cheekbones, the parts no expression moves. Matches beyond 12 mm are ignored, and only the shortest 80 percent of the rest are used. It ran 15 rounds.

  4. Amberg N-ICP-A

    Five stiffness stages from stiff to soft, a landmark term on A2's rigid points fading to zero, and the eye and lip vertices taken out of the distance term.

  5. Read out

    Each template landmark vertex is snapped to the nearest point of the full CT surface. The distance it had to travel is kept as a quality flag.

What we kept from the paper

The model, the cost and the solver are the paper's. One 3 by 4 affine map per vertex. Stiffness as the Frobenius difference of neighbouring maps with \(G = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, 1, \gamma)\) and \(\gamma = 1\). A landmark term with a weight that fades to zero. Each step a closest point search and one exact sparse solve of \(A^\top A X = A^\top B\). The data is normalised into a unit cube first, as the paper does. Without that, the stiffness and distance terms would sit at very different scales in millimetres.

What we changed and why

PartPaperOurs, A3Why
Zero weightsScan borders, normal disagreement, matches through the templateEvery eye vertex within 10 mm of an eye landmark (96 vertices) and every lip vertex within 12 mm of a lip landmark (100 vertices), alwaysThe CT eyes and lips are closed. The nearest CT point to an open template eyelid is the wrong tissue
Other dropsAs aboveA distance threshold per stage, 20, 12, 8, 6 and 5 mm, plus a soft normal agreement factorThe template only reaches for surface it is already close to, so the chin rest and neck cannot pull it
Schedule100 equal stepsFive stages. Stiffness 0.2, 0.08, 0.03, 0.01, 0.005 with landmark weight 12, 6, 3, 1, 0, up to 12 inner steps eachThe same stiff to soft, landmark led to surface led idea in fewer stages. Each stage runs until the error stops improving
StartRigid alignment on hand placed landmarksSimilarity Procrustes on A2's points, then trimmed rigid ICPFully automatic
TargetThe scanThe CT surface decimated to 150,000 facesThe closest point query is the cost, and 150,000 faces still resolve the face far below a millimetre

The zero weight on the eyes and lips is the paper's missing data mechanism used for a different reason. The CT is not missing those regions. Its shape there is simply not the shape the photo shows. Weight zero says "do not listen to the surface here" and lets the stiffness carry the template's open eyes across, shaped by the skin around them.

What A3 got

The five N-ICP-A stages took about 2.3 s in total. The residual of the fitted template against the CT, by region, is the clearest result of the whole method.

Region of the fitted MediaPipe templateverticesmedian distance to CT, mm
Chin120.020

Jaw100.026
Forehead120.046

In short, 0.02 to 0.07 mm on the stable regions and 1.4 to 1.5 mm at the eyes and lips. The means tell the same story, 1.47 mm on the eyes and 1.88 mm on the lips. Where the template was allowed to listen to the CT, it lies on it.

Where it was not, it stays about a millimetre and a half off, and that gap is the expression difference between the closed eyed CT and an open eyed face. ICT FaceKit, registered the same way, shows the same pattern, and its 12 shared landmarks agree with the MediaPipe template's to a median of 1.47 mm.

The transferred landmarks moved from A2's detected positions by 1.4 to 2.2 mm at the eye corners, which sit in the zero weight region, and by less than 0.5 mm on the cheekbones and jaw.

A3 also recovers the three jaw points A2 had dropped, because the template simply has them. So its camera solve uses all 22 rigid landmarks. Each landmark gets an uncertainty of \(\sqrt{1.5^2 + r^2}\) mm, where \(r\) is its snap distance and 1.5 mm is the accuracy reported in the literature for landmark transfer by template fitting. Landmarks in the zero weight regions get double that.

A2 40 render consensus6.431.3955810.7838.4025.37238.5

As a camera method A3 is mixed. Its contour matches A2 at 8.40 px. Its camera distance spread of 151.1 mm is tight for a method that solves each photo on its own. But it has the lowest cross view score of the landmark methods, 23.96 dB, because its two side focal lengths land far apart.

Its front focal length of 7298 px is also far above the 3300 to 4700 px range. A6 beats it on both counts, 25.56 dB and 145.9 mm, by solving the three cameras together. A3's lasting value is the measurement. Its residual map is the one place in the project where the expression mismatch is put into millimetres.

Watch out

A small residual is not a correct correspondence. On the stable regions the template lies within hundredths of a millimetre of the CT, but it could have slid along the surface while getting there. The landmark positions come from where the template ended up, so their accuracy is bounded by the template's shape prior, not by the residual.

Remember

One affine map per vertex, a cost of distance plus \(\alpha\) times neighbour difference plus \(\beta\) times landmarks.

With the closest points frozen it is \(\lVert AX - B\rVert_F^2\), solved exactly by \(A^\top A X = A^\top B\), while \(\alpha\) falls from stiff to soft.

Weight zero lets the template ignore bad data, and A3 used that to ignore the closed eyes and lips, which then measured the mismatch at 1.4 to 1.5 mm.

If they ask you

"What does non rigid ICP add over rigid ICP?"

Every vertex gets its own affine map, tied to its neighbours by a stiffness term. You start stiff, so it behaves like rigid ICP, and lower the stiffness so it can bend locally. Each step is still an exact solve, a sparse linear system, so it is stable.

"How did you deal with the closed eyes in the CT?"

I set the distance weight of the template's eye and lip vertices to zero, the paper's mechanism for missing data. They are carried by the stiffness from the skin around them. The leftover gap there, 1.4 to 1.5 mm against 0.02 to 0.07 mm elsewhere, measures the expression difference.

"Why is A3 not your recommended method?"

The registration itself is very tight, but as a camera it scored the lowest cross view of the landmark family, 23.96 dB, because the side photos' focal lengths came out far apart. Solving the three photos together with one shared focal length, A6 and A7, fixed that.

Building blocks used

ICP · Procrustes alignment · Least squares · Face landmarks · PnP

About 50 minutes

Paper P4Computer Graphics Forum 28(7), Pacific Graphics 2009Used in B2

Image-to-Geometry Registration: a Mutual Information Method exploiting Illumination-related Geometric Properties

Massimiliano Corsini, Matteo Dellepiane, Federico Ponchio and Roberto Scopigno. Visual Computing Lab, ISTI-CNR, Pisa.

You have a 3D scan of an object and a photo of it, and you want to know where the camera stood. This paper draws the scan from a guessed camera and scores the drawing against the photo. Then it moves the camera until the score peaks. Its real contribution is the choice of drawing. It draws the surface direction and how hidden each point is, because those two things decide how light falls on the object.

The short version
  • A grey scan and a colour photo never look alike, so you cannot compare them pixel by pixel.
  • Mutual information is a score that only asks whether one image predicts the other. It does not care if the two look alike.
  • Draw the scan as surface directions plus how hidden each point is. Those drawings predict photo brightness best.
  • Search the seven camera numbers with an optimiser that never needs a slope. It polishes a start that is already close.
  • Our B2 used the same loop. On our flat lit photo we had to swap mutual information for an edge direction score plus an outline term.

Read first Cameras and projection and Comparing two images.

In one minute

Museums scan statues with a laser scanner to get the shape. The colour comes from separate photos. To paint a photo onto the scan you need the exact camera of that photo. The trouble is that a photo and a grey scan look very different. The photo has paint, dirt and the room's light. The scan has none of that.

The authors borrow a tool from medical imaging. Doctors align a CT scan with an MRI scan, and the two machines show the same body with completely different brightness. The score they use is mutual information. It asks whether knowing one image's value at a pixel lets you predict the other image's value there.

The paper tests which drawing of the scan predicts photo brightness best. The options are the surface direction (a normal map), how hidden each point is from the open sky (ambient occlusion, new in this paper), the mirror direction (a reflection map), the plain outline (a silhouette map) and mixtures. An optimiser called NEWUOA moves the seven camera numbers to raise the score.

The mixture of ambient occlusion and normals is always close to the best single drawing. Starting 50 pixels off, it converged in 90 percent of runs on one carved capital, 76 percent on a painted capital and 82 percent on a bas relief. A run takes about 100 iterations and about 4 seconds.

Where this sits in our project

Our method B2 is this paper applied to our CT and our studio photo. We render geometry, compare it with the photo using a score that does not need the two to look alike, and search the camera without gradients from another method's start. We changed the optimiser, masked out the eyes, brows and lips, and replaced mutual information with an edge direction score plus an outline term. On our flat lit photo mutual information alone drifted 2 degrees.

B2 reached a 3.2 px outline error on the front photo, second only to B4 at 2.8 px. But it made the jaw worse, it only works from a close start, and a run takes 66 s. It is our classical reference, not our recommendation.

The problem they solve

You need this because a camera is what links a photo pixel to a point on the surface. The input is a triangle mesh of an object and one photo of it. The output is the camera that took the photo. Once you have it you can project every vertex into the photo and read off its colour. That is how a scanned statue gets its paint back, and how our CT face gets its skin.

The paper uses a pinhole camera with its image centre in the middle of the photo, square pixels and no skew. What is left is seven numbers. Three give the camera position, three give its rotation and one is the focal length, which is the zoom.

The goal as one equation

The paper writes registration as a search in seven dimensions (its equation 2).

\[ C^{*} = \arg\max_{C \in \mathbb{R}^7} I\big(I_A,\; I_B(C)\big), \qquad C = (t_x, t_y, t_z, \theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z, f) \]
C
the camera, seven numbers
I_A
the photo after conversion to grey
I_B(C)
a rendering of the model from camera C. It changes whenever C changes.
I( , )
the mutual information between the two images, explained below
arg max
"the C that makes this largest"

In words, try cameras, draw the model from each one, and keep the camera whose drawing best predicts the photo. Every try costs one rendering and one histogram. There is no formula for the slope, which is why the search has to work without one.

The method step by step

The paper splits registration into two jobs. Rough alignment gets a camera roughly right. Fine alignment polishes it. This paper only does fine alignment. The authors argue that a fine alignment that works from far away makes the rough job easy, since you can then try many starting views.

  1. Make the photo grey

    Each colour pixel becomes one brightness with the TV formula \(Y = 0.3R + 0.59G + 0.11B\) (their equation 4).

  2. Render the model at the current camera

    Draw a geometry map, not a realistic image. The options are in the next section.

  3. Build the joint histogram

    For every pixel of the whole rendered image, take the pair (photo value, render value) and count it in a 128 by 128 table.

  4. Compute mutual information

    Turn the table into probabilities and compute the score with equation 1.

  5. Update the camera

    NEWUOA proposes a new set of seven numbers that should score better.

  6. Repeat

    Go back to step 2 until the camera stops moving. This took about 100 iterations.

What to draw instead of a photo

This choice is the paper's main idea. You cannot render a realistic photo of the scan, because you do not know the paint, the material or the lights. So the authors ask which drawing of the bare geometry changes together with photo brightness, whatever the light is.

Why surface direction predicts brightness

A matte surface, like stone or skin, looks equally bright from every viewing angle. Its brightness depends only on how squarely it faces the light. That is Lambert's law.

\[ \text{brightness}(p) = \rho(p)\; \max\big(0,\; \mathbf{n}(p) \cdot \mathbf{l}\big) \]
p
a point on the surface
n(p)
the surface normal at p, a unit vector pointing straight out of the surface
l
the direction toward a distant light, also a unit vector
ρ(p)
the albedo, meaning how much light the paint or skin at p reflects

In words, a point is as bright as its colour times how directly it faces the light, and zero if it faces away.

A worked example. Let the light come from \(\mathbf{l} = (0.6, 0, 0.8)\), in front and to one side. A patch that faces the camera has \(\mathbf{n} = (0, 0, 1)\), so \(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{l} = 0.8\). A cheek patch turned toward the light has \(\mathbf{n} = (0.6, 0, 0.8)\) and gets \(1.0\). A patch turned away has \(\mathbf{n} = (-0.6, 0, 0.8)\) and gets \(0.28\). With the same albedo, the three brightnesses are in the ratio 0.8 to 1.0 to 0.28.

Here is the key point. If the albedo is roughly constant and there is one main light, brightness is a fixed function of the normal. You do not know that function, because you do not know \(\mathbf{l}\). But it exists. Mutual information rewards exactly that, a relation through any function.

The normal is three numbers, so the normal map is three images. The paper uses only the x and y images, since z follows from them (\(n_z = \sqrt{1 - n_x^2 - n_y^2}\) for a visible point). It computes mutual information for each and adds them.

Ambient occlusion

Some points get little light from any direction, like the inside of a nostril or the corner of an eye. They are dark in almost every photo, whatever the lighting. Ambient occlusion measures this. For each point it asks what share of the sky above the point is open, with directions near the normal counting more.

\[ A(p) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\Omega} V(p, \omega)\, (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omega)\; d\omega \]
Ω
all directions in the half sphere above the surface at p
V(p, ω)
1 if a ray from p in direction ω escapes, 0 if it hits the object
n · ω
directions near the normal count more, as they would for real light
1/π
makes a fully open point score exactly 1

In words, shoot rays out of the point in all directions and count the share that escape, giving more weight to rays that leave straight out. A point on a flat open cheek scores near 1. A point deep in a nostril scores near 0.

It does not depend on the camera, so the paper computes it once per vertex on the GPU and stores it as a vertex colour. This page estimates it with 60 directions.

Reflections, outlines and the mixture

A reflection map stores the mirror direction \(\mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v}\), where \(\mathbf{v}\) points from the surface to the camera. Shiny objects show highlights where \(\mathbf{r}\) points at a light, so this map helps on shiny objects. A silhouette map is white on the object and black elsewhere. It only knows the outline.

The mixture that the paper recommends weights the normal map by the ambient occlusion (their equation 3).

\[ C_{\text{comb}} = (1 - C_A)\, C_A + C_A\, C_N \]
C_A
the ambient occlusion value, from 0 (hidden) to 1 (open)
C_N
a normal map value, one component at a time, mapped to the range 0 to 1

In words, in hidden creases show the occlusion, and on open surfaces show the normal. In a deep crease \(C_A\) is near 0, so the pixel is dark. On an open surface \(C_A\) is near 1, the first term vanishes and \(C_{\text{comb}} \approx C_N\). A crease with \(C_A = 0.2\) and \(C_N = 0.7\) gives \(0.2 \times 0.8 + 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.30\). An open cheek with \(C_A = 0.9\) and the same normal gives \(0.9 \times 0.1 + 0.9 \times 0.7 = 0.72\).

Mutual information from scratch

This is the score that makes the whole method work, and you will meet it again on the comparing two images page. You need three ideas. Probability from a histogram, entropy, and the joint histogram.

Step 1. Probability and entropy of one image

Count how many pixels have each grey level and divide by the number of pixels. That gives the probability \(p(a)\) of level \(a\). Take a tiny image of 8 pixels with levels 0 to 3.

\[ A = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3] \quad\Rightarrow\quad p(0) = \tfrac{2}{8},\; p(1) = \tfrac{3}{8},\; p(2) = \tfrac{1}{8},\; p(3) = \tfrac{2}{8} \]

In words, two of the eight pixels are level 0, so level 0 has probability one quarter. Entropy then measures how unpredictable one pixel is.

\[ H(A) = -\sum_a p(a)\, \log_2 p(a) \]
p(a)
share of pixels with level a
log₂
logarithm base 2, so the unit is bits. Levels with p = 0 are skipped.

In words, entropy is the average number of yes or no questions you need to guess a random pixel's level. For the tiny image it is \(0.25 \times 2 + 0.375 \times 1.415 + 0.125 \times 3 + 0.25 \times 2 \approx 1.906\) bits. An image of one flat colour has entropy 0. An image with four equally common levels has entropy 2.

Step 2. The joint histogram

Now take two images of the same size, the photo \(A\) and the render \(B\). Walk over the pixels together and count each pair \((a, b)\). The result is a 2D table, the joint histogram. Dividing by the pixel count gives the joint probability \(p(a, b)\). Its row sums give \(p(a)\) and its column sums give \(p(b)\).

\[ H(A, B) = -\sum_{a, b} p(a, b)\, \log_2 p(a, b) \]

In words, this is how hard it is to guess the pair of values at a random pixel. If the images are aligned and related, each photo level goes with only a few render levels. The table is thin and \(H(A,B)\) is small. If they are misaligned, the table smears out and \(H(A,B)\) grows.

Step 3. Mutual information

Mutual information is how much more predictable the pair is than the two images taken apart.

\[ I(A, B) = H(A) + H(B) - H(A, B) = \sum_{a, b} p(a, b)\, \log_2 \frac{p(a, b)}{p(a)\, p(b)} \]
p(a,b)
share of pixels where the photo has level a and the render has level b
p(a) p(b)
what p(a,b) would be if the two images were unrelated

In words, it counts how many bits of the photo you get for free once you know the render. The right hand form is the paper's equation 1, and both forms give the same number. Three cases with the tiny image make it concrete.

  • \(B = A\). The table has four filled cells, so \(H(A,B) = H(A)\) and \(I = 1.906\) bits. This is the most \(I\) can be.
  • \(B = 3 - A\), the negative image. The four cells move, but there are still four with the same counts. So \(I\) is still 1.906 bits. Mutual information does not care that dark became bright, only that the pairing is consistent.
  • \(B = [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]\), unrelated to \(A\). Now \(H(B) = 1\) and \(H(A,B) = 2.75\). So \(I = 1.906 + 1 - 2.75 \approx 0.16\) bits, close to zero. With only 8 pixels a little fake structure always remains.

Compare it with two simpler scores. The sum of squared differences wants equal values. Normalised cross correlation wants a straight line relation. Mutual information accepts any consistent relation, straight, curved or inverted. In the paper's example, an image against itself scored 6.307 and against a rotated copy scored 1.109.

Why the background counts

Many earlier methods only counted pixels that the render covers. This paper counts the whole image, background included. If the backdrop has a different grey than the object, a render that spills over the outline pairs object values with backdrop values, and the table smears. So the outline helps for free.

The shape of the score

A good drawing gives one clear, smooth peak at the true camera, so the search can find it. To check this the authors walked away from the true camera in 30 random directions through the seven dimensional space and plotted the score along each line. They also rescaled the parameters so that one unit of any parameter moves the projected model by about one pixel, measured as the mean square distance between the projected vertices under the two cameras.

Searching for the camera with NEWUOA

The search decides whether the camera is found at all, and mutual information is a hard score to search. Histogram bins make it change in small jumps, so its slope is unreliable and slope based methods stall near the peak. Other papers smooth the score with Parzen windows or anti aliased rendering. This paper keeps the bumpy score and uses NEWUOA, an optimiser by Michael Powell from 2004 that never asks for a slope. The general family is on the searching without gradients page.

A quadratic model inside a trust region

NEWUOA keeps a bowl shaped model \(Q\) of the function \(F\) near the current best point \(x_k\). Here \(F\) is the negative mutual information, so lower is better.

\[ Q(x) = c + g^{\top}(x - x_k) + \tfrac{1}{2}(x - x_k)^{\top} H\, (x - x_k) \]
c, g, H
the model's value, slope and curvature, all fitted from function values, never from derivatives

In words, fit a smooth bowl through scores you already computed, and use the bowl to guess where the bottom is. The optimiser trusts the bowl only inside a ball of radius \(\Delta\), the trust region, and steps to its lowest point in that ball.

\[ x_{\text{new}} = \arg\min_{\lVert x - x_k \rVert \le \Delta} Q(x), \qquad \rho = \frac{F(x_k) - F(x_{\text{new}})}{Q(x_k) - Q(x_{\text{new}})} \]
Δ
the trust radius
ρ
real improvement divided by predicted improvement

In words, take the bowl's best point within reach, then check how much of the promised gain really arrived. If \(\rho\) is close to 1 the model was right, so the step is kept and \(\Delta\) may grow. If \(\rho\) is small or negative, \(\Delta\) shrinks. The only setting the authors tuned is the starting radius. They set it to 2.0 in all tests, about a tenth of the expected starting error in their one unit per pixel scaling.

A worked example in one dimension. Suppose \(F\) at \(x = -1, 0, 1\) is 5, 3 and 2. The parabola through them is \(Q(x) = 3 - 1.5x + 0.5x^2\), lowest at \(x = 1.5\). With \(\Delta = 1\) you may only go to \(x = 1\), where the model predicts 2. If the real \(F(1)\) is 2, then \(\rho = (3 - 2)/(3 - 2) = 1\). The step is kept and the radius can grow.

What they measured

These tests show which drawing to trust. They used five scanned objects with real photos. CAPITAL1 is a plain stone capital with complex carving. CAPITAL2 is similar but painted. DOGS and HORSE are shiny, and HORSE has a busy outline. The BAS-RELIEF is a carving on a flat wall, photographed in part, so it has no outline at all.

The reference cameras came from a semi automatic tool called TexAlign, good to about one pixel after scaling the photos to 800 pixels wide. For each object they shook the reference camera 300 times, by up to 50 pixels of error on an 800 by 600 view. A run counted as a success if it ended within 4 pixels. For CAPITAL1, 20 pixels of error can be more than 20 degrees of rotation.
