Percent of 300 runs that converged to within 4 px, selected rows of the paper's Table 1. The figure above has all 30 rows.

  • The outline alone is not enough. The silhouette map converged 0 to 23 percent of the time on CAPITAL1 and almost never on DOGS. Only HORSE, with its busy outline, did well with it.
  • Speed. On a 2009 machine (Intel Core Duo at 2300 MHz, NVidia 8600 GTS), convergence took about 100 iterations at 25 frames per second. That is about 4 seconds for a 1 million triangle model in an 800 by 600 view.

Weak points

  • Fine alignment only. It needs a start within tens of pixels. The authors say a fully automatic version is still being developed.
  • No clean way to combine maps. Mutual information values from different maps live on different scales, so simply adding them is unreliable. The authors leave this open.
  • It assumes shading comes from shape. If the light is flat and even, the photo's brightness is mostly paint or skin colour, and no geometry map predicts it well. Figure 6 shows this, and our photo has exactly this problem.
  • Narrow test set. Five rigid, statue like objects. Skin, faces and soft studio light are not tested.
  • Focal length and distance trade off. For a shallow object a longer lens further away looks almost the same, so the focal length is weakly held. The paper does not report focal errors separately.

How we used it

Our B2 is this recipe with no deep learning, which makes it an independent check on the learned methods.

  1. Render geometry at the current camera

    We render the CT with a ray caster as Lambertian shading under two fixed lights, depth and an ambient occlusion proxy. Depth was switched off in the score, because on a face its gradient is mostly the overall front to back slope.

  2. Pick the photo pixels

    We use grey levels inside the face skin, minus the eyes, brows and lips, plus a band along the jaw and cheek outline. The CT eyes are shut while the photo's are open, so those pixels compare two different things.

  3. Score

    Two scores were built. One is normalised mutual information, \(2I(A,B) / (H(A) + H(B))\), which lies between 0 and 1. The other is a normalised gradient field score, explained below. Both get a silhouette chamfer term. That is the average distance from each rendered outline pixel to the nearest photo outline pixel and back, which pulls the outline onto the photo's face mask. The interior fixes the nose and eye sockets, and the outline fixes the jaw.

  4. Search

    Seven numbers, a rotation in degrees, a translation in millimetres and the log of the focal length. CMA-ES does the wide search on a small render. It samples many cameras around the current guess and moves toward the better ones. Then Powell's method polishes on a larger render, improving one direction at a time.

  5. Start

    B2 starts from A5, our fused landmark camera. Like the paper, it is a refiner.

Why mutual information drifted on our photo

Our studio photo is lit flat and evenly. Its grey levels are almost all skin colour. Freckles, brows, lips and hair make the structure. The CT render is all shading and has no skin colour at all. So the paper's assumption, that brightness follows the geometry, fails. Mutual information alone drifted 2 degrees from a good camera. Figure 6 shows the same effect when you pick flat light and face only pixels.

A normalised gradient field (NGF) score held better. It ignores brightness and compares only the direction of edges. At each pixel it takes the image gradient and divides it by its length, softened by a small constant so that flat noise does not count.

\[ \mathbf{n}_A = \frac{\nabla A}{\sqrt{\lVert \nabla A \rVert^2 + \eta^2}}, \qquad \text{NGF}(A, B) \propto \sum_{\text{pixels}} \big(\mathbf{n}_A \cdot \mathbf{n}_B\big)^2 \]
∇A
the image gradient, how fast brightness changes in x and in y
η
the softening constant. In B2 it is 0.10 times the mean gradient length inside the mask.
squared dot
a bright edge in the photo can be a dark edge in the render, and squaring forgives that sign flip

In words, at every pixel ask whether the edges in the two images run the same way, ignoring how strong they are and which side is darker. The sum is scaled to lie between 0 and 1, where 1 means every edge points the same way in both images.

The silhouette term mattered even more. In one early setting, with no cap on how far the outline term could reach, the search turned the head 2.8 degrees to chase parts of the photo's face mask that have no partner in the CT outline. The contour score improved from 6.4 to 3.6 px, while the held out landmark error got 5.8 px worse and the jaw group went from 11 to 20 px. Capping the term at the band width fixed that.

Front photo for fit and contour. Silhouette IoU is how much the rendered and photographed face masks overlap, 1 being perfect. Cross view bakes a texture from the front photo, renders it at the side camera and compares with the real side photo, so higher dB is better. B2 ran only on the front photo, so its cross view borrows A5's side cameras and measures the pair, not B2 alone.

  • Outline. 3.2 px of contour, second only to B4's 2.8 px.
  • Interior. The nose, lip and eyelid edges score 9.07 px, the best interior edge score of all fifteen methods. The nose group improved from 9.0 to 6.4 px.
  • Jaw. B2's fit column is the reprojection error of A1's 22 rigid landmarks, which were never in B2's score, so it is a held out check. It rose to 9.58 px, mostly from the jaw.
  • Close start needed. Started from A1 instead of A5, it lands somewhere else entirely. The paper says the same of its own method.
  • Time. 66 s per photo, against about 4 s in the paper for a far simpler score loop.

Its sibling B1 tried the same idea with gradients, using the Mitsuba differentiable renderer. It moved only 0.03 degrees from its A1 start. Searching without gradients was the version that actually moved.

Watch out

Do not say that mutual information failed in general. It failed on a flat lit photo whose brightness is mostly skin colour, against a render that is all shading. With a key light, or with paint free objects such as the paper's stone capitals, it works well. The paper itself lists this assumption.

If they ask you

Why not just compare the render and the photo pixel by pixel?

They do not share brightness. The photo has skin colour and room light, the render has neither. Mutual information only asks whether one image predicts the other, so it works across that gap. Corsini borrowed it from CT to MRI registration.

Why did your B2 not use mutual information?

We tried it. Our photo is flat lit, so its grey levels are skin colour while the render is pure shading. Mutual information drifted 2 degrees. An edge direction score with a capped silhouette term held, and gave a 3.2 px outline.

Why is B2 not your recommended method?

It needs a close start, it makes the jaw landmarks worse, and it takes 66 s. Our A7 keeps a usable outline and scores best on the cross view test, 26.18 dB against 25.57.

Building blocks used

  • Cameras and projection, for the seven camera numbers and the pinhole model.
  • Rendering, depth and back projection, for drawing normals and ambient occlusion from a mesh.
  • Comparing two images, for mutual information, normalised gradient fields and silhouette distances.
  • Searching without gradients, for NEWUOA, CMA-ES and Powell's method.
  • Painting the surface, for what you do once the camera is known.

About 55 minutes

Paper P5ECCV 2024Used in B3 A7

FoundPose: Unseen Object Pose Estimation with Foundation Features

Evin Pınar Örnek, Yann Labbé, Bugra Tekin, Lingni Ma, Cem Keskin, Christian Forster and Tomas Hodaň. Technical University of Munich and Meta Reality Labs.

You have the 3D model of an object and one photo of it, and you need the object's exact position and rotation in that photo. Nobody trained a network on this object. FoundPose renders the model from many sides, describes every small patch of every render with a large pretrained network, matches those patches to the photo, and solves for the pose with classic geometry.

The short version
  • Render the model from hundreds of directions and keep each render's depth, so every pixel of a render knows its 3D point on the model.
  • Describe every 14 pixel patch, in the renders and in the photo, with DINOv2, a large network that was never trained on this object.
  • Pick the few renders that look most like the photo, then match photo patches to render patches. Each match is a 2D pixel paired with a 3D point.
  • Solve the pose from those pairs with PnP inside RANSAC, then polish it so the descriptors line up.
  • Our B3 is this recipe on the CT. Our recommended A7 runs it with the focal length held fixed and a guard that keeps the result only if it helps.

Read first Features, descriptors and DINOv2, PnP and RANSAC.

In one minute

Robots and headsets need the 6D pose of objects, three numbers of rotation and three of translation. Most strong methods are trained on each new object, or on millions of synthetic images. FoundPose asks what you can do with only the object's mesh and five minutes of preparation on one GPU.

The answer is a frozen foundation model, DINOv2. It was trained on a huge set of unlabelled images, and its patch descriptors happen to match well between clean renders and real photos. FoundPose renders 800 templates of the model, each with a depth image. At test time it finds the 5 templates most like the photo with a bag of visual words, matches photo patches to template patches, and turns those 2D to 3D links into a pose with PnP (the classic solve for a camera from point pairs) inside RANSAC (repeated tries on small random subsets, to ignore bad pairs). A last featuremetric refinement nudges the pose so that descriptors line up below patch size.

The test is BOP, a standard benchmark of seven datasets and 108 objects, scored by average recall (AR, the share of poses that are close enough, from 0 to 100). The coarse pose scored 37.2 AR with no training at all. The best trained coarse rival scored 27.6. Its own refinement raised that to 42.6. With a trained refiner from another method and 5 hypotheses it reached 59.6, the best RGB only result in their comparison.

Where this sits in our project

Our B3 reimplements this recipe on the CT and the photo. We match DINOv2 patches between the photo and a render of the CT, lift each render patch to an exact 3D point on the CT, and solve the camera with RANSAC PnP. The same code is the refinement step inside our recommended method A7.

In A7 we pin the focal length at A6's shared 4050 px so only the pose moves, and we keep the refined pose only if both the face outline and the interior edges improve. That guard is worth 1.47 dB on our cross view test. The right photo's outline goes from 31.8 px to 7.39 px, and A7 scores 26.18 dB, the best of any method with a usable outline.

The problem they solve

The task is pose estimation of unseen objects. You get a mesh of the object, one RGB photo and the camera's intrinsics, meaning its focal length and image centre. A separate method called CNOS gives a mask of the object's pixels. You must output the rotation \(R\) and translation \(t\) that take model points into the camera, \(x_{\text{cam}} = R\,X + t\). "Unseen" means the method never trained on this object. The BOP Challenge 2023 rules allow at most 5 minutes on one GPU to prepare a new object.

Two ideas you need first

Vision transformers, briefly

The descriptors come from a vision transformer, so you need a rough picture of one. A vision transformer (ViT) cuts an image into square patches, here 14 by 14 pixels. A 420 by 420 crop becomes a 30 by 30 grid, 900 patches. Each patch becomes a vector called a token. The network then runs a stack of identical layers. In each layer every token looks at every other token and mixes in what it finds useful. That step is called attention.

\[ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}} \right) V \]
Q, K, V
three linear maps of the tokens, called queries, keys and values. One row per token.
Q Kᵀ
a table of scores, how much token i should listen to token j
softmax
turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and sum to 1
d
the token length. Dividing by its square root keeps the scores in a sensible range.

In words, each token's new value is a weighted average of all tokens' values, with weights it chose itself. After a layer, a token still sits at its patch but carries information from the whole image. The output token of a patch, at any layer, can be used as that patch's descriptor.

DINOv2 is a ViT trained without labels. A student network learns to match a teacher network's output on different crops of the same image. FoundPose uses the large model, ViT-L/14 with registers, and reads the tokens of layer 18 out of 23. Each descriptor is shortened to 256 numbers with PCA, which keeps the directions along which descriptors vary most.

Bag of visual words, briefly

Comparing the photo with 800 templates patch by patch would be slow, so FoundPose first picks a short list. Search engines describe a document by how often each word appears. The same trick works for images if you invent a vocabulary. Group many patch descriptors into clusters with k-means, which places k centres so each descriptor is close to one. Each centre is a visual word. An image is then a histogram of how often each word appears. Two images that show the object from a similar direction use similar words in similar amounts.

The method step by step

FoundPose has an offline onboarding stage that runs once per object, and an online inference stage that runs per photo.

  1. Render templates

    Render 800 views of the model that cover all rotations evenly, about 25 degrees apart, each 420 by 420 pixels with a black background and fixed light. Keep the depth image of each.

  2. Describe and lift every template patch

    Run DINOv2 on each template. For each patch whose centre falls on the object, keep its descriptor and lift the centre to a 3D model point through the depth.

  3. Build the vocabulary

    Cluster all template descriptors of the object into 2048 visual words. Store each template's word histogram.

  4. Crop the photo

    Warp the photo to a virtual camera that looks straight at the CNOS mask, at the same size and padding as the templates.

  5. Retrieve templates

    Compute the crop's word histogram and keep the 5 templates with the most similar histograms.

  6. Match and solve

    For each retrieved template, match every crop patch to its nearest template patch, giving 2D to 3D links. Run PnP inside RANSAC. Keep the pose with the most inliers, the matches that agree with it.

  7. Refine

    Adjust that pose so that template descriptors, projected into the crop, land on matching crop descriptors.

Templates and lifting patches to 3D

Lifting is what gives every match an exact 3D side. It is the same idea as back projection. A rendered depth image tells you, at each pixel, how far the surface is. With the camera's intrinsics you can turn a pixel and its depth back into a 3D point.

\[ X_{\text{cam}} = d \; K^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (u - c_x)\, d / f \\ (v - c_y)\, d / f \\ d \end{pmatrix}, \qquad X_{\text{model}} = R_t^{\top} \big( X_{\text{cam}} - t_t \big) \]
(u, v)
the centre of a template patch, in pixels
d
the rendered depth at that pixel
K
the intrinsics matrix with focal length f and image centre (c_x, c_y)
R_t, t_t
the pose the template was rendered with. Undoing it moves the point into model coordinates.

In words, walk out from the camera through the pixel until you have gone the rendered depth, then undo the template's pose to land on the model.

A worked example. Take \(f = 500\) px and \(c = (210, 210)\) for a 420 px template. A patch centre at \((252, 168)\) with depth 400 mm lifts to \(X_{\text{cam}} = (42 \cdot 400/500,\; -42 \cdot 400/500,\; 400) = (33.6, -33.6, 400)\) mm. Every template patch is stored as a pair of descriptor and model point. With 800 templates of about 300 valid patches each, the paper's object takes 234 MB.

Which layer to read

The layer decides whether matches land on the correct side of the object. Early layers still know a lot about where a patch sits in the image. Late layers know more about what the patch means, like "a corner of a box" or "a cheek". The paper shows that patches on the left and right side of a symmetric part get different colours at layer 13 and the same colour at layer 23.

A symmetric or plain object, and a face is close to symmetric, gives late layer descriptors that cannot tell left from right. Matches then jump to the mirror image. Layer 18 kept enough position to stay on the right side. In the paper's ablation, layer 18 scored 37.2 AR and the last layer, 23, scored 23.5. Dense SIFT, a classic hand made descriptor, scored 7.6 and SAM's ViT-L scored 10.7.

Retrieving templates with a bag of words

Retrieval keeps the slow matching step to 5 templates out of 800. The paper builds 2048 words per object with k-means.

Each template \(t\) becomes a vector \(b_t = (b_1, \dots, b_k)\) with one entry per word (Sec. 3.2 of the paper).

\[ b_i = \frac{n_{i,t}}{n_t} \, \log \frac{N}{n_i} \qquad\qquad \text{sim}(q, t) = \frac{b_q \cdot b_t}{\lVert b_q \rVert \, \lVert b_t \rVert} \]
n_{i,t}
how often word i occurs in template t
n_t
the number of words in template t, so the first factor is a share
N, n_i
the number of templates, and how often word i occurs across them
sim
cosine similarity, the angle between the two vectors. It ignores their length, so a half hidden object can still match.

In words, a word counts more when it is common in this template and rare in the others, and two images are similar when their word counts point the same way. Each descriptor is also soft assigned to its 3 nearest words with weight \(\exp(-d^2 / 2\sigma^2)\), where \(d\) is its distance to the word. That softens the hard edges of the clusters.

A worked example with 4 words and 3 templates, counting \(n_i\) as the number of templates that contain the word. The counts are T1 = (6, 2, 0, 2), T2 = (0, 5, 5, 0) and T3 = (3, 3, 2, 2). Word 2 is in all three templates, so its factor is \(\log(3/3) = 0\). The other words appear in two templates and get \(\log(3/2) = 0.405\). A photo with counts (5, 3, 0, 2) becomes \(b_q = (0.203, 0, 0, 0.081)\). Its cosine similarity is 0.998 with T1, 0.856 with T3 and 0 with T2. T1 is retrieved first.

Matching and PnP inside RANSAC

This step turns matches into the coarse pose. For each retrieved template, every crop patch is matched to the template patch with the nearest descriptor. A match links a 2D crop point \(u_i\) to a 3D model point \(x_i\). Searching inside one template already removes most of the left and right confusion of symmetric objects.

PnP finds \(R, t\) so that the model points project onto their matched pixels. The paper uses the EPnP solver, a fast closed form version. Some matches are wrong, so PnP runs inside RANSAC. Pick 4 random matches, solve, count the matches that reproject within 10 px, repeat up to 400 times and keep the pose with the most inliers. The best of the 5 templates, by inlier count, becomes the coarse pose.

\[ \min_{R,\,t} \sum_{i \in \text{inliers}} \big\lVert \pi(R\,x_i + t) - u_i \big\rVert^2, \qquad \pi(X, Y, Z) = \Big( c_x + f \tfrac{X}{Z},\; c_y + f \tfrac{Y}{Z} \Big) \]
π
the pinhole projection, from a 3D point in camera coordinates to a pixel

In words, turn and move the model until each inlier's 3D point projects as close as possible to its matched pixel.

Why 400 tries is plenty. If half the matches are right, a random sample of 4 is all right with probability \(0.5^4 = 0.0625\). The chance that 400 samples all contain a wrong match is \((1 - 0.0625)^{400} \approx 6 \times 10^{-12}\). With only 30 percent right matches it would be \((1 - 0.0081)^{400} \approx 0.04\).

Featuremetric refinement

Patches are 14 pixels wide, so a match only says "somewhere in this square", and the coarse pose inherits that coarseness. FoundPose then refines the pose against the photo's descriptors instead of its raw colours, which is why it is called featuremetric rather than photometric.

\[ (R_r, t_r) = \arg\min_{R,\,t} \sum_{(p_i, x_i) \in \mathcal{T}_t} \rho\Big( \big\lVert p_i - F_q\big( \pi(R\,x_i + t) / s \big) \big\rVert \Big) \]
p_i, x_i
the descriptor and 3D model point of template patch i
F_q
the crop's feature map, all its patch descriptors in a grid, read between grid points by bilinear interpolation
π( ) / s
project the model point into the crop, then divide by the patch size s so the position is in feature map cells
ρ
Barron's robust loss with α = −5 and c = 0.5, which stops bad patches from pulling hard

In words, move the pose so that each template patch lands on a spot of the photo whose descriptor looks like its own.

Bilinear interpolation is what makes this smooth. Between grid cells the feature map is a weighted average of the four nearest descriptors, so the cost has a slope everywhere. A one number example. Let the feature map along a row be 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 and 0.7 at cells 0 to 3, and let a template patch have descriptor 0.8. Projected at 1.2, the map reads \(0.5 + 0.2 \times 0.4 = 0.58\), so the residual is 0.22. The slope there is 0.4 per cell. A Gauss-Newton step moves by \(0.22 / 0.4 = 0.55\) cells to 1.75, where the map reads \(0.5 + 0.75 \times 0.4 = 0.8\). The residual is now 0.

Levenberg-Marquardt does this for all six pose numbers at once. With residuals \(r\), their Jacobian \(J\) (how each residual changes with each pose number) and robust weights \(W\), it solves

\[ \big( J^{\top} W J + \lambda\, \text{diag}(J^{\top} W J) \big)\, \delta = -J^{\top} W r \]

and updates the pose by \(\delta\). In words, take the step that best cancels the residuals if the cost were a perfect bowl, but shorten it when that guess has been failing. A small \(\lambda\) gives a full Gauss-Newton step. A large \(\lambda\) gives a short, careful step downhill. After a good step \(\lambda\) shrinks and after a bad one it grows. The paper runs up to 30 iterations.

The robust loss. With α = −5 and c = 0.5 the loss is \(\rho(x) = 1.4 \big[ 1 - (1 + x^2/1.75)^{-2.5} \big]\). For small \(x\) it behaves like \((x/c)^2/2\). At \(x = 1\) it is 0.95 and at \(x = 2\) it is 1.33, and it never passes 1.4. A plain squared loss would give 2 and 8. So a patch that sits on background cannot pull the pose hard.

What they measured

These numbers show how far a model with no training on the object can go. BOP uses seven core datasets, LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, IC-BIN, ITODD, HB and YCB-V, from plain industrial parts to household objects in clutter. FoundPose used only the 3D models and the test images.

A pose counts as correct if its error is under a threshold. AR averages that over many thresholds and three error measures (VSD on the visible surface, MSSD on the 3D surface, MSPD in the image). Higher is better.

From the paper's Table 1. AR averaged over the seven datasets. Time is seconds per image, including about 0.3 s for CNOS. GigaPose's time was measured on a stronger GPU.

  • The featuremetric refinement adds about 5 AR (37.2 to 42.6). A trained render and compare refiner adds about 17 (to 54.7). The two together score best, so they help in different ways.
  • Speed. The coarse stage takes 1.7 s per image against 15.5 s for MegaPose's coarse stage. With the smaller ViT-S backbone it runs at about 1.3 s.
  • Retrieval. Bag of words beat retrieval by DINOv2's single summary token, 37.2 against 25.1 AR. Taking the top template's pose alone, with no matching, already scored 17.7.
  • Masks. With perfect masks instead of CNOS masks, the coarse scores rose by 6 to 19 AR. Bad masks are a main cause of failure.
  • Memory. 234 MB per object, 25 times less than earlier template methods, which need 5.6 GB. The template count, PCA size, vocabulary size and RANSAC iterations mattered only marginally.

Weak points

  • Mask dependence. Retrieval and matching both work inside the CNOS crop. A wrong mask breaks everything after it.
  • Known intrinsics. The method assumes the focal length is known. Ours is not, which is why our A7 had to borrow it from A6.
  • No guarantee from the refinement. The authors say plainly that featuremetric refinement can stop at a local minimum.
  • The best scores need training after all. The fully training free version scores 42.6 or 44.1. The 59.6 headline uses MegaPose's refiner, which was trained on more than 2 million synthetic images.
  • Rigid objects only. A face changes with expression. Our CT has eyes shut and a relaxed mouth, while the photo has eyes open.

How we used it

B3, the recipe on our CT

FoundPose gives what our landmark methods lack, hundreds of matches with an exact 3D side. Its code is under a non commercial licence, so B3 uses none of it. We rewrote the recipe from the paper on top of Apache licensed DINOv2 weights. B3 refines another method's camera, A5 by default.

  1. Crop and size

    Crop the photo to the face with a margin and resize so that one 14 px patch covers about 9 to 10 photo pixels, about the width of a nostril. The network input is capped at 1120 px, which is 80 by 80 patches. The render uses a matching crop camera so both show the same view.

  2. Descriptors

    We use the smaller ViT-B/14 and measured which of its 12 layers to read. Scored by the held out A1 landmark error after one round from A5 (9.86 px for A5 itself), layer 3 gave 11.6 px, layer 6 gave 9.8, layer 9 gave 11.1 and layer 12 gave 15.3. So we read layer 6. The last layer being worst is the paper's finding again.

  3. Match

    Cosine similarity between photo and render patches. A match is kept only if the two patches pick each other as best (mutual nearest neighbours) and the best is clearly better than any match at least 3 patches away (a ratio test). A parabola fitted to the similarity peak places each match below patch size. Eyes and lips are masked out on the photo side, because the CT eyes are shut.

  4. Lift

    Each render patch centre is lifted by casting a ray against the CT mesh. The 3D side of every match is exact, not a detector's guess.

  5. Solve

    RANSAC with EPnP at an 8 px threshold, then a robust Huber least squares PnP (big errors count linearly instead of squared) that may also adjust the focal length inside a narrow window. A solution rotated more than 25 degrees from the start is rejected, since a near symmetric face invites mirrored answers.

  6. Repeat instead of featuremetric LM

    We replaced the Levenberg-Marquardt step with rounds. Render again at the new camera, match again, solve again, up to 3 rounds, stopping when the inlier error stops improving. This needs no gradients through the renderer.

B3 finds 180 to 260 matches per round with an inlier residual of 4.6 px, about a third of a patch. Its front contour error is 5.0 px. On the side photos the right chin group goes from 40 px to 4 px. Its cross view score is 25.75 dB and its three camera distances agree within 126.5 mm. A run takes 25 to 45 s per photo.

It has two limits. It overfits if it runs too many rounds. And a good camera moved 10 degrees and 100 mm away does not come back. So B3 is a refiner, not an initialiser. An optional LoFTR stage, another learned matcher, added nothing.

A7, the same refinement with the focal held

A6 solves all three photos together with one shared focal length, 4050 px. Its cameras agree, but the right photo's own geometry wants a shorter focal, so its pose absorbs the compromise and its outline lands 31.8 px off. B3 fixes poses well but lets each photo move its own focal, so the three cameras drift apart again (B3's front focal is 4893 px).

A7 combines them. It pins A6's 4050 px and runs B3's refinement with only the six pose numbers free. Then a guard asks two questions that are not part of the matching score. Did the projected outline move closer to the photographed one? Did the nose, lip and eyelid edges not move further away? The refined pose is kept only if both answers are yes.

Front photo for fit, IoU and contour, which is why A7 equals A6 there. The guard kept A6's front pose. IoU is the overlap of the rendered and photographed face masks. Cross view bakes a texture from the front photo, renders it at a side camera and compares it with the real side photo, mean over directions, higher is better. Distance spread is across the three photos. C4's fit is on its own matches and is not comparable.

  • The gain is in one direction. Front to right goes from 24.49 dB to 26.35 dB, because the right camera is the one the shared focal broke. Its IoU goes from 0.742 to 0.791.
  • The guard is worth 1.47 dB. Without it, A7 scores 24.71 dB. On the front photo the refinement moved the outline from 6.40 to 7.80 px. On the left photo it improved the outline from 6.39 to 3.40 px while the interior edges went from 11.45 to 11.73 px, and the cross view test scores that pose 1.9 dB worse. An outline only guard would have accepted it.
  • Why only C4 scores higher. C4 wins the cross view column with 26.39 dB, but its outline is 16.6 px off. A7 is the best cross view score with a usable outline, and its camera distances agree within 107 mm, the tightest of the landmark family.
  • Cost. About 14 s per photo.
Watch out

The dense refiner has its own resting point and mostly ignores where it starts. Measured by A1's held out landmarks on the left and right photos, B3 from A5 went from 20.3 and 23.2 px to 22.6 and 19.7 px. A7 from A6 went from 6.7 and 8.0 px to 19.9 and 19.1 px. So the refinement helps a camera that is worse than its resting point and hurts one that is better. That is why A6 needs a guard around it, and why the right photo's held out landmark error rose from 8.05 to 19.08 px even as its outline improved. Those landmarks are the set A6 was fitted to, so they flatter A6.

If they ask you

What does FoundPose bring that landmarks do not?

Hundreds of matches whose 3D side is exact. Each render patch is lifted through the render's depth, so no detector has to guess a point on the CT. Our B3 found 180 to 260 matches per round at 4.6 px inlier error.

Why hold the focal length in A7?

Zoom and distance can mimic each other on a face, and FoundPose assumes the focal is known anyway. A6 gives one focal for all three photos, 4050 px. Holding it keeps the cameras consistent, and only the six pose numbers move.

Why the two part guard?

The dense step can line up the outline by sliding the face across it. On the left photo it did, 6.39 to 3.40 px outline but worse interior edges and 1.9 dB worse cross view. Checking both outline and interior edges makes the guard worth 1.47 dB.

Building blocks used

  • Features, descriptors and DINOv2, for patch descriptors and vision transformers.
  • Rendering, depth and back projection, for lifting template patches to 3D.
  • PnP and RANSAC, for the coarse pose.
  • Least squares and robust fitting, for Levenberg-Marquardt and robust losses.
  • Cameras and projection, for intrinsics and why focal length and distance trade off.

About 50 minutes

Paper P6CVPR 2024Used in C1

DUSt3R: Geometric 3D Vision Made Easy

Shuzhe Wang, Vincent Leroy, Yohann Cabon, Boris Chidlovskii and Jerome Revaud. Aalto University and Naver Labs Europe.

Give the network two ordinary photos with no camera information, and for every pixel of both it tells you where that pixel sits in 3D. Both answers come out in the first camera's frame, so the two views are already lined up. Depth, focal length, camera pose and pixel matches then fall out with a little simple math.

The short version
  • A pointmap is an image where each pixel stores the 3D position of the surface it sees.
  • DUSt3R is one transformer network that takes two photos and outputs a pointmap for each, both in the first camera's frame.
  • The focal length, the second camera's pose and pixel matches are then read off the points with small closed form fits.
  • For more than two photos, a short optimisation puts all the pairwise answers into one shared frame.
  • Our C1 used a successor of DUSt3R and registered its face cloud to the CT. The cameras agreed with each other but the side cameras were wrong.

Read first Cameras and projection, Rendering, depth and back projection and Procrustes.

In one minute

The classic way to build 3D from photos is a long chain. Find keypoints, match them, estimate the cameras, triangulate, then fill in dense depth. Each link adds its own errors, and the chain breaks with few photos, shiny surfaces or little camera motion. Most links also need the focal length up front. DUSt3R, short for Dense and Unconstrained Stereo 3D Reconstruction, replaces the chain with one network.

The output is a pointmap per photo plus a confidence per pixel. The network is trained on 8.5 million image pairs with known 3D, using a simple 3D distance loss with the scale normalised away. For more than two photos, a short global alignment puts all pairwise pointmaps into one frame.

It set new results on multi view pose estimation. On CO3Dv2, 96.2 percent of image pairs had a rotation error under 15 degrees, against 80.5 for the previous best. Its 3D reconstructions on the DTU lab benchmark were 2.7 mm from the true surface on average without any known camera, which the authors say is still behind methods that are given the cameras.

Where this sits in our project

Our C1 runs MapAnything, an Apache licensed successor of DUSt3R, on our three photos with the background masked. We register the resulting face cloud to the CT with a similarity ICP (ICP that may also change the scale) on the stable regions, then carry the network's cameras into CT coordinates. C1 gave one shared focal of 5311 px, 2.66 mm median surface distance on the stable regions, and camera distances that agree within 99.4 mm, the second tightest of all fifteen methods.

But its side outlines were 28 to 30 px off and its cross view score was 23.06 dB, second lowest of the table. Family C lost because a similarity fit can hide a wrong focal length inside a wrong scale and a wrong distance. Figure 8 shows how.

The problem they solve

This is the setting of our three photos, which came with no camera data. The input is a pair of RGB images \(I^1, I^2\) of the same scene. Nothing else is known. Not the focal length, not the image centre, not where either camera stood. The output, for each image, is a pointmap and a confidence map. Everything else people usually want from 3D vision is computed from those.

Pointmaps

The pointmap is the paper's key idea, so it pays to be exact about it. An ordinary image stores a colour at each pixel. A depth map stores one number per pixel, the distance along the camera's viewing axis. A pointmap stores three numbers per pixel, the full 3D position \((x, y, z)\) of the surface seen there. So a \(W \times H\) photo has a \(W \times H \times 3\) pointmap. The paper assumes each pixel sees one surface, so glass and smoke are out.

From depth to pointmap, and between frames

If you knew the intrinsics \(K\) and a depth map \(D\), the pointmap in the camera's own frame would be

\[ X_{i,j} = K^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} i\, D_{i,j} \\ j\, D_{i,j} \\ D_{i,j} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (i - c_x)\, D_{i,j} / f \\ (j - c_y)\, D_{i,j} / f \\ D_{i,j} \end{pmatrix} \]

In words, walk out from the camera through pixel \((i, j)\) until you reach the depth. The pointmap of camera \(n\) written in camera \(m\)'s frame is (the paper's equation 1)

\[ X^{n,m} = P_m\, P_n^{-1}\, h\big(X^n\big) \]
(i, j)
pixel coordinates, i across and j down
D_{i,j}
depth at that pixel
K, f, c
the intrinsics matrix, its focal length and image centre
P_n
camera n's world to camera pose, a 3 by 4 matrix [R | t]
h
appends a 1, \((x, y, z) \to (x, y, z, 1)\), so a 3 by 4 matrix can rotate and shift in one product. This is a homogeneous coordinate.

In words, take camera \(n\)'s points out into the world with \(P_n^{-1}\), then into camera \(m\)'s frame with \(P_m\).

A worked example. With \(f = 500\) px and centre \((256, 192)\), the pixel \((306, 142)\) at depth 2 m gives \(X = (50 \cdot 2/500,\; -50 \cdot 2/500,\; 2) = (0.2, -0.2, 2)\) m. The point is 20 cm right of the axis, 20 cm up (since j grows downward) and 2 m out.

DUSt3R never sees \(K\), \(D\) or \(P\) at test time. It predicts \(X^{1,1}\) and \(X^{2,1}\) directly. Because both are in camera 1's frame, the network has to work out how the two cameras relate, and the answer is hidden inside its output.

The network

The network is where the matching and the geometry are learned, so it helps to see how the two images talk to each other. It follows CroCo, an earlier model from the same lab, pretrained to fill in one view of a scene from another. It has two branches, one per image, each with an encoder, a decoder and a head. Attention, the step where tokens look at each other, is explained on the features and DINOv2 page and in the FoundPose page.

  1. Encoder, shared

    Each image is cut into patches and encoded by the same vision transformer (ViT-Large) with the same weights for both. This is called a Siamese encoder. It gives token sets \(F^1\) and \(F^2\).

  2. Decoders that talk to each other

    Two ViT-Base decoders run side by side. Each decoder block does self attention within its own image, then cross attention to every token of the other image, then a small fully connected network. Information flows between the branches in every block.

  3. Heads

    A head per branch reads the decoder tokens and outputs a pointmap and a confidence map. The final model uses a DPT head, which combines tokens from several layers into a full resolution output.

\[ G^1_i = \text{DecoderBlock}^1_i\big(G^1_{i-1},\, G^2_{i-1}\big), \qquad G^2_i = \text{DecoderBlock}^2_i\big(G^2_{i-1},\, G^1_{i-1}\big) \] \[ X^{1,1}, C^{1,1} = \text{Head}^1\big(G^1_0, \dots, G^1_B\big), \qquad X^{2,1}, C^{2,1} = \text{Head}^2\big(G^2_0, \dots, G^2_B\big) \]
G_i
the tokens after decoder block i, with \(G^1_0 = F^1\) and \(G^2_0 = F^2\)
B
the number of decoder blocks

In words, each decoder block updates one image's tokens using both images' tokens from the block before, and each head turns all its branch's layers into a pointmap with confidence. Nothing here forces the output to obey real camera geometry. The authors chose this on purpose, so that a generic architecture can use strong pretraining.

Training: regression with the scale taken out

Training decides what the output means, including why it has no real scale. Training pairs come with true pointmaps \(\bar X^{1,1}\) and \(\bar X^{2,1}\), built from known depth, intrinsics and poses. The loss is simply the 3D distance between prediction and truth at each valid pixel. There is one catch. From photos alone a small near object and a big far one look the same, so the true scale cannot be predicted. Both pointmaps are therefore divided by their own average distance to the origin before comparing.

\[ \ell_{\text{regr}}(v, i) = \Big\lVert \tfrac{1}{z} X^{v,1}_i - \tfrac{1}{\bar z} \bar X^{v,1}_i \Big\rVert, \qquad z = \frac{1}{|D^1| + |D^2|} \sum_{v \in \{1,2\}} \sum_{i \in D^v} \big\lVert X^v_i \big\rVert \]
v, i
view 1 or 2, and a valid pixel of that view
z, z̄
the mean distance to the origin of the predicted and of the true points
D^v
the pixels where the truth is defined

In words, shrink both clouds so their average distance from the camera is 1, then measure how far each predicted point is from its true point. A worked example. If the truth is a face 46 cm away (\(\bar z \approx 46\)) and the network predicts the same shape at 62 percent of the size (\(z \approx 28.5\)), the raw distance per point is many centimetres. After dividing, both have mean distance 1 and the error is only the shape difference. The network is never punished for scale. The flip side is that its output has no scale in millimetres. You must fix scale from something else, and we did that with ICP against the CT.

Confidence

Some pixels are hard, like sky or areas seen in only one view. The network also predicts a confidence \(C_i\) and the loss becomes (the paper's equation 4)

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{conf}} = \sum_{v} \sum_{i \in D^v} \Big( C^{v,1}_i\, \ell_{\text{regr}}(v, i) - \alpha \log C^{v,1}_i \Big), \qquad C = 1 + e^{\tilde C} > 1 \]

In words, a pixel's error counts more when the network claims high confidence, and claiming low confidence costs a fixed penalty. Look at one pixel. The term \(C\ell\) wants \(C\) small, and \(-\alpha \log C\) wants \(C\) large. Setting the slope to zero, \(\ell - \alpha / C = 0\), gives \(C^* = \alpha / \ell\). So where the error \(\ell\) is small the best confidence is high, and where the error is large it is low. The network learns confidence with no labels for it. Because \(C > 1\) always, it can never switch a pixel off completely, which forces it to guess even in hard areas.

α
a hyperparameter that sets how much low confidence is penalised
C̃
the raw network output before it is mapped above 1

The 8.5 million training pairs come from eight datasets (Habitat, MegaDepth, ARKitScenes, Static Scenes 3D, BlendedMVS, ScanNet++, CO3Dv2 and Waymo), indoor and outdoor, real and synthetic. The network starts from CroCo v2 weights. It trains first at 224 by 224 and then at 512 pixels on the long side, with random crops so that it sees many focal lengths.

Getting cameras back from pointmaps

The focal length

The focal length is the number our whole project hinges on, so this read off matters most to us. Camera 1 sits at the origin of \(X^{1,1}\) and looks along its z axis. If the network is right, projecting each 3D point with the true focal length should land it back on its own pixel. So the focal is the zoom that best does that. The paper assumes the image centre is the middle and pixels are square.

\[ f_1^{*} = \arg\min_{f} \sum_{i=0}^{W} \sum_{j=0}^{H} C^{1,1}_{i,j} \left\lVert (i', j') - f\, \frac{\big(X^{1,1}_{i,j,0},\, X^{1,1}_{i,j,1}\big)}{X^{1,1}_{i,j,2}} \right\rVert, \qquad i' = i - \tfrac{W}{2},\; j' = j - \tfrac{H}{2} \]
(i', j')
the pixel measured from the image centre
X_{i,j,0}, X_{i,j,1}, X_{i,j,2}
the x, y and z of that pixel's 3D point. Dividing by z is the pinhole projection.
C
confidence weights, so hard pixels count less

In words, find the one zoom that puts each 3D point back on its own pixel, trusting confident pixels more. Write \(p_k = (i', j')\) and \(q_k = (x/z, y/z)\) for pixel \(k\). The model is \(p_k \approx f\, q_k\), one unknown number fitted to many 2D vectors. If the norm were squared, the answer would be closed form, \(f = \sum C_k\, p_k \cdot q_k \,/\, \sum C_k\, q_k \cdot q_k\). The paper uses the plain norm, which is more robust to bad pixels, and solves it with the Weiszfeld algorithm. It repeats the closed form with weights \(C_k / \lVert p_k - f q_k \rVert\), so pixels that fit badly count less in the next round.

A worked example with two pixels and unit weights. Pixel 1 has \(p = (100, 50)\) and \(q = (0.2, 0.1)\). Pixel 2 has \(p = (-60, 120)\) and \(q = (-0.12, 0.25)\). Then \(\sum p\cdot q = 20 + 5 + 7.2 + 30 = 62.2\) and \(\sum q \cdot q = 0.05 + 0.0769 = 0.1269\), so \(f = 490\) px. Pixel 1 alone says exactly 500. Pixel 2 says 500 for its x part but about 480 for its y part, and the fit splits the difference.

For camera 2's focal, run the network again on the swapped pair \((I^2, I^1)\) and apply the same formula to \(X^{2,2}\).

The relative pose

Run the pair both ways and you have photo 2's points twice, as \(X^{2,2}\) in its own frame and as \(X^{2,1}\) in camera 1's frame. The rigid transform between those two clouds is camera 2's pose relative to camera 1. The paper finds it with a confidence weighted Procrustes alignment, which has a closed form.

\[ R^{*}, t^{*} = \arg\min_{\sigma, R, t} \sum_i C^{1,1}_i C^{1,2}_i \big\lVert \sigma (R X^{1,1}_i + t) - X^{1,2}_i \big\rVert^2 \]
σ
a free scale, since each prediction has its own lost scale
C
confidences, so only points both predictions trust count much

In words, find the turn, shift and scale that lay one cloud of photo 2's points on the other. Procrustes is sensitive to noise and outliers, so the more robust option is to recover the focal first and run PnP inside RANSAC. The 2D side is the pixel grid of image 2, and the 3D side is \(X^{2,1}\). Pixel matches are just as easy. Take nearest neighbours in 3D between the two pointmaps and keep the pairs that pick each other.

Global alignment for more than two photos

We had three photos, so this is the step that applies to us. The network only sees pairs. For \(N\) photos, build a graph whose edges are pairs that overlap, either from image retrieval or by running all pairs and keeping the confident ones. A pair takes about 40 ms on an H100 GPU. Each pair \(e\) gives pointmaps in its own frame and its own lost scale. The goal is one pointmap \(\chi^n\) per photo in a shared world frame.

\[ \chi^{*} = \arg\min_{\chi,\, P,\, \sigma} \sum_{e \in E} \sum_{v \in e} \sum_{i=1}^{HW} C^{v,e}_i \big\lVert \chi^v_i - \sigma_e P_e X^{v,e}_i \big\rVert, \qquad \prod_e \sigma_e = 1 \]
e, v
a pair, and one of its two views
P_e, σ_e
a rigid transform and a scale per pair, which move that pair's predictions into the world frame
χ^v_i
the world position of pixel i of view v, which every pair containing v must agree on
∏ σ_e = 1
stops the trivial answer where every scale shrinks to zero

In words, find one world point per pixel and one move and scale per pair, so that every pair's prediction of a pixel lands on that pixel's world point. Unlike bundle adjustment, the classic joint camera and point solve, which compares 2D reprojection errors, this compares 3D positions. The paper runs plain gradient descent, which converges in a few hundred steps and a few seconds on a GPU. Replacing \(\chi\) with depth maps seen through pinhole cameras recovers every camera's intrinsics, pose and depth at once.

What they measured

These show how good a camera free network is at the tasks we care about, pose and depth. All results use one model, DUSt3R 512, never fine tuned on a test task.

  • Localisation. As a pure matcher on 7Scenes and Cambridge, with known query intrinsics, it was comparable to dedicated methods, for example 3 cm and 0.97 degrees on the Chess scene, without training for this task.
  • Ablations. CroCo pretraining and the higher 512 pixel resolution both helped on every task.
  • DTU. They do not reach the best methods, which use the true cameras and train on DTU, but argue 2.7 mm is useful for a plug and play method.
Watch out, two different 2.7 mm numbers

The paper's DTU 2.677 mm and our C1 2.66 mm look alike by coincidence. DTU accuracy is the mean distance from every reconstructed point to a laser scanned reference of small lab objects. Our 2.66 mm is the median distance between MapAnything's face cloud and our CT, on the forehead, nose and cheekbones only, after our own similarity ICP. Do not compare them.

Weak points

  • Regression is less precise than triangulation. The authors say so. Classic methods with known cameras reach sub pixel accuracy.
  • No real scale. Every pointmap is up to an unknown scale. You need something else, like a CT, to fix millimetres.
  • No enforced geometry. The pointmaps need not match any real pinhole camera. A focal length read off them is only as good as the network's depth.
  • Pairs grow quickly. N photos give up to N(N-1)/2 pairs, each needing a strong GPU.
  • Plain surfaces. Few photos of smooth, textureless surfaces, like skin, give it less to work with.
  • Intrinsics per image. Even for a sequence from one camera, the paper never forces the focal lengths to be equal.

How we used it

Our C1 is the only one of our methods that uses all three photos at once from the start. The idea of family C is to build a 3D surface from the photos themselves, register it to the CT, and read the cameras off the registration. That gives thousands of 2D to 3D pairs on the CT surface, each point paired with the photo pixel it came from.

  1. Mask the inputs

    The front photo and both three quarter photos go in with everything except face skin, body skin and hair painted grey. The backdrop has checkerboard markers and stayed still while the head turned. An unmasked run concludes that the camera never moved.

  2. Run MapAnything

    We used MapAnything with its Apache 2.0 checkpoint, with VGGT (another successor) and DUSt3R as fallbacks. It runs in its own environment, since its dependencies clash with ours. It returns a pointmap with confidence and a camera per photo, all in its own frame.

  3. Start from landmarks

    MediaPipe landmarks of the front photo are lifted to 3D through the front pointmap and paired with our A2 consensus CT landmarks on the rigid subset. A similarity Procrustes fit on those pairs gives the first transform.

  4. Similarity ICP on stable regions

    Point to point ICP with a free scale on the confident points of all three views settles the scale. Then a robust point to plane ICP runs with the scale frozen, ignoring pairs more than about 2 mm apart (a Tukey kernel). On the CT side only the forehead, nasal bridge and cheekbones count. On the photo side the eyes and lips are removed, because the expression in a photo cannot match the CT.

  5. Chain the cameras

    Each network camera is carried through the same similarity into CT coordinates. Then a joint robust PnP over all three photos refines them with one shared focal length, using the dense pairs.

Front photo for fit, IoU and contour. Cross view is the mean over directions. Distance spread is how much the three camera to face distances disagree, smaller is better. C3 and C4 fit their own matches, so their fit columns are not comparable.

  • The surface is the weak part. 2.66 mm median distance on the stable regions. That is worse than a clinical bar and worse than phone photogrammetry. Hair has to be excluded from the ICP, and letting ICP choose its own scale was worse than taking the scale from landmarks.
  • The cameras agree with each other. The three camera to face distances agree within 99.4 mm, second only to C3's 89.3 mm, because all three come from one joint solve.
  • The focal is high. The shared focal came out at 5311 px. Four independent estimates (C3, C4 and the learned focal estimators GeoCalib and Depth Pro) cluster at 3300 to 4700 px, so C1 sits above that range.
  • The front looks fine, the sides do not. Front IoU 0.761 and contour 8.59 px are respectable. The side cameras inherit the registration error and land 28 to 30 px off. The cross view score, 23.06 dB, is the second lowest of the table, above only C2's 22.33.

Why family C lost

This is the lesson of the page for our project. Seen from the front, a face is shallow compared to its distance from the camera. For a shallow object, doubling the focal length and doubling the distance makes almost the same picture. Only the strength of the perspective changes. So a focal length read off a face is weakly held, and a reconstruction with a wrong focal is mostly stretched or squashed in depth.

A similarity fit has one free scale and a free shift. It cannot undo a depth stretch. It picks a compromise scale and slides the cloud along the front camera's axis until the front view matches. The front photo cannot see a shift along its own axis. A camera 25 degrees to the side sees about \(\sin 25^\circ \approx 0.42\) of that shift as a sideways move, and its outline lands off. That is exactly our pattern, a front contour of 8.59 px and side contours of 28 to 30 px. Our C1 code notes predicted it before the run.

So our A6 solves all three photos jointly with one focal length directly against the CT landmarks, with no free scale in between, and A7 refines each pose with that focal held. Family C still helped. Its methods agree on the focal length across photos much better than single photo PnP did, and that agreement pointed at the joint solve that became A6.

If they ask you

What is a pointmap?

An image sized grid of 3D points. Pixel (i, j) stores where its surface is, in camera 1's frame. DUSt3R predicts one for each of two photos in the same frame, so the views come out aligned, and depth, focal and pose can be read off.

Is your 2.66 mm the same as DUSt3R's 2.7 mm on DTU?

No. DTU's is a mean distance on lab objects. Ours is a median on the stable face regions after our own similarity ICP to the CT. The closeness is a coincidence.

Why did C1 lose if its cameras agree so well?

Agreement is not correctness. A similarity fit can absorb a wrong focal into a wrong scale and a wrong distance along the front axis. The front photo cannot see that, the side photos can. Side outlines were 28 to 30 px off and the cross view score 23.06 dB.

Building blocks used

  • Cameras and projection, for intrinsics, homogeneous coordinates and the focal versus distance trade.
  • Rendering, depth and back projection, for depth maps and how a pointmap relates to them.
  • Procrustes alignment, for relative pose and the similarity fit.
  • ICP, for registering the cloud to the CT.
  • PnP and RANSAC, for robust poses from pointmaps.
  • Features, descriptors and DINOv2, for transformers and attention.
  • Least squares and robust fitting, for the Weiszfeld iterations and the confidence weighted losses.

About 25 minutes

Wrap up X1All six papers

The papers side by side

The six papers solve different problems, but each one is a way to match a 3D shape with images. This page lines them up so you can say in one sentence how any two of them differ, and which one to reach for on a new case.

The short version
  • Every paper needs matches, but they match different things. Landmarks (Park, Paulsen), dense patches (FoundPose), whole images (Corsini) or surfaces (Amberg, and Park's last step).
  • Matches between pixels and 3D points give a camera through PnP. Matches between two 3D shapes give a rotation, shift and maybe scale through Procrustes or ICP.
  • The papers also differ in where learning sits. Amberg and Corsini learn nothing. DUSt3R is a network from end to end.
  • Landmark methods need no start but stop at landmark accuracy. Dense and image based methods are more exact but need a good start.
  • So our A7 chains them. Landmarks give the start, and dense matching refines it under a guard.

Read first the six paper pages, starting with Park et al.
