What gets matched

The first way to tell the papers apart is the unit of a match. Every paper needs to know which part of one thing goes with which part of the other. A correspondence, or match, is one such pair.

  • Landmarks. A few named points, such as the nose tip. Park and Paulsen work this way. Few matches, but each one is meaningful, so the geometry is simple. The cost is that a detector's error goes straight into the answer.
  • Dense patches. Hundreds of small squares matched by a learned descriptor. FoundPose works this way. Many matches, each one weak, and RANSAC sorts out the wrong ones.
  • Image similarity. No explicit match at all. Corsini renders the model at a guessed camera and scores the whole picture against the photo with mutual information, then searches for the best camera.
  • Surface fitting. Points on one surface pair with the closest points on the other, as in ICP. Amberg works this way, and Park uses it to finish.

2D to 3D, or 3D to 3D

The second difference is where the match lives, because that decides what you solve for. In a 2D to 3D match, one side is a pixel and the other is a 3D point. The unknown is a camera, and you solve it with PnP (finding the camera from point pairs). Corsini and FoundPose work here, and so does our whole pipeline.

In a 3D to 3D match, both sides are 3D points. The unknown is a rotation and a shift, sometimes with a scale. You solve it with Procrustes (the best fit for matched point sets) or ICP. Park, Paulsen and Amberg work here. DUSt3R turns photos into 3D first and then works here too.

The choice matters for our task. A 3D to 3D route needs a 3D face from the photos first. That rebuilt face carries its own errors, and its scale is free. In our family C, a similarity ICP (ICP that may also scale) absorbed a wrong focal length into scale and depth instead of correcting it.

Learned or classical

The third difference is how much of each method is learned, which decides what breaks on a new kind of data. A learned step is a neural network trained on data. A classical step is a formula or an optimiser you could write by hand. Most of these papers mix both. The useful question is where the learning sits.

  • Park uses a pretrained landmark detector and trains nothing. Everything after the detector is geometry.
  • Paulsen trains its own CNN. That is its main cost on a new kind of scan.
  • Amberg and Corsini are fully classical.
  • FoundPose uses a pretrained feature network as is, with no training on the new object. The pose itself comes from classical RANSAC PnP.
  • DUSt3R is learned end to end, trained on about 8.5 million image pairs. The geometry is what the network learned to output.

For us, the learned parts that helped were the ones that stayed off the critical path. MediaPipe and DINOv2 feed matches into a classical solver, and the solver can reject them. The fully learned routes in family C rebuilt the face well but placed the camera worse.

Two questions that sort the papers

Two questions decide most of how a method behaves on a new case. How much does it trust landmarks? How close a start does it need? The map places each paper on both. The positions are our reading of each paper, not measured numbers.

The pattern is simple. Methods that lean on landmarks start from nothing and land close, but never closer than the landmarks allow. Methods that ignore landmarks can be more exact, but only from a good start. So the practical recipe is to chain them. Start with landmarks, then refine with something dense.

A decision guide for this problem

  1. Is the focal length known?

    If the photo has EXIF (camera data stored in the file) or the lens is known, fix it. Most of our trouble came from not knowing it. If not, solve all photos jointly with one shared focal, as A6 does, and check the value against a learned estimator.

  2. Get a start from landmarks.

    Render the CT and detect landmarks, as Park does. Use many renders and a consensus, as Paulsen does, to drop the sliding outline points.

  3. Keep the expression out.

    Fit only on rigid regions. Give the eyes and lips zero weight, as Amberg allows.

  4. Refine with dense matches, under a guard.

    Use FoundPose style patch matching with the focal fixed. Keep the result only if checks it was not fitted to also improve, such as the outline.

  5. Use image similarity as a check, not a driver.

    Corsini style scores need shading in the photo. Under flat studio light, mutual information drifted for us.

  6. Use rebuild and register when you have many photos.

    DUSt3R style methods shine with many views and a free scale is acceptable. With three near frontal photos they lost on the outline.

Remember

Landmarks give a start, dense matching gives precision, and a guard decides whether to trust the refinement. 2D to 3D solves a camera. 3D to 3D solves a transform and needs a 3D face from the photos first.

About 15 minutes

Wrap up X2254 terms

Glossary

Every term used on this site, in plain words. Each one links to the page that explains it properly. Type in the box to filter the list. The filter also searches inside the definitions, so a word like "focal" finds every related term.

#ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXZ

#

3D morphable model
A face model built from many 3D face scans. A handful of numbers bend it into almost any face shape. Our C3 fits one to the photo with 3DDFA_V3. Family C
3DDFA_V3
A free network that fits a 3D morphable model to a single face photo. It runs our C3, which lands about 1 mm from the CT on stable regions. Family C
6D pose
The full placement of a rigid object. Three numbers say how it is turned and three say where it is. FoundPose outputs one. FoundPose

A

A1 to A7, B1 to B4, C1 to C4
The names of our 15 methods. Family A works from landmarks (A1 single render, A2 multi view consensus, A3 template landmark transfer, A4 geometric snapping, A5 fusion, A6 joint solve, A7 refined and recommended). Family B refines by comparing images (B1 differentiable rendering, B2 render and compare, B3 DINOv2 dense correspondence, B4 optical flow loop). Family C rebuilds the face from photos and registers it (C1 MapAnything, C2 Depth Pro, C3 3DDFA_V3, C4 COLMAP). Our methods
Ablation
A test where you remove one part of a method and measure how much worse it gets. It shows which parts matter. FoundPose
AbsRel and δ<1.25
Two scores for predicted depth. AbsRel is the average depth error as a fraction of the true depth, so lower is better. δ<1.25 is the share of pixels within 25 percent of the true depth, so higher is better. DUSt3R
Adam
A popular downhill optimiser that adapts its step size for each unknown as it goes. B1 used it to follow the slope of its differentiable renderer. Searching without gradients
Affine transform
A map that can turn, stretch, shear and shift, while keeping straight lines straight. In 3D it has 12 numbers. Amberg gives every template vertex its own one. Amberg et al.
Alar base
The side of the nostril, where it joins the cheek. MediaPipe points 129 and 358 sit there. Face landmarks
Albedo
The surface's own colour, with the effect of light taken out. A flat lit photo shows mostly albedo, while a CT render shows only shading. That mismatch is why mutual information drifted on our case. Comparing two images
Ambient occlusion
How hidden a point is from the open space around it. Creases and nostrils come out dark, much as they look in a photo. Corsini renders it to compare with photos. Corsini et al.
AR (average recall)
The score of the BOP pose benchmark, from 0 to 100. It is roughly the share of poses close enough to the truth, averaged over many strictness levels and three error measures (VSD, MSSD and MSPD). Higher is better. FoundPose
Attention
The step inside a transformer where each token looks at every other token and takes a weighted mix of their content. Each token sends a query, every token offers a key and a value, and the weights say how well each key answers the query. Features and DINOv2

B

Back projection
Going from a pixel back to a 3D point, also called lifting. Follow the pixel's ray out of the camera until it reaches the depth that the render stored, and you land on the surface. Rendering and back projection
Backbone
The main feature network inside a bigger system. For example, FoundPose can run with a small or a large ViT as its backbone. Features and DINOv2
Bag of words
A fast way to compare whole images. Sort all patch descriptors into a fixed set of typical ones, called visual words, and count how often each appears. FoundPose uses these counts to pick the most similar templates. FoundPose
Bake
Writing colours from the photos into the texture image once, so the mesh carries its colour without the photos. Painting the surface
Barycentric coordinates
Three weights that describe a point inside a triangle as a mix of its corners. They add up to 1. The same weights carry depth, colour or UV from the corners to the point. Painting the surface
Basin
The set of starting guesses from which an optimiser still slides into the right answer. Start outside it and you end up in a wrong dip. Searching without gradients
Benchmark
A public test set with agreed scores, so different methods can be compared fairly. BOP, BU-3DFE and DTU are examples. The papers side by side
Bilinear sampling
Reading an image at a point between pixel centres by blending the four nearest pixels, each weighted by how close it is. Also called bilinear interpolation. Painting the surface
BOP
The standard public benchmark for object pose. It has seven datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, IC-BIN, ITODD, HB and YCB-V) and 108 objects, from plain industrial parts to household objects in clutter. It is scored by AR. FoundPose
BU-3DFE
A public set of 3D face scans of people making several expressions, with hand placed landmarks. Paulsen reports a 2.42 mm mean landmark error on it. Paulsen et al.
Bundle adjustment
One big least squares over all cameras and all 3D points at once. It moves them all to make every reprojection error small. COLMAP runs it inside our C4. Least squares

C

Camera frame
Coordinates measured from the camera. The camera sits at the origin and looks along one axis, so the depth of a point is simply one of its coordinates. Cameras and projection
Camera pose
Where a camera stands and which way it points. Three numbers for the turn and three for the position. Cameras and projection
Canonical face
MediaPipe's generic average face mesh, with 468 points and 898 triangles. Every drawing on this site uses it, never patient data. Face landmarks
CBCT
Cone beam CT, the compact 3D X ray scanner used in dental clinics. Park lines up CBCT surfaces with face scans, from a RAYSCAN Studio CBCT and a RayFace 200 face scanner. Park et al.
Chamfer distance
The average distance from each point of one set to the nearest point of the other set, often taken both ways. Our contour metric and B2's outline score are chamfer distances. Comparing two images
Chart
One piece of a mesh after it is cut for unwrapping. Each chart lies flat somewhere in the texture image. xatlas cut our CT into 4371 charts. Painting the surface
Chin rest
The plate the patient's chin sits on during the scan. On our CT it is fused into the skin surface and must not receive skin colour. The task
CMA-ES
A search that needs no gradient. It throws a cloud of guesses around the current best, keeps the better ones, and moves and reshapes the cloud toward them. A running memory of past moves, the evolution path, helps it pick up speed along a valley. B2 uses it. Searching without gradients
CNN
Convolutional neural network. A stack of layers of small learned filters that slide over an image. Early layers find edges, and later layers find whole parts like an eye. Features and DINOv2
CNOS
A separate method that marks which pixels of a photo belong to an object, using only its 3D model. FoundPose crops the photo around the CNOS mask. FoundPose
CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, NYUD-v2 and other data sets
Public test sets used in the DUSt3R paper. The first two are videos used to score camera poses. NYUD-v2 is indoor photos with measured depth. DUSt3R trained on eight collections, such as MegaDepth, ARKitScenes, BlendedMVS and ScanNet++. DUSt3R
COLMAP
A classic structure from motion program. It finds cameras and sparse 3D points from a set of overlapping photos. Our C4 uses it. Family C
Confidence map
A per pixel score of how sure a network is about its output. DUSt3R outputs one next to each pointmap. DUSt3R
Contour distance
Our landmark free metric. The median distance between the rendered head outline and the photo's face outline along the jaw and cheeks, in pixels. Lower is better. How to read each number
Convolution
Sliding a small grid of weights (a kernel) over an image and, at each spot, adding up weight times pixel. The result is a new image called a feature map. Features and DINOv2
Coordinate descent
Improving a score along one axis at a time, then the next, round and round. It zigzags slowly in a diagonal valley, which Powell's method fixes. Searching without gradients
Coordinate frame
A choice of origin, axes and units. We use three, the CT frame, the camera frame and the image frame. The task
Correspondence
A pair that says this point in one thing is that point in the other. Also called a match. Every method on this site is a way to get correspondences. PnP
Corsini's test objects
Five scanned objects with real photos, CAPITAL1 and CAPITAL2 (carved stone capitals), DOGS and HORSE (shiny objects) and a BAS-RELIEF (a carving on a wall). The reference cameras came from a semi automatic tool called TexAlign. Corsini et al.
Cosine similarity
A closeness score for two vectors, the cosine of the angle between them. 1 means they point the same way and 0 means they are at right angles. Features and DINOv2
Covariance
A matrix that says how spread out a cloud of points is in each direction, and which directions vary together. CMA-ES learns one to shape its cloud of guesses. Searching without gradients
CPD and FPFH
Two classic ways to roughly line up two 3D surfaces without landmarks. Park compares against both, each followed by ICP. Park et al.
CroCo
An earlier network from the DUSt3R lab, trained to fill in one view of a scene from another. DUSt3R starts from its weights. DUSt3R
Cross attention
In a transformer, the tokens of one input look at the tokens of another input. DUSt3R relates its two photos this way. DUSt3R
Cross covariance matrix
In Procrustes, the 3 by 3 matrix that adds up how the centred points of one set line up with those of the other. Its SVD gives the best rotation. Procrustes
Cross view PSNR
Our fairest metric. Paint the CT from one photo, render it at another photo's solved camera, and compare with that real photo. A wrong camera that fits one photo fails it. Higher is better. Comparing two images
CT
Computed tomography. X ray measurements turned into a 3D grid of density values. The skin surface is pulled out of that grid as a mesh. The task
Curvature
How sharply a surface bends at a point. A4 uses a curvature measure, the shape index, to place the eye corners and the sides of the nostrils. Family A

D

Decibel (dB)
A log scale for ratios. For PSNR, higher is better, and every 6 dB halves the typical pixel error. 25 dB means a typical error of about 14 grey levels out of 255. Comparing two images
Decimation
Making a copy of a mesh with fewer triangles that keeps the same overall shape. xatlas runs on a decimated copy of our CT to save time. Painting the surface
Degenerate set
A set of points that cannot pin down the answer, for example points all on one line, which leave the turn about that line free. Procrustes
Dense correspondence
Hundreds or thousands of matches spread over the whole image, instead of a few landmarks. B3 and B4 work this way. Features and DINOv2
Depth map
An image that stores, at each pixel, how far away the surface is instead of a colour. Rendering and back projection
Depth Pro
Apple's network that predicts depth in real units and a focal length from a single photo. It runs our C2, whose depth came out 9 percent long, and gave focal estimates of 3319, 4474 and 4391 px. Family D
Descriptor
A list of numbers that sums up what a small image patch looks like, so that similar patches get similar lists. Matching compares descriptors. Features and DINOv2
Determinant
One number computed from a square matrix. For a 3 by 3 matrix it says how much the matrix scales volume. A rotation has determinant 1, and a mirror flip has determinant minus 1. Procrustes
DICOM
The standard file format of medical scanners. It also fixes the patient axes we call LPS. The task
Differentiable rendering
A renderer that also reports how the image would change if you nudged the camera, so an optimiser can follow the slope downhill. Our B1 uses the Mitsuba renderer this way. Family B
DINOv2
A vision transformer trained without labels on a huge image collection. Its patch features match photos to renders well with no extra training. B3 and A7 are built on it. Features and DINOv2
Distance spread
How far apart the three solved camera to face distances are. The camera did not move between photos, so smaller is better. How to read each number
Dlib
A free software library with a face landmark detector. Park runs it on renders of both scans. Park et al.
DLT
The direct linear transform. It finds a camera from six or more point pairs by writing projection as linear equations and solving them with SVD. PnP
Dolly zoom
Moving the camera back while zooming in, so the face stays the same size. The face changes only slightly, which is why focal length and distance are hard to tell apart from one photo. Cameras and projection
Dot product
Multiply two vectors entry by entry and add up. It is large when they point the same way and zero when they are at right angles. Cameras and projection
DTU
A lab benchmark of small objects scanned with a precise reference surface. Without knowing any camera, DUSt3R scores 1.7 mm overall on it. DUSt3R
DTU-3D
A public set of 601 face scans with 73 hand placed landmarks each. Paulsen tests on it. Paulsen et al.
DUSt3R
A 2024 network that takes two photos with no camera data and outputs a 3D point for every pixel. Our C1 uses its successor MapAnything. DUSt3R
DUSt3R's rivals (PoseDiffusion, PixSfM, DPT, GeoMVSNet)
The best other methods in DUSt3R's results tables, each specialised for one task such as camera pose or depth. DUSt3R

E

Encoder and decoder
The two halves of many networks. The encoder turns the input into features, and the decoder turns features into the output. A head is the last small part that writes the final numbers. DUSt3R has one shared encoder and two decoders that talk to each other. DUSt3R
Entropy
How spread out a set of values is, measured in bits. It is the average number of yes or no questions needed to guess a value. Mutual information is built from entropies. Comparing two images
EPnP
A fast PnP solver that writes every 3D point as a mix of four control points and solves for those. Our RANSAC runs it. PnP
Euler angles (yaw, pitch, roll)
Three turns about fixed axes that together describe a rotation. Yaw turns the head left or right, pitch nods it up and down, and roll tilts it toward a shoulder. Cameras and projection
EXIF
Camera data stored inside a photo file, usually including the focal length. Our photos had none. The task
Extrinsics
The rotation and translation that carry world points into the camera frame. Another name for the camera pose. Cameras and projection

F

Feature (keypoint)
A spot in an image worth describing, such as an eye corner. In networks the word also means the vector of numbers a network gives each patch. Features and DINOv2
Feature map
The image that a convolution or a network layer outputs. Each pixel says how strongly a pattern was found there. Features and DINOv2
Featuremetric refinement
Polishing a pose by lining up learned features instead of raw pixel colours. FoundPose does this with Levenberg Marquardt. FoundPose
Field of view
How wide an angle the camera sees. A long focal length gives a narrow field of view. Cameras and projection
Fill mask
An image the same size as the texture that records, for every texel, whether its colour came from a photo, a mirror or inpainting. It keeps invented skin honest. Painting the surface
Fit px
Our column for the reprojection error of each method's own landmarks. It rewards agreeing with MediaPipe, not being right. How to read each number
Focal length
How zoomed in a lens is, measured here in pixels. A larger focal length means a narrower view. Ours settled at 4050 px. Cameras and projection
Foundation model
A large network trained once on huge data and then reused for many tasks without retraining. DINOv2 is one. FoundPose
FoundPose
A 2024 method that finds the pose of an object it was never trained on, by matching DINOv2 patches between the photo and rendered views of the model. Our B3 follows its recipe. FoundPose

G

Gauss Newton
A least squares solver. At each step it replaces the residuals by their straight line approximation from the Jacobian, solves that easy problem, and moves. Least squares
Gaussian
The bell shaped curve that random errors often follow. A Gaussian window weights the pixels near its centre most. Least squares
GeoCalib
A learned estimator of focal length and the direction of gravity from one photo. It gave 4665, 4192 and 3800 px for our three photos. Family D
Geometric median
The point with the smallest total distance to a set of points. Stray points pull it much less than they pull the mean. A2 uses it for each landmark. Paulsen et al.
Global alignment
DUSt3R's step for more than two photos. It puts all the pairwise pointmaps into one shared 3D frame, by solving one move and one scale per pair so that every pair agrees on each pixel's 3D point. DUSt3R
GPU
Graphics processing unit, the chip that runs networks and rendering fast, much faster than the main processor (the CPU). The H100 is a large data centre GPU. DUSt3R
Gradient
The vector of slopes of a function, one per unknown. It points where the function rises fastest, so optimisers step against it. Least squares
Gradient descent
Take a small step downhill along the negative gradient and repeat. Simple, but slow in narrow curved valleys. Least squares
Gradient field
The arrow of brightness change at every pixel of an image. NGF compares two such fields by direction. Comparing two images
Grazing angle
Seeing a surface nearly edge on. One photo pixel then covers a long strip of skin, so our bake ignores triangles whose facing cosine is below 0.35, about 70 degrees. Painting the surface
Ground truth
The known correct answer used to score a method. Our case has none for the camera, which is why we use landmark free checks. Our methods and results
Guard
Our acceptance test in A7. A refined pose is kept only if the outline and the interior edges both line up better. On our case it is worth 1.47 dB. Why A7

H

Heatmap
An image a network outputs for one landmark, bright where the landmark probably is. The brightest pixel is the guess. Face landmarks
Homogeneous coordinates
A point with an extra 1 added at the end, so (x, y) becomes (x, y, 1). Projection and shifts then become plain matrix products. Cameras and projection
Huber loss
A loss that counts small residuals squared and large ones only linearly, so one bad match pulls less. Our PnP switches over at 4 px by default. Least squares

I

ICP
Iterative closest point. Pair each point with the nearest point on the other surface, solve the best rigid motion for those pairs, move, and repeat. ICP
ICT FaceKit
A second public face model. A3 bends it onto the CT as a cross check on the MediaPipe template. Family A
Image plane
The flat sheet in front of a pinhole camera where the picture forms. Every pixel is a spot on it. Cameras and projection
Inlier
A match that agrees with the fitted model to within a threshold. The inlier threshold, such as 8 px, decides how close counts as agreeing. RANSAC
Inner and outer loop
The two loops of Amberg's method. The inner loop refinds closest points and solves again at a fixed stiffness. The outer loop then lowers the stiffness and runs the inner loop again. Amberg et al.
Inpainting
Filling a hole in an image by growing colour inward from its edges. Our code uses OpenCV's Telea method for skin no photo saw. Painting the surface
Intrinsics
The lens settings, the focal length and the principal point, collected in a 3 by 3 matrix called K. Cameras and projection
IoU
Intersection over union. The area two regions share divided by the area they cover together. 1 is a perfect overlap. It hides small outline errors. How to read each number
IRLS
Iteratively reweighted least squares. Solve a weighted least squares, lower the weight of each point with a big residual, and solve again. It is how a robust loss such as Huber is minimised. Least squares
Isosurface
The surface where a 3D grid of values crosses a threshold. The CT skin is the isosurface where tissue density crosses the skin level. Face landmarks

J

Jacobian
The table of first derivatives of every residual with respect to every unknown. It says how each error moves when you nudge each unknown. Gauss Newton and Levenberg Marquardt are built on it. Least squares
Joint histogram
A table that counts, for every pair of brightness bins, how many pixels have that brightness in image A and that one in image B. Mutual information is computed from it. Comparing two images
Joint solve
Solving several unknowns in one least squares so they share information. A6 solves three camera poses and one shared focal length together. Family A

K

k-means
A simple method that sorts items into k groups of similar items. It moves k group centres until they settle. FoundPose uses it to build its visual words. FoundPose
Kabsch algorithm
The SVD recipe for the best rotation between two matched point sets, after both are centred, with the scale fixed. Procrustes
Kernel
The small grid of weights a convolution slides over the image. A kernel like [-1, 0, 1] responds to vertical edges. Features and DINOv2
Kronecker product
A way to build a big matrix from two small ones. Each entry of the first is replaced by that entry times the whole second matrix. Amberg uses it to write the stiffness term. Amberg et al.

L

L-BFGS-B
A general purpose gradient based optimiser that accepts bounds on the unknowns. On Amberg's problem it stalls, because the cost can jump as matches appear. Amberg et al.
Lambert's law
A matte surface looks brightest when it faces the light and darker as it turns away. Its brightness follows the cosine of the angle to the light. A surface that obeys it is called Lambertian. Rendering and back projection
Landmark
A named point you can find on any face, such as the nose tip or an eye corner. Face landmarks
Least squares
Choosing the unknowns that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Least squares
Leave one out and corruption tests
Two checks in A5. Leave one out solves again with each landmark removed. The corruption test pushes one landmark and watches the camera move. Together they show which points hold the answer. Family A
Levenberg Marquardt
A least squares solver that blends Gauss Newton with small downhill steps. It steps carefully when the fit is far off and fast when it is close. Least squares
Licences (Apache, CC BY-NC)
The terms under which code and weights may be used. Apache allows commercial use. CC BY-NC forbids it, which is why B3 re implements FoundPose instead of using its code. Features and DINOv2
Line search
Finding the lowest point along one straight direction, for example by shrinking a bracket around it (golden section). Powell's method is built from line searches. Searching without gradients
Linear light
Brightness values before the camera's gamma curve, where twice the light means twice the number. Our texture polish fits its gains there. Painting the surface
Local minimum
A dip that is lower than everything near it but not the lowest overall. An optimiser that starts nearby can get stuck in it. Searching without gradients
LoFTR
Another learned image matcher. B3's optional LoFTR stage added nothing. Features and DINOv2
Loss
The number an optimiser tries to make small, built from the residuals. Squared loss and Huber loss are examples. Least squares
LPS
The DICOM patient frame. x points to the patient's left, y to the back of the head and z up. Our CT is in this frame. The task

M

MapAnything
An Apache licensed successor to DUSt3R that rebuilds 3D from several photos. Our C1 runs it on the three photos, with 2.66 mm stable region surface distance. VGGT, another successor, was a fallback. DUSt3R
Mask
A black and white image that marks which pixels belong to something, such as the face. A render gives its mask for free, and a photo needs a segmenter. Comparing two images
MDCT
Multi detector CT, the hospital CT scanner. Park reports 0.37 mm mean surface error on MDCT cases. Park et al.
Median
The middle value once values are sorted. Unlike the mean, one wild value barely moves it. How to read each number
MediaPipe
Google's free face landmark detector. It finds 478 points on a photo. Its canonical face model, used in our drawings, has 468. Face landmarks
MegaPose, GigaPose and GenFlow
Trained pose methods that FoundPose compares against. Before refinement they score 20.8, 27.6 and 23.5 AR against FoundPose's 37.2. FoundPose
Mesh
A surface made of small triangles. The triangle corners are vertices and their sides are edges. Rendering and back projection
Minimal set
The smallest number of matches that fixes a model, such as 3 point pairs for a camera with a known lens. RANSAC fits each guess to one random minimal set. RANSAC
Mirror fill
Filling an unseen texel with the colour of its mirror point across the face midline, if the camera saw that point. Painting the surface
Mitsuba
A research renderer that can also return gradients. Our B1 used it, and it moved only 0.03 degrees from its start. Family B
Monocular depth
Depth predicted from a single photo by a network, with no second view. Depth Pro does this. Family C
MRI
Magnetic resonance imaging, a scanner that shows soft tissue. Its images look different from CT, so registering the two needs a measure like mutual information. Comparing two images
MSE and RMSE
Mean squared error, the average of the squared pixel differences. RMSE is its square root, a typical error in grey levels. PSNR is RMSE on a log scale. Comparing two images
MTL
The small text file next to an OBJ that names the texture image and how to light it. Painting the surface
Mutual information
How much knowing one image's value at a pixel tells you about the other image's value there, by any rule. It does not need the two images to look alike. NMI is its version scaled to 0 to 1. Comparing two images
Mutual nearest neighbour
A match kept only if each side is the other's closest descriptor. It drops many ambiguous matches. Features and DINOv2

N

N-ICP-A and N-ICP-T
Amberg's non rigid ICP with an affine map per vertex (A), and a faster version with only a shift per vertex (T). NRICP is a general short name for non rigid ICP. Amberg et al.
NCC
Normalised cross correlation. It removes each image's mean brightness and contrast and then asks whether the two rise and fall together. 1 means a perfect match up to brightness. Comparing two images
Nearest neighbour
The closest item to a given one, for example the closest descriptor in the other image or the closest point on the other surface. Features and DINOv2
Neural network
A long chain of simple steps, each with adjustable numbers called weights. Training adjusts the weights so the output does something useful. A layer or block is one link of the chain. Features and DINOv2
NEWUOA
A search that needs no gradient. It builds a bowl shaped model of the score from past tries and jumps to the bowl's lowest point inside a safe radius. Corsini uses it, with one tuning number, RHOBEG. Searching without gradients
NGF
Normalised gradient field. It compares the directions of the edges in two images and ignores how strong they are. B1, B2 and our cross view test use it. Comparing two images
Node-arc incidence matrix
A matrix with one row per mesh edge and one column per vertex. Each row holds minus 1 and plus 1 at the edge's two ends, so it compares neighbouring vertices. Amberg's stiffness term uses it. Amberg et al.
Non rigid ICP
ICP where different parts of the surface may move differently, held together by a stiffness term. Amberg's method. Amberg et al.
Normal
The direction a small piece of surface faces, an arrow of length 1 at right angles to it. Rendering and back projection
Normal equations
The square linear system you get by setting the derivative of a least squares cost to zero. Solving it gives the best fit in one step. Least squares
Normal map
A render that stores the surface direction at each pixel as a colour. Corsini compares several such geometry pictures with photos, including normal, reflection (mirror direction) and silhouette maps. Paulsen also renders a curvature map, which shades each point by how sharply the surface bends. Corsini et al.

O

OBJ
A plain text mesh file with vertices, UV coordinates and faces. A companion MTL file names the texture image. Our output is face.obj. Painting the surface
Octree
A way to split space into nested boxes so that the nearest point can be found fast. Paulsen et al.
Onboarding
FoundPose's one time preparation per object. It renders 800 template views and stores their patch features, before any photo arrives. FoundPose
OpenCV, SciPy, Open3D and trimesh
Free software libraries we use. OpenCV does image work and the first PnP solves, SciPy does the final least squares, and Open3D and trimesh handle meshes and point clouds. Other names on the site, such as OpenGL (drawing), TensorFlow (networks) and UMFPACK (sparse equations), are libraries of the same kind. PnP
Optical flow
A field that says where each pixel of one image moved to in another. Our B4 uses DIS flow between a shading render and the photo. Family B
Orthographic camera
A camera model with no perspective, where far things do not shrink. It is close to true when the subject is far away compared with its depth. Cameras and projection
Outlier
A match that disagrees with the model, usually because it is wrong. RANSAC
Overfitting
Fitting the noise or your own mistakes instead of the truth. B3 drifts if it runs too many rounds, and A7's guard exists because of this. Features and DINOv2

P

P3P
The PnP solver for the smallest case, 3 point pairs with a known lens. Three points can fit more than one camera, so a fourth point picks the right one. AP3P is a variant of it, and SQPnP is another solver in the same family. PnP
Patch
A small square of an image. DINOv2 works on 14 by 14 pixel patches. Features and DINOv2
PCA
Principal component analysis. It finds the few directions along which a set of vectors varies most. Used to shrink descriptors and to paint features as colours. Features and DINOv2
Perspective
The way far things look smaller, because every ray passes through one point. A pinhole camera has perspective, and an orthographic one does not. Cameras and projection
Pinhole camera
The simple camera model where every ray passes through one point. It gives u = f X / Z + c_x for the horizontal pixel. Cameras and projection
Plateau
Our word for the range of focal lengths over which the camera fit barely changes. On our case it spans a factor of 3.7 to 6.8. The task
PNG and JPEG
Two common image file formats. PNG stores pixels exactly, and JPEG compresses them with small losses. Our texture is a PNG. Painting the surface
PnP
Perspective n point. Finding the camera pose from n 3D points and the pixels where they appear. PnP
Point cloud
A set of 3D points with no triangles joining them. DUSt3R
Point to plane
An ICP distance measured only along the target surface's normal, so the two surfaces can slide along each other. It usually converges in fewer rounds. ICP
Point to point
The plain ICP distance, the straight gap from a point to its paired point. ICP
Pointmap
An image that stores a 3D point at each pixel instead of a colour. It is what DUSt3R outputs. DUSt3R
Position code
Numbers added to each token in a transformer so it knows where its patch came from in the image. Features and DINOv2
Powell's method
A search that needs no gradient. It improves the score along one direction at a time, then adds the total move of each round as a new direction. B2 finishes with it. Searching without gradients
Pretrained
Already trained by someone else, on other data, and used as is. Park's Dlib detector and FoundPose's DINOv2 are pretrained. The papers side by side
Principal point
The pixel where the camera's central axis meets the image. We keep it at the image centre. Cameras and projection
Prior
Extra knowledge added to a solve as a soft pull toward a likely value. A6 adds a weak prior on focal length from the learned estimators. Family A
Procrustes
Finding the rotation, shift and possibly scale that best line up two matched point sets. The rotation part alone is called the orthogonal Procrustes problem. It has an exact one step answer through SVD. Procrustes
Projection
Mapping a 3D point to a pixel by dividing by its depth and scaling by the focal length. Cameras and projection
Projection matrix
The 3 by 4 matrix that does the whole projection in one product, the intrinsics times the rotation and translation. Cameras and projection
PSNR
Peak signal to noise ratio, in decibels, 10 log10 of 255 squared over the mean squared error. Higher means a smaller error. Comparing two images

Q

Quaternion
Four numbers that describe a rotation. They make it easy to blend smoothly between two rotations. Horn's Procrustes method uses them. Procrustes

R

RANSAC
Random sample consensus. Fit a model to many small random sets of matches, count how many matches agree with each fit, and keep the best. RANSAC
Ratio test
Dropping a match when its best distance is almost the same as the second best, because then the match is ambiguous. B3 uses a threshold of 0.92. Features and DINOv2
Ray
A straight line out of the camera's centre through one pixel. Everything on it lands on that pixel. Cameras and projection
Ray casting
Shooting a ray from the camera through a pixel and finding where it first hits the mesh. The Möller and Trumbore test is the standard fast way to hit one triangle. Rendering and back projection
Reflection
A mirror flip. A rotation fit must refuse it, or the left and right of the face swap without warning. Procrustes
Registration
Bringing two datasets into the same coordinates, such as a CT and a face scan, or a CT and a photo's camera. The task
Regression
Predicting numbers directly. DUSt3R regresses a 3D point for every pixel. DUSt3R
Rendering
Drawing a 3D model as an image from a chosen camera. A render of the CT shows shape only, since the CT has no colour. Rendering and back projection
Reprojection error
The distance in pixels between where a 3D point projects and where it was seen in the photo. PnP
Residual
The leftover error of one measurement under the current guess, such as the pixel gap between a projected point and its detection. Least squares
RGB
The red, green and blue values of a colour pixel. A grey value can be made from them, for example Y = 0.3R + 0.59G + 0.11B. Corsini et al.
Rigid landmarks
The 22 MediaPipe points that barely move with expression, used in our camera solve. Eyelids, lips and most of the face outline are left out, and the jaw points get a low weight. Face landmarks
Rigid transform
A rotation plus a shift, with no stretching. Also called a rigid transformation. Six numbers in 3D. Procrustes
RMS
Root mean square. Square the values, average them and take the square root. It is a typical size that weights big values more. Least squares
Robust loss
A loss that lets big residuals count less than their square would, so a few wrong matches cannot drag the whole fit. The Huber loss is one. Robust PnP and robust ICP use such a loss. Least squares
Rotation matrix
A 3 by 3 matrix whose columns have length 1 and are at right angles, with determinant 1. Multiplying a point by it turns the point about the origin. Cameras and projection
Rotation vector
Three numbers for a rotation. The direction is the axis and the length is the angle. The Rodrigues formula turns it into a rotation matrix. Solvers use it because it has no extra numbers. PnP
Rough and fine alignment
Rough alignment gets close from far away, often from landmarks. Fine alignment polishes a nearly right answer, as ICP or mutual information do. Fine methods need a rough one first. The papers side by side
RRA, RTA and mAA
Camera pose scores in the DUSt3R paper. RRA and RTA are the share of camera pairs whose relative turn, or direction of travel, is within a threshold such as 15 degrees. mAA averages that accuracy over thresholds. DUSt3R

S

Seam
A line where two charts of a texture meet, or where colour from one photo meets another. A colour jump there is what the texture polish removes. Painting the surface
Segmentation mask
An image that marks which pixels belong to a class, such as face skin. A segmenter is the network that makes it. MediaPipe's selfie mask is one, with a coarse edge. Comparing two images
Self supervised learning
Training without human labels. DINOv2 learns by making a student network agree with a teacher network on different crops of the same image. Features and DINOv2
Shading
How bright a surface looks because of the light hitting it, as opposed to its own colour. Rendering and back projection
Shape index
A curvature measure that says whether a spot is shaped like a cap, a ridge, a saddle, a rut or a cup. A4 uses it to place eye corners. Family A
SIFT
A classic hand designed keypoint detector and descriptor built from gradient directions. In C4 it found only 44 points on skin. Features and DINOv2
Sigma (σ)
The usual symbol for a standard deviation, the typical size of the spread around the mean. A5 gives each landmark its own sigma as its uncertainty. Family A
Silhouette
The outline of an object against its background. Comparing two images
Similarity transform
A rigid transform plus one overall scale. Seven numbers in 3D. Family C needs one, because a face rebuilt from photos has no true size. Procrustes
Singular matrix
A square matrix that flattens some direction to zero, so its equations have no unique answer. It shows up when the points give too little information. Least squares
Softmax
Turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, giving the largest score the most weight. Features and DINOv2
SSD
Sum of squared differences between two images, pixel by pixel. Zero only for identical images. Comparing two images
SSIM
Structural similarity index. It compares local brightness, contrast and pattern between two images. 1 means identical. Comparing two images
Stable regions
The parts of the face that barely change with expression, the forehead, nose and cheekbones. We align rebuilt faces to the CT on them only. ICP
Stiffness
In non rigid ICP, how strongly neighbouring vertices are made to move together. Amberg starts stiff and softens step by step. Amberg et al.
STL
A mesh file of bare triangles with no colour and no UV coordinates. Our CT surface came as a binary STL. The task
Structure from motion
Recovering camera positions and sparse 3D points from many overlapping photos of a still scene. COLMAP does it. Family C
SVD
Singular value decomposition. It writes any matrix as a turn, a stretch along the axes and another turn. It gives the best rotation in Procrustes and solves the DLT. Procrustes
Symmetry plane
The plane that splits the face into mirror halves. A4 finds it by mirroring the CT and aligning the copy with ICP. Family A
Synthetic data
Data made up in code, with a known right answer, used to test a method. Every figure on this site runs on synthetic data from the generic face. Start here

T

Taubin smoothing
A gentle mesh smoothing that does not shrink the surface. It cut our xatlas charts from 5674 to 4371. Painting the surface
Template
A generic model with known structure. In A3 and Amberg it is a mesh bent onto a scan. In FoundPose it is one rendered view of the object. Amberg et al.
Template retrieval
Picking, from many stored template views, the few that look most like the photo. FoundPose does it with a bag of words. FoundPose
Texel
One pixel of a texture image. Painting the surface
Texture
An image wrapped onto a mesh to give it colour. Painting the surface
Token
One vector in the list a transformer works on. In a vision transformer each image patch becomes one token. Features and DINOv2
Training and inference
Training is adjusting a network's weights on example data. Inference is running the finished network on new input. Paulsen and DUSt3R need training, FoundPose and our B3 only run inference. The papers side by side
Transformer
A network that splits its input into tokens and lets every token look at every other one through attention. Features and DINOv2
Triangulation
Finding a 3D point from two or more rays that see it from different places. Park et al.
Trimmed ICP
ICP that ignores the worst share of pairs in each round, so parts that do not overlap cannot pull the fit. ICP
Trust region
A limit on how far one optimiser step may go. It grows when the local model predicts well and shrinks when it does not. Corsini et al.

U

Umeyama
The Procrustes recipe that also solves one overall scale, giving a similarity transform. Procrustes
Unwrapping
Cutting a mesh into charts and laying them flat in a texture square, so every triangle gets UV coordinates. Painting the surface
UV map
The 2D coordinates, from 0 to 1, that say where each triangle corner sits in the texture image. Painting the surface

V

Venues (CVPR, ECCV, ACCV, MICCAI)
Conferences named on this site. CVPR, ECCV and ACCV are computer vision conferences, where Amberg, DUSt3R, FoundPose and Paulsen appeared. MICCAI is a medical imaging conference. Start here
Vertex
A corner point of a mesh. The CT skin surface has about 300,000. Rendering and back projection
View angle weight
How much one photo counts at a texel when several photos see it. It is the facing cosine, faded to zero near the 0.35 cutoff, so head on views count most. Painting the surface
Visibility
Whether a camera really sees a surface point. It must face the camera, not be hidden behind other skin, and fall inside the skin mask. Painting the surface
Visual word
One typical descriptor in a bag of words. Every patch is labelled with the visual word it is closest to. FoundPose
ViT
Vision transformer. A transformer whose tokens are image patches. ViT-S, ViT-B and ViT-L are small, base and large sizes. DINOv2 is one. Features and DINOv2
Voxel
A 3D pixel, one small cube of a scan grid. The CBCT scans in Park's tests had 0.3 mm voxels. Park et al.

W

Weights
The adjustable numbers inside a network that training sets. Also any numbers that say how much each item counts in a sum. Features and DINOv2
Weiszfeld's algorithm
A simple loop that finds the geometric median. It repeats a weighted mean, where each point's weight is one over its distance, so far points count less. Paulsen et al.
White balance
The colour tint a camera applies so white looks white. It differed between our photos, which the texture polish corrects. Painting the surface

X

xatlas
A library that cuts a mesh into charts and packs them into a texture square. It cut our surface into 4371 charts. Painting the surface

Z

Z depth and ray length
Two ways to store depth. Z depth is the distance along the camera's viewing axis. Ray length is the distance along the pixel's own ray, which is a little longer away from the image centre. Rendering and back projection

No term matches. Try a shorter word.

Remember

If a word on any page is new, its dotted underline links to the page that teaches it. This list is the one line version for quick lookups.
